docs.title: Nawaqid al-Wudu (Invalidators of Wudu)
docs.text:
Wudu is broken (yantaqidu al-wudu) when any one of the following nine things occurs:

1. Something exits from one of the two private parts (السَّبِيلَيْن) - Urine, excrement, or wind — all break wudu - Applies to exit from the front or back private part

2. Blood, pus, or wound fluid that moves from its place - If blood, pus, or clear wound liquid comes out and crosses (تَجَاوَزَ) to an area beyond the wound itself (i.e., reaches skin that would normally require cleaning), wudu is broken - Key condition: The substance must move on its own from its place - If the blood stays within the wound and does not flow outward, wudu remains intact - This same ruling applies to pus and the clear fluid that seeps from a healing or unhealed wound

3. Blood from the mouth that equals or exceeds the saliva - If blood from anywhere in the mouth is more than (غَلَبَ) the saliva, or equal to it (أَوْ سَوَاهُ), wudu is broken - If saliva is more than the blood, wudu remains intact - Practical example: brushing teeth after wudu — if gums bleed heavily (blood ≥ saliva), wudu must be remade

4. Vomiting a mouthful - Wudu is broken if one vomits: food, water, a blood clot (عَلَق), bile (مَرَّة), or phlegm — provided it is a mouthful (مِلْءُ الْفَمِ) - Definition of mouthful: the vomit fills the mouth to the point that speech is difficult or impossible - A small burp that brings up a little food is NOT a mouthful — wudu is not broken - Stomach acid is included in this ruling, as it is something being vomited up

5. Falling asleep such that the buttocks leave the ground - If a person falls asleep while sitting and their backside does not remain stable on the ground (they keep tipping/swaying over), wudu is broken - Likewise, if the buttocks of a sleeping person rises off the ground before they awaken (i.e., they are in a deep sleep and fall over), wudu is broken - The key criterion: buttocks are no longer firm and stable on the ground

6. Fainting (الإغماء) - If a person loses consciousness (أُغْمِيَ عَلَيْهِ), wudu is broken

7. Losing one's sanity (الجنون) - If a person becomes insane (جُنَّ), wudu is broken

8. Becoming intoxicated (السُّكر) - If a person becomes intoxicated (سَكِرَ), wudu is broken

9. Laughing out loud during salah (القَهْقَهَة) - Conditions for this to break wudu: 1. The person must be mature (بَالِغ — has reached puberty) 2. The person must be awake (يَقْظَان — not asleep) 3. It must occur during salah (فِي صَلَاة) 4. The salah must contain bowing and prostration (ذَاتُ رُكُوعٍ وَسُجُود) — i.e., any fard or nafl salah (not Salat al-Janaza or Sajdat al-Tilawa) - Wudu is not broken by laughing out loud in the following cases: - A child laughs out loud - A sleeping person laughs out loud during salah (even in a lighter sleep, as it is not a conscious act) - Laughing out loud during Salat al-Janaza (no ruku/sujud) - Laughing out loud during Sajdat al-Tilawa (no ruku/sujud)

docs.title: Things That Resemble Nawaqid but Do NOT Break Wudu
docs.text:
1. Blood appears but does not move from its place - Blood comes to the surface of a wound but stays within it — wudu intact

2. Flesh falls from the body without blood flowing - Example: 'Irq al-Madani (عِرْقُ الْمَدَنِي / "Naru") — a skin disease, common in hot regions, where pieces of flesh fall off - As long as no blood flows from the wound, wudu is intact - The main condition is: blood does not come out (لَمْ يَسِلْ مِنْهُ الدَّم)

3. A worm exits from a wound or from the ear - This does not break wudu

4. Vomiting less than a mouthful - If a person vomits, but it is not a mouthful, wudu does not break

5. Vomiting phlegm (بَلْغَم) - Whether the phlegm is a little or a lot, vomiting phlegm alone does not break wudu

6. A person performing salah falls asleep while in a valid prayer position - If a person falls asleep while standing, sitting, bowing (ruku), or prostrating (sujud), and remains in the correct form (على صِفَةِ السُّنَّة) — i.e., still appears to be praying — wudu does not break - If, however, his hands drop loose (no longer in proper form while standing), wudu breaks, and therefore salah also breaks

7. A person with wudu falls asleep with their buttocks firm on the ground - If a person with wudu falls asleep while sitting and their backside remains firm (مُتَمَكِّنَة) on the ground, wudu does not break

8. Touching one's own private part - Touching one's own private part with the hand does not break wudu (Hanafi position)

9. Touching a woman - Touching a woman does not break wudu (Hanafi position)

10. Swaying while asleep - If a sleeping person sways (as long as their backside remains on the ground), wudu does not break

docs.title: Fara'id al-Ghusl (Obligatory Acts of Ghusl)
docs.text:
There are three obligatory acts of ghusl. If any one is missed, ghusl is invalid:

  1. Al-Madmada (الْمَضْمَضَة) — Rinsing the mouth
  2. Al-Istinshaq (الِاسْتِنْشَاق) — Cleaning/sniffing water into the nose
  3. Isal al-Ma' ila Jami' al-Badan (إِيصَالُ الْمَاءِ إِلَى جَمِيعِ الْبَدَنِ) — Making water reach every part of the body, such that not a single dry spot remains

docs.title: Sunnan al-Ghusl (Recommended Acts of Ghusl)
docs.text:
Observing these sunnahs completes the ghusl in the best manner (عَلَى وَجْهٍ أَكْمَل):

  1. Reciting Bismillah before beginning the ghusl
  2. Making the intention (niyyah) for ghusl — to attain purity (tahara)
  3. Washing the hands up to and including the wrists first, just as one does in wudu
  4. Washing away any impurities on the body or clothing before beginning the ghusl
  5. Performing wudu before ghusl — however, if standing in a lowered/steep place where water gathers (مُنْخَفِض) at the feet, one delays washing the feet until the end (so the feet are washed clean after all impure pooled water has been cleared)
  6. Pouring water over the entire body three times
  7. Pouring water in the following order: first over the head, then right shoulder (مَنْكِب أَيْمَن), then left shoulder (مَنْكِب أَيْسَر)
  8. Rubbing the body (دَلْك) while washing — not merely pouring water over it
  9. Washing the body continuously (مُتَوَالِيًا) — such that the first limb/area does not dry before the second is washed

Note on flowing water: If a person enters a flowing body of water (river, stream) or a large reservoir that is considered in the ruling of flowing water, remains in it, and rubs their body — they have completed the sunnah of ghusl.

docs.title: Conditions for Laughing Out Loud (Qahqaha) Breaking Wudu
docs.text:
All four conditions must be met simultaneously:

Condition Detail Maturity (بُلُوغ) Must be a mature person (post-puberty); does not apply to children Wakefulness (يَقَظَة) Must be awake; sleeping person laughing is not a conscious act During Salah Must occur while in the prayer Prayer contains Ruku & Sujud Applies to all fard and nafl salah; excludes Janaza and Sajdat al-Tilawa

docs.title: Conditions for Blood/Pus Breaking Wudu
docs.text: State of Blood/Pus Ruling Appears on wound surface but stays in place Wudu intact Moves (flows) from its place by itself Wudu broken From the mouth — saliva is more Wudu intact From the mouth — blood = or > saliva Wudu broken

docs.title: Conditions for Sleep Breaking Wudu
docs.text: Sleep Scenario Ruling Asleep sitting, backside firm on ground Wudu intact Asleep sitting, swaying/tipping (backside unstable) Wudu broken Asleep, buttocks rise off ground before waking Wudu broken Asleep lying down Wudu broken Asleep in salah in correct form (standing, sitting, ruku, sujud) Wudu intact Asleep in salah, hands fall (loses sunnah form) Wudu broken

docs.title: Scholarly Opinions
docs.text:
• The rulings covered follow the Hanafi madhab, as is the standard for this course.
  • The ruling that touching a woman or touching one's own private part does not break wudu is specific to the Hanafi position (contrasting with Shafi'i and Maliki positions where these do break wudu).
  • The ruling on qahqaha (loud laughter in salah breaking wudu) is a position particular to the Hanafi school. Other madhabs do not hold this view.

docs.title: Lessons & Practical Application
docs.text:
1. Brushing teeth after wudu: Check the amount of blood vs. saliva when brushing. If gums bleed lightly and saliva is clearly more, wudu remains. If there is a significant amount of blood (equal to or more than saliva), remake wudu before salah.

  2. Wounds during wudu/salah: A cut or wound does not break wudu unless the blood actually flows out from the wound. As long as blood stays within the wound site, one may continue salah.

  3. Vomiting: A small reflux or burp with a little food is not a mouthful and does not break wudu. Only when the vomit fills the mouth (making speech difficult) is it considered a mouthful.

  4. Dozing off: Nodding off while seated with one's backside on the ground (e.g., during a lecture or after salah) does not break wudu. Falling into a deep sleep where one falls over does.

  5. Salah with drowsiness: If a person is very sleepy in salah and sways but maintains proper form, their wudu and salah are intact. The moment the proper form is lost (e.g., hands drop while standing), wudu breaks.

  6. Ghusl practice: Begin ghusl with Bismillah and niyyah, wash hands first, remove any impurities, perform wudu (delaying feet if water pools), then pour water over the head, right shoulder, and left shoulder — rubbing the body throughout — and wash continuously without letting any part dry.

  7. Ghusl in a shower: The sunnah of delaying washing the feet applies when water pools at one's feet (e.g., a clogged drain). Wash feet last so that accumulated used water on the floor can be washed away cleanly.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered Aqsam al-Ghusl (the types/categories of ritual bath). The lesson systematically categorized ghusl into three levels of obligation — fard, sunnah, and mandub/mustahab — and detailed the specific occasions that fall under each category. A brief discussion also addressed the ruling on washing a martyr (shaheed) and the ruling on a new Muslim performing ghusl.

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
• The three-tier classification of ghusl: obligatory, recommended (sunnah), and preferred (mustahab)
  • The four causes that make ghusl obligatory (fard)
  • The four occasions that make ghusl a sunnah
  • The eighteen occasions where ghusl is mustahab/mandub
  • The distinction between the ruling on a shaheed dying in battle vs. other forms of martyrdom
  • The ruling on a new Muslim performing ghusl based on their state of purity at the time of conversion

docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning أَقْسَامُ الْغُسْل (Aqsam al-Ghusl) The categories/types of ritual bath غُسْل (Ghusl) Full ritual bath/purification فَرْض (Fard) Obligatory سُنَّة (Sunnah) Prophetically recommended مَنْدُوب / مُسْتَحَب (Mandub / Mustahab) Preferred/desirable (not obligatory) جَنَابَة (Janabah) State of major ritual impurity جُنُب (Junub) A person in the state of janabah حَيْض (Haydh) Menstrual bleeding نِفَاس (Nifas) Postnatal bleeding (after childbirth) شَهِيد (Shaheed) Martyr إِحْرَام (Ihram) State of consecration for Hajj or Umrah عَرَفَة (Arafah) The plain of Arafah (Hajj station) زَوَال الشَّمْس (Zawal al-Shams) Midday (when the sun passes its zenith) لَيْلَة النِّصْف مِنْ شَعْبَان (Laylat al-Nisf min Sha'ban) The 15th night of Sha'ban اسْتِسْقَاء (Istisqa) Prayer for rain (performed during drought) فَزَع (Faza') Fear/panic ظُلْمَة (Dhulmah) Darkness رِيح شَدِيدَة (Rih Shadida) Severe/strong wind تَوْبَة (Tawbah) Repentance حِجَامَة (Hijamah) Cupping therapy مُزْدَلِفَة (Muzdalifah) Station between Arafah and Mina during Hajj يَوْم النَّحْر (Yawm al-Nahr) Day of sacrifice (10th of Dhul Hijjah) طَوَاف الزِّيَارَة (Tawaf al-Ziyarah) The obligatory tawaf of Hajj صَبِيحَة (Sabihah) The morning of الْمَدِينَة الْمُنَوَّرَة (al-Madinah al-Munawwarah) The illuminated city of Madinah مَكَّة الْمُشَرَّفَة (Makkah al-Musharrafah) The noble city of Makkah

docs.title: Classification of Ghusl
docs.text: Ghusl is divided into three categories: 1. فَرْض (Fard) — Obligatory 2. سُنَّة (Sunnah) — Recommended 3. مَنْدُوب / مُسْتَحَب (Mandub / Mustahab) — Preferred/desirable

docs.title: Fard Ghusl — The Four Causes
docs.text:
يُفْتَرَضُ الْغُسْلُ بِوَاحِدٍ مِنْ أَرْبَعَةِ أُمُورٍ "Ghusl is obligatory due to one of the following four reasons:"

# Cause Arabic 1 A person is in the state of janabah (major ritual impurity) إِذَا كَانَ جُنُوبًا 2 A woman becomes pure from her menstrual cycle (haydh) إِذَا طَهُرَتْ مِنَ الْحَيْض 3 A woman becomes pure from postnatal bleeding (nifas) إِذَا طَهُرَتْ مِنَ النِّفَاس 4 It is obligatory upon the living to wash a deceased Muslim يُفْتَرَضُ تَغْسِيل الْمَيِّت عَلَى الْأَحْيَاء

Note on washing the deceased (Cause #4): - The obligation of washing the deceased falls on the living, not the deceased person himself. - A shaheed (martyr) who dies in battle is not washed; he is buried in his clothes and salah is performed over him. - There are two types of shaheed: one who died in actual battlefield combat (kukman shaheed) and one who died through other means (e.g., drowning, collapsing building, killed in self-defense). Their rulings differ regarding washing, salah, and burial — to be confirmed.

docs.title: Sunnah Ghusl — The Four Occasions
docs.text:
يُسَنَّ الْغُسْلُ لِأَرْبَعَةِ أَشَاءٍ "Ghusl is sunnah for four things:"

# Occasion 1 For Salat al-Jumu'ah (Friday prayer) 2 For Eid prayer (Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha) 3 For a person entering into the state of Ihram 4 For a pilgrim (haji) in the plain of Arafah after zawal al-shams (mid-afternoon)

docs.title: Mustahab/Mandub Ghusl — The Eighteen Occasions
docs.text: # Occasion 1 On the 15th night of Sha'ban (Laylat al-Nisf min Sha'ban) 2 On Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power — on the nights most likely to be it) 3 Before the solar eclipse prayer (Kusuf) 4 Before the lunar eclipse prayer (Khusuf) 5 Before Salat al-Istisqa (prayer for rain during drought) 6 During a time of fear (عند فَزَع) 7 During a time of darkness (عند ظُلْمَة) 8 During severe winds (عند رِيح شَدِيدَة) 9 When wearing new clothing (عند لُبْس ثَوْب جَدِيد) 10 When making tawbah (repentance) from a sin 11 Upon returning from a journey (للَّذِي قَدِمَ مِنْ سَفَر) 12 When intending to enter al-Madinah al-Munawwarah 13 When intending to enter Makkah al-Musharrafah 14 When staying in Muzdalifah on the morning of Yawm al-Nahr (10th of Dhul Hijjah) 15 Before performing Tawaf al-Ziyarah (the obligatory tawaf of Hajj) 16 After washing a deceased person (للَّذِي غَسَّلَ مَيِّتًا) 17 After hijamah (cupping therapy) 18 Upon recovering from insanity, fainting, or intoxication

docs.title: Ruling on the New Muslim Performing Ghusl
docs.text:
Scenario Ruling A person accepts Islam while already in a state of purity Ghusl is mustahab (preferred, not obligatory) A person accepts Islam while in a state of janabah (major ritual impurity) Ghusl is fard (obligatory) upon him

Arabic text: - أَمَّا إِذَا كَانَ الَّذِي أَسْلَمَ جُنُوبًا فَيُفْتَرَضُ عَلَيْهِ الْغُسْلُ - "As for the one who accepts Islam while in a state of janabah, ghusl is obligatory upon him."

docs.title: Summary Table — Three Levels of Ghusl
docs.text: Level Arabic Number of Occasions Obligatory فَرْض 4 causes Sunnah سُنَّة 4 occasions Preferred مُسْتَحَب / مَنْدُوب 18 occasions

docs.title: Key Conditions to Note
docs.text:
• The obligation to wash the deceased (Cause #4 of fard ghusl) is a communal obligation (fard kifayah) — it falls on the living as a community, not on the deceased.
  • The mustahab occasions of ghusl are largely connected to worship, acts of obedience, or entry into sacred spaces — indicating that a person should present himself in a state of complete cleanliness before acts of worship or drawing near to Allah.
  • Non-Muslims do not have Islamic purification procedures for janabah. If they embrace Islam while in that state, ghusl immediately becomes fard upon them.

docs.title: Scholarly Opinions
docs.text:
• The distinction between the two types of shaheed (battlefield martyr vs. other forms of martyrdom, e.g., drowning, crushed under rubble, killed in self-defense) results in differing rulings regarding:
  • Whether ghusl is performed
  • Whether janazah salah is prayed
  • How the body is buried
  • The teacher noted he would verify the precise distinctions between the two types (kukman shaheed vs. actual battlefield martyr) for a future class.

docs.title: Lessons & Practical Application
docs.text:
1. Ghusl has a hierarchy — not every occasion requiring ghusl carries the same legal weight. Knowing the difference between fard, sunnah, and mustahab allows a Muslim to prioritize correctly and avoid sin where there is an obligation.

  2. Cleanliness before worship — the 18 mustahab occasions of ghusl are largely tied to moments of worship or approaching Allah (tawbah, salah, entering sacred cities). This reinforces the Islamic principle that external purity reflects and supports internal readiness for worship.

  3. Istisqa reminder — Salat al-Istisqa is performed during drought as a communal act of humility before Allah, going out in simple clothing to make du'a for rain. Ghusl before this salah is mustahab.

  4. New Muslims — if someone accepts Islam while in janabah, ghusl is immediately fard. Da'ees (callers to Islam) and community members should be aware of this ruling to guide new Muslims properly.

  5. This chapter (Aqsam al-Ghusl) is the last chapter before the chapter of Salah. The class will continue from here in the next session, possibly after completing the remaining four hadiths in the Hadith class.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This was the final Fiqh class of the academic year. The session covered three major topics: (1) the legal basis (mashru'iyyah) and conditions (shurut) of Tayammum, its integrals (arkan), sunnahs, method of performance, and its invalidators; (2) wiping over leather/thick socks (masah 'ala al-khuffayn) — its conditions, time periods, and invalidators; and (3) wiping over wound dressings and casts (masah 'ala al-'isabah wal-jabirah). The session also included miscellaneous rulings connecting intention to validity of Tayammum for various acts of worship.

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
• Tayammum is a divinely granted concession enabling worship when water is unavailable or harmful to use
  • The validity of Tayammum depends strictly on eight conditions, particularly the correctness of intention (niyyah)
  • Intention must be made for an ibadah maqsudah (a purposive act of worship) for Tayammum to be valid for Salah
  • Masah 'ala al-khuffayn is a concession granted by Shari'ah to ease the practice of Wudu — not an independent act of worship
  • Islamic law consistently removes hardship (haraj) from worship, as evidenced by rulings on tayammum, masah, and wound dressings
  • The same invalidators that break Wudu break Tayammum and Masah al-khuffayn

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning تَيَمُّم (Tayammum) Linguistically: intention / to intend. Legally: purification using clean earth, involving wiping the face and hands including elbows صَعِيد (Sa'id) Dirt / earth طَيِّب (Tayyib) Clean / pure مَشْرُوعِيَّة (Mashru'iyyah) Legality within Shari'ah; the subject's place in Islamic law شُرُوط (Shurut) Conditions (plural of shart) أَرْكَان (Arkan) Integrals / pillars (plural of rukn) سُنَن (Sunan) Recommended acts / traditions نَوَاقِض (Nawaqid) Invalidators (plural of naqid) حَدَث (Hadath) State of ritual impurity حَدَث أَصْغَر (Hadath Asghar) Minor ritual impurity (requiring Wudu) إِبَاحَة الصَّلَاة (Ibahatu al-Salah) Permissibility of performing Salah عِبَادَة مَقْصُودَة (Ibadah Maqsudah) A purposive act of worship — one that yields reward and cannot be validly performed without purification عِوَض ('Iwad) In replacement of / in lieu of مَفْقُود (Mafqud) Unavailable / missing مَعْذُور (Ma'dhur) One who has a valid excuse حَائِل (Ha'il) Barrier (between skin and wiping) مَسْح عَلَى الخُفَّيْن (Masah 'ala al-Khuffayn) Wiping over leather/thick socks in place of washing the feet during Wudu خُفَّيْن (Khuffayn) Leather socks (dual) كَعْبَيْن (Ka'bayn) The two ankles خَرْق (Kharq) Hole / tear (in a sock) عِصَابَة ('Isabah) Wound dressing / bandage / gauze جَبِيرَة (Jabirah) Splint or cast رَمَدَ (Ramada) To suffer from sore eyes حَادِق (Hadiq) Skilled / experienced التِّلَاوَة (Al-Tilawah) Recitation of the Qur'an مُحْدِث (Muhdith) One in a state of hadath مُقِيم (Muqim) Resident (non-traveler) مُسَافِر (Musafir) Traveler صُفُوف (Sufuf) Rows تُرْبَة (Turbah) Soil / earth طَهُور (Tahur) Purifying (that which purifies) مَسْجِد (Masjid) Place of prostration / prayer (in the hadith, meaning any place on earth) شَمَّرَ (Shammara) To pull up one's sleeves سَاعِد (Sa'id) Forearm مِرْفَق (Mirfaq) Elbow اسْتِبَاحَة (Istibahah) Making something permissible for oneself through a valid act

docs.title: Qur'anic Evidence for Tayammum
docs.text:
Surah al-Nisa (4:43) / al-Ma'idah (5:6):

"...wa in kuntum marda aw 'ala safarin aw ja'a ahadun minkum min al-gha'it aw lamastumu al-nisa'a falam tajidu ma'an fatayyamamu sa'idan tayyiban famsahu biwujuhikum wa aydikum. Inna Allaha kana 'afuwwan ghafura."

"If you are sick, or on a journey, or any of you has used the restroom, or has had intimate relations and you find no water, then perform Tayammum with clean earth — wipe your faces and hands. Indeed Allah is Most Pardoning, Most Forgiving."

docs.title: Hadith Evidence for Tayammum
docs.text:
The Prophet ﷺ said:

"Fuddiina 'ala al-naas bi-thalathin: ju'ilat sufufuna kasufuf al-mala'ikah, wa ju'ilat lana al-ardu kulluha masjidan, wa ju'ilat turbataha lana tahuran idha lam najid al-ma'."

"We have been given virtue over people in three things: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels; the entire earth has been made a place of prayer for us; and its soil has been made purifying for us when we do not find water."

docs.title: Reason Tayammum Was Legislated
docs.text: Tayammum was prescribed because human beings sometimes cannot use water — either due to water being unavailable (mafqud) or due to illness — so that people are not deprived of performing acts of worship (like Salah) that require purification.

docs.title: Hadith Evidence for Masah al-Khuffayn
docs.text:
The Prophet ﷺ said:

"Al-mashu 'ala al-khuffayn lil-musafir thalathu ayyamin wa layaliyha, wa lil-muqim yawm wa laylah."

"Wiping over leather socks is permissible for a traveler for three days and nights, and for a resident for one day and one night."

docs.title: Qur'anic Evidence for Concessions (Masah over Wound Dressings)
docs.text: "Wa ma ja'ala 'alaykum fi al-dini min haraj." "He has not placed any hardship upon you in the religion." (Surah al-Hajj 22:78)

docs.title: Conditions of Valid Tayammum (8 Conditions)
docs.text:
1. Niyyah (Intention) Tayammum is invalid without intention. The intention must be for one of three things: - Purification from hadath - The permissibility of Salah (istibahatu al-salah) - An ibadah maqsudah — a purposive act of worship that cannot be validly performed without purification (e.g., Salah, Sajdatu al-Tilawah)

Key rulings on intention: - It is not necessary to specify which hadath in the intention - If a person makes Tayammum with the intention of touching the Mus'haf: Salah will not be valid, because merely touching the Qur'an is not an ibadah in itself — the actual ibadah is tilawah (recitation) - If a person makes Tayammum with the intention of calling the Adhan or Iqamah: Salah will not be valid, as Adhan and Iqamah are not stand-alone ibadah maqsudah - If a person makes Tayammum with the intention of recitation of Qur'an while in a state of hadath asghar: Salah will not be valid, because recitation of Qur'an — though it is an ibadah maqsudah — can be performed without Wudu - If a person makes Tayammum with the intention of Salah: all other acts (touching the Qur'an, reciting, Sajdatu al-Tilawah) become permissible under that same Tayammum

2. Presence of a Valid Excuse One of the following excusable circumstances must exist: 1. Water is more than a mile away 2. A skilled Muslim doctor informs the person that using water will cause illness, worsen existing illness, or delay recovery 3. The person overwhelmingly fears that using cold water (the only water available) will cause death or severe harm 4. The person fears thirst for himself or a companion if water is used for Wudu (water is insufficient for both drinking and purification) 5. No instrument (bucket, rope) is available to extract water from a well 6. An enemy — human or carnivorous animal (hayawan muftaris) — stands between the person and the water 7. The person overwhelmingly fears that performing Wudu will cause him to miss 'Eid Salah or Salatu al-Janazah (prayers with no qada)

Important distinction: If a person fears missing a regular Fard Salah or Jumu'ah due to performing Wudu, Tayammum is not permissible. He must perform Wudu, pray, and make qada of the missed obligatory prayer. For Jumu'ah specifically, he will pray Zuhr as a substitute ('iwadan 'an al-Jumu'ah).

3. Use of a Pure Earthy Substance Tayammum must be performed with something from the earth (jins al-ard): dirt (turab), stone (hajar), or thick dust (raml). Tayammum is not valid with wood, silver, or gold.

4. Wiping the Entire Face and Both Arms Including Elbows The entirety (or majority) of the full hand must be used. If a person uses only two fingers to wipe — even if he covers the entire arm — the Tayammum is not valid because the majority of the hand was not used.

5. [Implicit from text] The wiping must be with both hands on both body parts.

6. Two Strikes with the Inner Palms (Darbatayn bi-batin al-kaffayn) A person must perform two strikes — one for the face, one for the arms. If a person strikes twice in the same place, or dirt falls onto his body and he wipes it without striking, the Tayammum remains valid.

7. No Barrier Between Wiping and Skin Nothing must be present between the hand and the skin: wax (sham'), grease (shahm), thick paint, super glue, nail polish (for sisters), etc. These must be removed before wiping. If present and not removed, Tayammum is invalid.

8. No Ongoing Invalidator Nothing that invalidates Tayammum should occur during the performance of Tayammum, such as: - Menstrual bleeding (hayd) - Postnatal bleeding (nifas) - Hadath occurring mid-performance (passing wind, vomiting, bleeding — unless the person is ma'dhur)

docs.title: Integrals (Arkan) of Tayammum
docs.text: There are only two physical integrals (plus intention as the internal integral): 1. Wiping the entirety of the face (mashu jami' al-wajh) 2. Wiping both arms including the elbows (mashu al-yadayn ma'a al-mirfaqayn)

docs.title: Sunnahs of Tayammum
docs.text:
1. Reciting Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim at the beginning
  2. Following the order: face first, then right arm, then left arm
  3. Not separating the wiping of the face and hands with a foreign action (fi'l ajnabi)
  4. Moving the hands forwards and backwards (iqbal wa idbar) in the dirt to get a good amount on the hands
  5. Dusting off the hands (nafd) after lifting them from the dirt, before wiping
  6. Keeping the fingers spread apart when placing the hands in the dirt

docs.title: Method of Performing Tayammum (Kayfiyyah)
docs.text:
1. Pull sleeves up above the elbows (shammara 'an sa'idayhi)
  2. Recite Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim
  3. Make intention (niyyah) — e.g., for permissibility of Salah (istibahatu al-salah)
  4. Place the inner palms on pure earth with fingers spread apart, moving hands forward and backward
  5. Raise hands and dust them off
  6. Wipe the entire face with both hands
  7. Place hands on earth a second time in the same manner
  8. Wipe the right arm entirely (including elbow) with the entire left hand
  9. Wipe the left arm entirely (including elbow) with the right hand
  10. Tayammum is now complete — one may now perform as many Fard and Nafl prayers as desired

docs.title: Invalidators (Nawaqid) of Tayammum
docs.text:
1. Everything that invalidates Wudu also invalidates Tayammum
  2. Finding and gaining the ability to use water (al-qudrah 'ala isti'mal al-ma')
  3. The disappearance of the excuse that originally made Tayammum permissible (e.g., enemy is gone, illness resolved, water found)

docs.title: Miscellaneous Rulings on Tayammum
docs.text: Situation Ruling Tayammum made for entering a Masjid Cannot perform Salah with it (not an ibadah maqsudah; also Wudu not required to enter Masjid) Tayammum made for I'tikaf I'tikaf itself is not the issue — but Ghusl (if in janabah) still does not permit Salah without intention for Salah Tayammum made with intention of visiting graves or burying the deceased Salah is not permissible with this Tayammum Person hopes to find water before Salah time exits It is mustahab to delay Tayammum and wait Someone has promised to bring the person water It is wajib (yajib) to wait for the water Person has little water needed for kneading flour (making bread) He should make Tayammum and use the water for food Person has little water needed for making gravy/curry He must use the water for Wudu — gravy is liquid and not a substitute survival need in the same category Seeking water from a companion Obligatory to ask if in a place where people are generally not stingy with water; not obligatory if people in the area are known to be stingy Performing Tayammum before Salah time enters Permissible if the person is not in the ma'dhur category and has no expectation of finding water Person whose hands and feet are amputated and whose face is injured Prays without any purification Majority of limbs are injured Performs Tayammum, then wipes over the injured parts Majority of limbs are uninjured Performs Wudu and wipes over the injured parts

docs.title: Conditions for Masah 'ala al-Khuffayn (6 Conditions)
docs.text:
1. The socks must have been put on while in a state of Taharah (Wudu) — specifically, the feet must have been washed before putting them on. If a person washes his feet, puts on the socks, then completes Wudu — this is valid, as long as Wudu was not broken between washing the feet and completing Wudu.
  2. The socks must cover the ankles (ka'bayn) — ankle socks do not qualify.
  3. The socks must be free of holes equal to or larger than the size of the three smallest toes (thalathu asabi' min asghar asabi' al-qadam). If the holes are that large or larger, the socks cannot be used for masah.
  4. The socks must stay on the feet without needing to be tied (yastamsika 'ala al-rijlayn biduni shadd) — they must not fall off when the foot is lifted.
  5. The socks must prevent water from reaching the feet — they must be waterproof.
  6. A person must be able to walk consistently while wearing them.

docs.title: The Obligatory (Fard) and Sunnah Amount of Masah al-Khuffayn
docs.text: Ruling Fard (minimum): Equivalent of the three smallest fingers of the hand (min asghar asabi' al-yad) wiped on the top (zahir) of each foot Sunnah: Keep fingers spread wide and wipe from the tips of the toes up to the shin (saq), starting from the bottom upward on the top of the foot

docs.title: Time Periods for Masah al-Khuffayn
docs.text:
Person Duration Resident (Muqim) 1 day and 1 night = 24 hours Traveler (Musafir) 3 days and 3 nights = 72 hours

When does the clock start? The time period begins from the first time Wudu breaks after putting on the socks while in a state of Taharah — not from when the socks were put on or when Wudu was completed.

docs.title: Transitioning Between Resident and Traveler Status
docs.text: Situation Ruling Resident begins traveling before his 24 hours expire He completes the remaining time up to 72 hours (the traveler's period) Traveler returns home (becomes resident) after 48 hours of wiping He must remove socks and restart; his time period ends when he becomes a resident Traveler returns home within 24 hours (still within resident period) He completes the 24-hour resident period and then is done Musafir wiped for less than 1 day then becomes a resident He completes 1 full day and night (yawm wa laylah) as the resident period

docs.title: Invalidators of Masah al-Khuffayn
docs.text:
1. Everything that invalidates Wudu
  2. Removing either or both socks (naz' al-khuff) — even one sock requires restarting
  3. Majority of the foot slipping out of the top of the sock (saq al-khuff)
  4. Expiry of the time period (intiha' muddatihi)
  5. Water reaching the majority of one foot inside the sock (sock is no longer waterproof)

docs.title: What Cannot Be Used for Masah
docs.text:
Item Ruling Turban ('imamah) Masah over it is not permissible in place of wiping the head Topi / head cap (qalansuwah) Not permissible for masah of the head Burqa / face veil (burqu') Not permissible for masah of the head Gloves (quffazayn) Not permissible for masah in place of washing the hands

The only concession for wiping over a covering is for the feet, using socks that meet the specified conditions.

docs.title: Masah over Wound Dressings ('Isabah) and Casts (Jabirah)
docs.text:
Conditions and Rulings:

  • If a person cannot wash or wipe a body part due to injury, he may wipe the majority of the wound dressing or cast from on top
  • This continues until the wound heals (ila an yalta'ima al-jurh)
  • It is not a condition that the dressing be tied upon a state of Taharah (impurity such as blood under the bandage does not affect validity)
  • The same applies to a cast (jabirah): wipe over it until healed; no condition of Taharah for putting it on
Situation Ruling One foot has a cast, the other is healthy Wipe over the cast on the injured foot; wash the other foot normally Cast falls off before wound heals Masah remains valid; no need to rewipe (if already wiped once) Cast is changed to a new one Not obligatory to wipe the new cast, but it is better (afadal) to wipe it Person has sore eyes and skilled Muslim doctor forbids washing eyes Wiping over the eyes is permissible

docs.title: Niyyah in Masah
docs.text: Act Niyyah Required? Masah 'ala al-Khuffayn Not required Masah 'ala al-Jabirah (cast) Not required Masah of the head (in Wudu) Not required Tayammum Required — the only act among these where Niyyah is a condition

docs.title: Scholarly Opinions
docs.text:
• The Hanafi position (implied throughout) is that Tayammum is a full substitute for Wudu and Ghusl when valid excuses exist, and a single Tayammum made for Salah covers all subsidiary acts of worship
  • The ruling that adhan and iqamah are not ibadah maqsudah is consistent with the position that Wudu is not obligatory for them (though it is recommended), and missing them does not require qada
  • The ruling distinguishing between fear of missing 'Eid/'Janazah (permits Tayammum) versus fear of missing Fard/Jumu'ah (does not permit Tayammum) reflects the principle that prayers with qada can be made up, while those without cannot

docs.title: Lessons & Practical Application
docs.text:
1. Intention determines validity: Before performing Tayammum, be clear about what ibadah you are performing it for. Intending Salah covers the broadest scope of subsequent worship acts.

  2. Know your excuses: Tayammum is not freely done — a specific, valid excuse from the list must be present. The most common in daily life are unavailability of water, illness, or fear of harm from water.

  3. The earth is your purifier: The Prophet ﷺ reminded us that the entire earth is a Masjid and its soil is tahur. This is a unique blessing of this ummah.

  4. Masah al-Khuffayn is a real concession: In cold weather or travel, wiping over thick socks that meet the six conditions is a fully valid and legitimate alternative to washing the feet. Learn the conditions and time periods carefully.

  5. Injured individuals are not excused from worship: Rather, they are given accommodation. A person with a cast does not skip Wudu — they simply wipe over the cast. A person with amputated limbs still performs Salah.

  6. The deen removes hardship: All of these concessions — Tayammum, masah, wiping over casts — reflect the Qur'anic principle: "Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship." Fiqh is not a set of obstacles but a framework of facilitation.

  7. Practical Tayammum sequence to memorize: Roll up sleeves → Bismillah → Niyyah → Strike earth (fingers spread) → Move hands forward and back → Lift and dust off → Wipe face → Strike earth again → Wipe right arm with left hand → Wipe left arm with right hand.

  8. Seeking water is itself obligatory: If a companion has water, asking for it is wajib (in places where people do not withhold water). If promised water, waiting is wajib. Tayammum is not a shortcut — it is a last resort.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This was the first session of Fiqh 201, serving as an orientation and introduction to the course. The teacher began by congratulating students on completing their first year, acknowledging the difficulty of balancing learning with work and other responsibilities. The bulk of the session covered: (1) the definition and scope of Ilm al-Fiqh, (2) the four sources of Islamic legal rulings with their evidences, (3) an overview of the four Imams and their madhabs, and (4) a brief introduction to the key Hanafi scholars relevant to the main text (Quduri). The class text, Mukhtasar al-Quduri, will begin on Saturday. No chapter of the book was covered today.

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
1. The purpose and structure of Ilm al-Fiqh — Fiqh is the knowledge of subsidiary legal rulings derived from detailed evidences; it does not deal with matters of belief (Aqidah).
  2. The four sources (Masadir) of Fiqh — Quran, Hadith, Ijma, and Qiyas, each with its own dalil.
  3. Mukallaf — not every ruling applies to every person; the concept of legal responsibility defines on whom a ruling falls.
  4. The progression of Fiqh books in the curriculum — Quduri (year 2) → Hidayah (year 3–4) → Daura-e-Hadith (year 6), each building on the last.
  5. The four Imams and their schools — their lives, teachers, students, and key contributions, presented chronologically.
  6. Adab of learning — respect for books, maintaining wudu, punctuality, active participation, and sincerity of intention.

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning Fiqh (فِقْه) Linguistically: to open/clarify. Technically (Istilahi): the knowledge of subsidiary legal rulings derived from their detailed evidences Faqih (فَقِيه) One who clarifies and opens the door of understanding for others in matters of Deen Ahkam (أَحْكَام) Rulings/laws Ahkam Asli / Ahkam I'tiqadi (أَحْكَام أَصْلِي / اعْتِقَادِي) Root/foundational rulings pertaining to belief (Aqidah) — e.g., Tawhid, Prophethood, Day of Judgment Ahkam Shar'iyyah Fari'iyyah (أَحْكَام شَرْعِيَّة فَرْعِيَّة) Subsidiary legal rulings; the domain of Fiqh Furu' (فُرُوع) Branches/subsidiaries; refers to practical (amal-based) rulings Usul (أُصُول) Foundations/principles Ibadat (عِبَادَات) Acts of worship (Salah, Zakat, Hajj, Sawm) Mu'amalat (مُعَامَلَات) Social/financial transactions and interpersonal dealings Mukallaf (مُكَلَّف) A legally responsible person upon whom Shari'ah rulings apply Dalil / Dalail (دَلِيل / دَلَائِل) Evidence; legal proof for a ruling Ijma (إِجْمَاع) Consensus of qualified scholars Qiyas (قِيَاس) Analogical reasoning; applying a known ruling to a new situation based on shared underlying cause Sunnah (سُنَّة) The established practice of Rasulullah ﷺ — includes his words (Qawl), actions (Af'al), approvals (Taqrir), and outward character (Sifa) Qawl (قَوْل) The verbal statements of the Prophet ﷺ Af'al (أَفْعَال) The physical actions of the Prophet ﷺ Matan (مَتْن) The body/text of a hadith Sanad (سَنَد) The chain of transmission of a hadith Zahir al-Riwayah (ظَاهِر الرِّوَايَة) The six most authoritative books of Hanafi Fiqh, all authored by Imam Muhammad Rahimullah Tadwin al-Fiqh (تَدْوِين الفِقْه) The formal codification/compilation of Fiqh — a key contribution of Imam Muhammad Rahimullah Usul al-Fiqh (أُصُول الفِقْه) The principles and methodology of Islamic jurisprudence Usul al-Hadith (أُصُول الحَدِيث) The science of Hadith methodology and terminology Khalkh al-Qur'an (خَلْق القُرْآن) The theological controversy of whether the Quran is created — the trial faced by Imam Ahmad Rijal (رِجَال) The science of narrators; the biographical study of hadith transmitters Takhwij (تَخْرِيج) The process of tracing a hadith back to its original source Masadir (مَصَادِر) Sources (here: the four sources of Fiqh) Istilahi (اصْطِلَاحِي) Technical/terminological meaning (as opposed to linguistic) Riwayatan / Dirayatan (رِوَايَةً / دِرَايَةً) Two modes of hadith teaching: riwayatan (transmission/reading aloud) and dirayatan (deep explanation and analysis) Amal (عَمَل) Action/deed Wahdaniyyah (وَحْدَانِيَّة) The Oneness of Allah Fard (فَرْض) Obligatory act established by definitive evidence Wajib (وَاجِب) Near-obligatory act established by less definitive evidence Sunnah Mu'akkadah (سُنَّة مُؤَكَّدَة) Emphasized Sunnah Sunnah Ghayr Mu'akkadah (سُنَّة غَيْر مُؤَكَّدَة) Non-emphasized Sunnah Nafl / Mustahab (نَفْل / مُسْتَحَب) Voluntary/recommended act Haram (حَرَام) Prohibited act Makruh Tahrimi (مَكْرُوه تَحْرِيمِي) Prohibitively disliked act Dinar / Dirham (دِينَار / دِرْهَم) Gold/silver coins used in early Islamic trade Khilafah (خِلَافَة) The Islamic caliphate Mazhab / Madhab (مَذْهَب) A school of Islamic jurisprudence

docs.title: Definition of Fiqh (Istilahi)
docs.text:
الْعِلْمُ بِالْأَحْكَامِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ الْفَرْعِيَّةِ عَنْ أَدِلَّتِهَا التَّفْصِيلِيَّة

"The knowledge of subsidiary Shari'ah rulings derived from their detailed evidences."

Breakdown of the definition: - "Knowledge" — Ilm; this is a formal, structured discipline. - "Subsidiary" (Fari'iyyah) — pertains to the Furu', i.e., practical acts, not foundational beliefs. - "Shari'ah rulings" — restricted to what Shari'ah has addressed. - "Detailed evidences" — each ruling traced to a specific Quranic verse, hadith, Ijma, or Qiyas.

docs.title: The Four Sources (Masadir) of Fiqh
docs.text:
# Source Description 1 Quran Primary and foremost source 2 Hadith/Sunnah Words, actions, approvals, and character of Rasulullah ﷺ 3 Ijma Consensus of qualified scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah 4 Qiyas Analogical reasoning applied by qualified scholars

Dalil for Qiyas and the first three sources — Hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal:

When the Prophet ﷺ dispatched Mu'adh ibn Jabal رضي الله عنه to Yemen, he asked him: "How will you give rulings?" - Mu'adh: "By the Book of Allah." - Prophet ﷺ: "What if you do not find it there?" - Mu'adh: "By the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." - Prophet ﷺ: "What if you do not find it there either?" - Mu'adh: "I shall practice my own reasoning (Qiyas)." - The Prophet ﷺ patted his chest and said: "All praise to Allah who gave success to the messenger of the Messenger of Allah in achieving what pleases the Messenger of Allah."

This hadith establishes Quran, Sunnah, and Qiyas as sources. (Referenced as a well-known hadith of Mu'adh.)

Dalil for all four sources — Hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (from Nasa'i):

"Whoever is faced with an issue, he should decide by the Book of Allah. If an affair comes to him not in the Book of Allah, then by what the Prophet ﷺ decided. If an affair comes to him that is not in the Book of Allah nor decided by the Prophet ﷺ, then by what the righteous (Sahaba) decided [Ijma]. And if an affair comes to him that none of the above covers, then he should decide using his own reasoning [Qiyas]."

This hadith from Sunan al-Nasa'i explicitly names all four sources.

docs.title: Scope of Ilm al-Fiqh
docs.text:
• Fiqh does not apply to Ahkam I'tiqadi (matters of belief): Wahdaniyyah of Allah, Prophethood, Day of Judgment. Issues in these areas relate to Iman itself, not Fiqh.
  • Fiqh applies to Ahkam Shar'iyyah Fari'iyyah — all practical actions a Muslim performs after accepting Islam: Salah, Zakat, Hajj, Sawm, trade, Nikah, and all of Mu'amalat.

docs.title: On Salah Being Fard
docs.text:
• Dalil: Surah al-Baqarah, Ayah 43 — "And establish Salah."
  • This establishes the obligation of Salah, but the ruling applies specifically to the Mukallaf — not to every person without qualification.

docs.title: The Mukallaf — Conditions for Legal Responsibility
docs.text:
A person is Mukallaf (legally responsible for a ruling) when applicable conditions are met. Examples of those excluded from certain rulings:

Category Ruling Non-Muslim Salah is not applied as a Fiqhi obligation upon them (though theoretically addressed in Quran) Insane person Salah does not apply — lacks legal capacity Child (before maturity) Salah not obligatory; parents should habituate them at a prescribed age to build the habit Severely intoxicated person Not Mukallaf for the duration of intoxication — Quran (referring to Sukara) says do not come to Salah in that state

Example — Hajj: Being wealthy alone does not immediately make one Mukallaf for Hajj; other specific conditions must also be met.

docs.title: Categories of Rulings Applied to the Mukallaf
docs.text:
The goal of Fiqh is to correctly categorize every human action into one of the following:

Category Description Fard (فَرْض) Obligatory — established by definitive Quranic or Mutawatir evidence Wajib (وَاجِب) Near-obligatory — established by strong but slightly less definitive evidence Sunnah Mu'akkadah Emphasized Sunnah — regularly practiced by Rasulullah ﷺ Sunnah Ghayr Mu'akkadah Non-emphasized Sunnah Nafl / Mustahab Voluntary/recommended Haram (حَرَام) Absolutely prohibited Makruh Tahrimi Prohibitively disliked (close to Haram) Makruh Tanzahi Mildly disliked

docs.title: On Ijma — What Qualifies
docs.text:
• Not the consensus of scholars of a single city, country, or locality.
  • Must be agreed upon by the majority of Ulama of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah across the Muslim world.
  • Strongest form: consensus of the Sahabah. After them: Tabi'een. After them: the majority of qualified Ulama globally.

docs.title: On Qiyas — Who May Perform It
docs.text:
• Qiyas is not for the general Muslim to perform independently.
  • It requires extremely deep knowledge of Deen — it is the domain of qualified Mujtahids.
  • Once established by qualified scholars and accepted by the Ummah, it becomes a binding source.
  • Examples given:
  • Cryptocurrency: no direct ruling exists; a scholar looks at the closest analogous ruling (e.g., currency, gold/silver trading) and applies the underlying principle.
  • Marijuana: no explicit text; the ruling on intoxicants is applied via Qiyas because it produces the same effect (intoxication/loss of discernment) as khamr.

docs.title: 1. Imam Abu Hanifa Rahimullah (Hanafi Madhab)
docs.text:
Detail Information Full name Nu'man ibn Thabit Born 80 AH, Kufa Died 150 AH, Baghdad Lifespan ~70 years Key teachers Ibrahim al-Nakha'i Rahimullah, Hammad ibn Sulayman Rahimullah Famous students Imam Abu Yusuf, Imam Muhammad, Abdullah ibn Mubarak Rahimullah
  • Never wrote books himself.
  • The six books of Zahir al-Riwayah (the most authoritative books of Hanafi Fiqh) were all written by Imam Muhammad Rahimullah.
  • Imam Muhammad Rahimullah performed two foundational services: (1) established/codified Hanafi Fiqh, and (2) was the first to formally define and lay down Usul al-Fiqh.
  • The Hanafi school emerged from Kufa (Iraq), which became the center of Islamic learning after Ali رضي الله عنه moved the Khilafah there. Major Sahabah including Abdullah ibn Mas'ud settled there.
  • Key principle of Ahnaf: Hanafi rulings are not whimsical — they follow defined Usul. Differences between Madhabs arise from different but internally consistent principles, not personal preference.

docs.title: 2. Imam Malik Rahimullah (Maliki Madhab)
docs.text:
Detail Information Full name Malik ibn Anas Born 95 AH, Medina Died In Medina (spent his entire life there) Key teachers Nafi' Rahimullah (among many — reportedly over 900 teachers) Famous students Qatan Rahimullah, Abdullah ibn Mubarak Rahimullah Key work Muwatta Imam Malik
  • Core Usul of Imam Malik: The practice ('Amal) of the people of Medina takes precedence — even over a Sahih hadith — because Medina is where Rasulullah ﷺ lived and died, and its people preserved his Sunnah through lived practice better than any other locality.
  • Muwatta is considered by many Muhaddithin to deserve inclusion among the Sihah Sittah (six canonical hadith books).

docs.title: 3. Imam Shafi'i Rahimullah (Shafi'i Madhab)
docs.text:
Detail Information Full name Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i Born 150 AH (the year Imam Abu Hanifa passed away), Asqalan Died 204 AH, Misr (Egypt) Key teachers Imam Malik Rahimullah, Imam Muhammad Rahimullah (Hanafi), Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna Rahimullah Famous students Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ali ibn Madini, Ishaq ibn Rahoya Key works Al-Risala, Kitab al-Umm
  • Studied under Imam Malik in Medina first; Imam Malik then directed him to study under Imam Abu Yusuf. By the time he arrived, Imam Abu Yusuf had also passed away, so he studied under Imam Muhammad.
  • Thus, Imam Shafi'i uniquely mastered both the Hanafi and Maliki schools before establishing his own.
  • His opinions in certain matters (e.g., recitation behind the Imam) shifted after he moved to Egypt, because of his exposure to the Sahabah's legacy there.
  • Was the first to formally write on Usul al-Fiqh — Al-Risala is considered the first work in this field.

docs.title: 4. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal Rahimullah (Hanbali Madhab)
docs.text:
Detail Information Born 164 AH, Baghdad Died 241 AH Key teachers Imam Abu Yusuf Rahimullah, Imam Shafi'i Rahimullah, Yahya ibn Qattan Famous students Imam Bukhari, Imam Muslim, Imam Abu Dawud, Abdullah ibn Ahmad Key work Musnad Imam Ahmad (127,000 hadith)
  • Studied directly under Imam Abu Yusuf (could not study under Imam Abu Hanifa, who passed away 14 years before his birth).
  • The Madhabs were codified before the major Hadith collections — Imam Bukhari, Imam Muslim, and Abu Dawud were students of Imam Ahmad; the canonical Hadith books came after the Madhabs were established.
  • Faced severe persecution over the Khalq al-Quran (createdness of the Quran) controversy — was imprisoned and beaten for firmly holding that the Quran is the uncreated speech of Allah.
  • Musnad Imam Ahmad contains 127,000 ahadith (compare: Sahih Bukhari ~6,700–6,800 hadith).
  • Imam Bukhari himself memorized over 600,000 ahadith with complete Sanad — a level of memorization far beyond the Matan alone.

docs.title: The Two Key Hanafi Imams (Sahibayn)
docs.text:
(Full detail deferred to Saturday; mentioned as essential to Quduri study)

  • Imam Abu Yusuf Rahimullah — student of Imam Abu Hanifa; his opinions are cited throughout Quduri alongside Imam Abu Hanifa's.
  • Imam Muhammad Rahimullah — author of the six Zahir al-Riwayah books; studied under both Imam Abu Hanifa and was a teacher to Imam Shafi'i.

In Quduri, students will regularly see: - Imam Abu Hanifa's opinion — the primary Hanafi position - Imam Abu Yusuf's opinion — sometimes differs - Imam Muhammad's opinion — sometimes differs

In Hidayah (year 3–4), all four Madhabs are compared with their underlying evidences.

docs.title: Adab (Etiquettes) of Seeking Knowledge
docs.text:
1. Maintain wudu during class — many senior scholars would not even write the name of Rasulullah ﷺ without being in a state of wudu.
  2. Make du'a before class — the time immediately after a class of Deen is a time of acceptance of du'a.
  3. Wear perfume (where appropriate) — with the note that women should avoid heavy fragrances as it falls under their hijab in public settings.
  4. Respect the books of Deen — keep a designated place for them; do not place anything (pens, phones, other books) on top of them.
  5. Anecdote of Anwar Shah Kashmiri Rahimullah: He would physically reposition himself to read the marginalia of a book rather than move the book itself — his reverence for the written Deen is credited as a source of his vast knowledge.
  6. Read actively in class — builds the habit needed for Daura year, where students read hadith aloud and the teacher explains.
  7. Punctuality — attend on time as a basic adab.

docs.title: Mindset for This Course
docs.text:
• Do not measure yourself by exam marks — measure by how much Deen has entered your life, how much you apply, and how much you convey to others.
  • Imam Shafi'i Rahimullah said: "If you do not give your 100% to the Deen of Allah, this Deen will not come to you — and even when you give 100%, only a fraction of it may return."
  • Encouragement to persevere even when not understanding — the teacher shared his own experience of nearly giving up in first year upon Mufti Yaseer's advice: "Even if you do not understand, continue. There will come a time — perhaps not this month, perhaps not this year — but stay and you will get it."
  • Hadith principle: "Whomever Allah wants good for, He gives them the understanding of Deen." (Agreed upon — Bukhari and Muslim) — our being here is solely from the mercy of Allah.

docs.title: Course Structure Going Forward
docs.text:
Year Fiqh Text Focus Year 1 Nur al-Idah / Fiqh al-Muyassar (or similar) Opening level — basic Masail Year 2 (now) Mukhtasar al-Quduri Hanafi opinions of the three Imams with basic reasoning; goal: complete in 3 semesters Year 3–4 Al-Hidayah (4 volumes; 1–2 may be covered) All four Madhabs compared; underlying evidences explored Year 5–6 (Daura) Siha Sittah Hadith behind the Masail — the "bigger picture" opens
  • Ibadat vs. Mu'amalat: Most public Islamic education covers Ibadat (worship). Mu'amalat — trade, Nikah, financial dealings, disputes — makes up approximately 80% of Fiqh Masail but is almost never taught publicly. This course will open that space through Quduri.
  • WhatsApp group for Fiqh class specifically will be created — for sharing hadith references, questions outside of class time.
  • Next class: Saturday, same time (7:00–8:30 PM CST) — Quduri begins.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered three main areas: (1) a review of the four sources of Islamic law and the role of the madhabs, (2) biographical introductions to Imam Abu Yusuf and Imam Muhammad al-Shaybani (the two primary students of Imam Abu Hanifa), and (3) a foundational introduction to the Ahkam al-Shar'iyyah — the legal categories of Islamic rulings — covering both the Azimat (positive/obligatory) and Mahi (prohibitory) categories. The session also included a detailed biographical introduction to Imam al-Quduri, the author of the primary text (Mukhtasar al-Quduri), and a brief orientation to the Zahir al-Riwayah (the six foundational books of Hanafi fiqh).

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
1. The necessity of knowing the dalil (evidence) behind every ruling — knowing a mas'ala is incomplete without knowing its source and how it was derived.
  2. The hierarchical categories of Islamic legal rulings (Ahkam) — the distinction between Fard, Wajib, Sunnah, and Nawafil on the positive side, and Haram and Makruh on the prohibitory side.
  3. The distinction between Fard and Wajib — a defining feature of Hanafi fiqh not found as explicitly in other madhabs.
  4. The caliber and contribution of the Hanafi Imams — particularly Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, and how their roles shaped Hanafi fiqh.
  5. The unique shura (consultative council) methodology of Imam Abu Hanifa — every mas'ala was discussed and agreed upon by 40 senior scholars before being recorded.
  6. The importance of scholarly humility — even Imam Malik said "I don't know" to the majority of questions posed to him; students of fiqh must exercise caution before issuing verdicts.
  7. The greatness of Imam al-Quduri and his Mukhtasar — the miracle of his revision at the Ka'bah and the book's 12,000 masa'il.

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning Fiqh Islamic jurisprudence; the detailed legal rulings derived from the sources Mas'ala (pl. Masa'il) A legal question or ruling Dalil (pl. Dala'il) Evidence or proof for a ruling Madhab A school of legal thought (e.g., Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki, Hanbali) Usul Foundational principles from which rulings are derived Qawa'id Legal maxims; a level above Usul Ijtihad Independent legal reasoning by a qualified scholar Istinbat The extraction/derivation of a ruling from the sources Mujtahid / Mustanbit A scholar qualified to perform ijtihad Ijma' Scholarly consensus; the third source of Islamic law Qiyas Analogical reasoning; the fourth source of Islamic law Ahkam Islamic legal rulings/categories Azimat Rulings that are firmly established obligations Rukhsah A concession or relaxation granted due to hardship Fard An absolute obligation proven by definitive evidence Fard al-'Ayn An individual obligation upon every qualifying person Fard al-Kifayah A collective obligation; discharged if fulfilled by some Wajib An obligation proven by probable (zanni) evidence; one level below Fard in Hanafi fiqh Sunnah An action regularly practiced by Rasulullah ﷺ Sunnah al-Mu'akkadah An emphasised Sunnah which Rasulullah ﷺ performed consistently Sunnah Ghayr Mu'akkadah A non-emphasised Sunnah; equivalent to Mandub/Nawafil Sunnah al-Huda Sunnahs related to acts of worship (Ibadat) Sunnah al-Zawaid Sunnahs from Rasulullah's ﷺ non-devotional personal habits Nawafil (sing. Nafl) Supererogatory acts done above and beyond the obligatory Haram Absolutely prohibited; established by definitive evidence Makruh Disliked/discouraged action Makruh Tahrimi Strongly disliked; established by zanni evidence; closer to Haram in practice Makruh Tanzihi Mildly disliked; permissible but should be avoided when possible Dalil Qat'i Absolute, definitive evidence (Quran or Hadith Mutawatir) Dalil Zanni Probable evidence (e.g., Khabar al-Wahid) Hadith Mutawatir A hadith narrated by so many chains that fabrication is inconceivable Khabar al-Wahid A hadith narrated by a smaller number of chains Zahir al-Riwayah The six foundational books of Hanafi fiqh, authored by Imam Muhammad Nawad al-Riwayah Secondary narrations from Imam Muhammad outside the six books Sanad The chain of narrators of a hadith Matan The text/content of a hadith Rawi (pl. Ruwat) A narrator of hadith Muhaddith A scholar specialising in hadith Faqih A scholar of fiqh Mufassir A scholar of Quranic exegesis Mufti A scholar qualified to issue legal verdicts (fatawa) Fatwa A legal verdict/opinion Qadi / Qadhi A judge in an Islamic court Iftah Specialisation in issuing legal verdicts Nisbah An epithet derived from one's origin, city, tribe, or profession Kuniyah An honorific name (e.g., "Abu Hussain") Nasab Lineage name Shuruhaat Commentaries (on a book) Miras / 'Ilm al-Miras Inheritance law Muamalat / Kitab al-Buyu' Commercial/transactional law Ibadat Acts of worship Qadha 'Umri Lifetime make-up of missed prayers Witr The odd-numbered prayer after 'Isha; Wajib in Hanafi fiqh Sadaqah al-Fitr Obligatory charity at the end of Ramadan Ahnaf The followers of the Hanafi madhab Tanning Drying/treating animal skin; a chapter in fiqh with specific rulings Khilaf / Ikhtilaf Scholarly disagreement Mufta Bihi The position adopted for fatwa (operative opinion) Ayimma Arba'ah The four Imams of the four madhabs Ayimma Thalatha The three Imams (Shafi'i, Ahmed, Malik) — used in certain mas'ail Shaykhain Imam Abu Hanifa and Imam Abu Yusuf Sahibain Imam Abu Yusuf and Imam Muhammad Tarafain Imam Abu Hanifa and Imam Muhammad Salaf (of Fuqaha) The period of Imam Abu Hanifa through Imam Muhammad Khalaf The later period of Hanafi scholars, from after Imam Muhammad onward

docs.title: The Four Sources of Islamic Law
docs.text: All rulings in every madhab are ultimately derived from one of four sources: 1. Quran 2. Sunnah (Hadith) of Rasulullah ﷺ 3. Ijma' — scholarly consensus 4. Qiyas — analogical reasoning

docs.title: Principle: Dalil Must Match the Ruling's Level
docs.text:
• For a ruling to be Fard, the dalil must be Qat'i (absolute) — from the Quran or Hadith Mutawatir.
  • For a ruling to be Wajib, the dalil may be Zanni — such as Khabar al-Wahid.
  • For a ruling to be Haram, the dalil must also be Qat'i; one cannot declare something haram based on zanni evidence alone.
  • For Makruh Tahrimi, the dalil is Zanni — hence it does not reach the level of Haram, but the practical obligation to avoid it is treated similarly.

docs.title: Example — Witr Prayer
docs.text:
• There is a hadith supporting Witr, but it comes through Khabar al-Wahid (not Mutawatir).
  • Therefore, in Hanafi fiqh, Witr is Wajib, not Fard.
  • Practical implication: when making up missed prayers (Qadha 'Umri), one must also make up Witr alongside Fard prayers.

docs.title: Example — Sadaqah al-Fitr
docs.text: • Similarly established through Khabar al-Wahid → classified as Wajib.

docs.title: Example — Timing of Salah
docs.text:
• Jibril led Rasulullah ﷺ in prayer over two days — early time on Day 1, late time on Day 2 — establishing that both times are valid.
  • Sahabah who settled in different regions (e.g., Abdullah ibn Mas'ud in Kufa) passed on the practice they followed, leading to regional differences in timing.
  • This is the origin of Hanafi prayers being performed slightly later — both timings are authentically established.

docs.title: Example — Chess
docs.text: • Playing chess is Makruh Tahrimi — established by zanni dalil, not categorised as Haram, but must be treated with near-Haram avoidance.

docs.title: Example — Shrimp
docs.text: • In Hanafi fiqh, the majority position is that eating shrimp is Makruh Tanzihi — it should be avoided, but one who eats it cannot be told it is Haram.

docs.title: Example — Haram with Rukhsah
docs.text:
• Alcohol/wine is Haram in all circumstances. Exception: if a person is extremely ill and the only available medicine contains it, the Shari'ah permits taking the medically prescribed amount.
  • Gelatin from swine in capsules: Haram ordinarily; permitted only when it is the sole available treatment.

docs.title: Skins — Absolute Prohibitions (No Tanning Exception)
docs.text: Two skins are impermissible under any circumstances (unlike other animal skins which become permissible after tanning): 1. Skin of a pig 2. Skin of a human being (Full discussion will come in the chapter on Tanning.)

docs.title: Preference of Opinions in Hanafi Fiqh by Domain
docs.text: Domain Preferred Opinion Ibadat (worship) Imam Abu Hanifa Mu'amalat / Kitab al-Buyu' (transactions) Imam Abu Yusuf (due to his 10–12 years as Qadi) 'Ilm al-Miras (inheritance law) Imam Muhammad al-Shaybani

docs.title: The Full Framework of Ahkam al-Shar'iyyah
docs.text:
AHKAM
├── AZIMAT (Obligatory/Positive Side)
│   ├── 1. FARD
│   │     ├── Dalil: Qat'i (Quran or Hadith Mutawatir)
│   │     ├── Fard al-'Ayn — obligatory on every individual
│   │     └── Fard al-Kifayah — collective obligation; some fulfilling it exempts others
│   ├── 2. WAJIB
│   │     ├── Dalil: Zanni (Khabar al-Wahid)
│   │     ├── Must be treated practically like Fard
│   │     └── Denying it does NOT make one a kafir (unlike denying a Fard)
│   ├── 3. SUNNAH
│   │     ├── Sunnah al-Huda (related to Ibadat)
│   │     │     ├── Sunnah Mu'akkadah (emphasised — e.g., 2 rak'at after Maghrib)
│   │     │     └── Sunnah Ghayr Mu'akkadah (non-emphasised; level of Mandub/Nafl)
│   │     └── Sunnah al-Zawaid (non-devotional habits of Rasulullah ﷺ)
│   └── 4. NAWAFIL
│         └── Any additional act above Fard and Wajib
│               (Linguistically: "addition on top of something")
│
└── MAHI (Prohibitory Side)
    ├── 1. HARAM
    │     ├── Dalil: Qat'i (Quran or Hadith Mutawatir)
    │     ├── Absolutely impermissible
    │     └── Rukhsah possible in extreme necessity (e.g., medicine)
    └── 2. MAKRUH
          ├── Makruh Tahrimi
          │     ├── Dalil: Zanni
          │     ├── Must be treated practically like Haram in avoidance
          │     └── Denying it does NOT make one a kafir
          └── Makruh Tanzihi
                ├── Mildly disliked
                └── One has the option; avoidance is preferred but not at the level of Tahrimi

docs.title: Fard vs. Wajib — The Hanafi Distinction
docs.text: Aspect Fard Wajib Dalil Qat'i (Quran/Mutawatir) Zanni (Khabar al-Wahid) Practical obligation Must be done Must be treated like Fard practically Denying its obligation Makes one a Kafir Does NOT make one a Kafir Example All five daily prayers Witr, Sadaqah al-Fitr

docs.title: Makruh Tahrimi vs. Makruh Tanzihi
docs.text: Aspect Makruh Tahrimi Makruh Tanzihi Dalil Zanni Zanni (weaker application) Avoidance level Treat like Haram in practice Avoid when possible; latitude exists Kafir if denied? No No Example Chess Eating shrimp (Hanafi position)

docs.title: On the Shura Council of Imam Abu Hanifa
docs.text: Imam Abu Hanifa did not derive rulings alone. He assembled a council of 40 of the finest scholars of his time — muftis, fuqaha, muhaddithun, mufassirun, and linguists. Each mas'ala was discussed, sometimes for weeks, until consensus was reached. He would not record a ruling until all agreed — and he would even wait for the return of Qadi 'Afiyah specifically before finalising a mas'ala.

docs.title: On Imam Abu Yusuf's Authority in Mu'amalat
docs.text: After the passing of Imam Abu Hanifa, Imam Abu Yusuf served as Chief Qadi (judge) for approximately 10–12 years. His practical judicial experience led him to revise certain opinions of Imam Abu Hanifa in the domain of commercial transactions. Therefore, in Kitab al-Buyu', the mufta bihi (adopted fatwa position) often follows Imam Abu Yusuf over Imam Abu Hanifa.

docs.title: On Imam Muhammad in Inheritance Law
docs.text: The detailed coverage of inheritance ('ilm al-miras) in Hanafi fiqh follows Imam Muhammad al-Shaybani's opinions. Miras is defined directly in the Quran with no other source — making it one of the most precisely defined areas of fiqh.

docs.title: On Ikhtilaf within Hanafi Fiqh
docs.text: Unlike the ikhtilaf between the four madhabs (which is extensive), differences of opinion between the Hanafi Imams are comparatively rare — a testament to the shura methodology. Where differences do exist (particularly in Imam Abu Yusuf or Imam Muhammad differing from Imam Abu Hanifa), they are rooted in the same usul but reflect changed circumstances or additional judicial experience.

docs.title: On Later Hanafi Scholars Revising Earlier Masa'il
docs.text: Imams such as Imam al-Quduri and Sahibi Hidayah (Imam al-Marginani) — writing 3–4 generations after Imam Abu Hanifa — sometimes recorded a different ruling than what the first generation wrote, not by abandoning the usul, but by applying the same principles to changed circumstances. This occurred primarily in Kitab al-Buyu' (transactional law), not in Ibadat. Such revisions required the consensus of the Hanafi muftis and fuqaha of their time.

docs.title: On Scholarly Humility — The Example of Imam Malik
docs.text: When Imam Malik traveled to Kufa, approximately 70 masa'il were presented to him. He responded "I don't know" to the majority of them. This is cited as the model: a scholar of the highest rank openly acknowledging the limits of his knowledge rather than issuing an unfounded verdict.

docs.title: Imam Abu Yusuf (Rahimullah)
docs.text:
• Real name: Ya'qub bin Ibrahim
  • Born: 113 AH, Kufa/Baghdad
  • Passed away: 182 AH, Baghdad
  • Primary teacher: Imam Abu Hanifa
  • Famous students: Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Imam Muhammad al-Shaybani, Yahya ibn Ma'in
  • Major works:
  • Kitab al-Athar
  • Kitab al-Kharaj (on land tax/state revenues)
  • Distinction: Served as Qadi for ~10–12 years after Imam Abu Hanifa's death; his opinions in Mu'amalat are given priority in Hanafi fatawa.

docs.title: Imam Muhammad al-Shaybani (Rahimullah)
docs.text:
• Real name: Muhammad bin Hasan
  • Born: 132 AH, Shayban (hence "al-Shaybani")
  • Passed away: 189 AH, Ra'id
  • Primary teachers: Imam Abu Hanifa, Imam Abu Yusuf, Sufyan al-Thawri/al-Sari
  • Famous students: Imam al-Shafi'i, Yahya ibn Ma'in, Abu Hafiz
  • Major works (the Zahir al-Riwayah — 6 books):
  • Al-Mabsut (also known as Al-Asl)
  • Al-Ziyadat
  • Al-Jami' al-Saghir
  • Al-Jami' al-Kabir
  • Al-Siyar al-Saghir
  • Al-Siyar al-Kabir
  • Note on Siyar: The last two books (al-Siyar al-Saghir and al-Kabir) deal with international relations and constitutional principles; various national military codes and constitutional frameworks have drawn from them.
  • Also wrote: Muwatta' Imam Muhammad, Nawadir al-Riwayah
  • Distinction: Primary author of the Zahir al-Riwayah. His opinions in 'Ilm al-Miras are given priority in Hanafi fatawa. Included in Imam Abu Hanifa's council of 40 despite his young age (~18 at the time of Imam Abu Hanifa's death).

docs.title: Imam al-Quduri (Rahimullah) — Author of the Primary Text
docs.text:
• Full name: Imam Abul Husain Ahmad bin Muhammad bin Ahmad al-Baghdadi al-Quduri
  • Born: 362 AH, Baghdad
  • Passed away: 428 AH, Baghdad (Sunday, 5 Rajab), age 66
  • Primary teacher in fiqh: Rukn al-Islam Abu 'Abdillah Muhammad bin Yahya bin Mahdi al-Jorjani
  • Chain to Imam Abu Hanifa: Al-Jorjani ← Abu Bakr al-Jassas ← Abu al-Hasan 'Ubaidullah Archi ← Abu Sa'id Badra'i ← 'Allama Musa Razi ← Imam Muhammad al-Shaybani ← Imam Abu Hanifa (approximately 6–7 teachers removed)
  • Teachers in Hadith: Muhammad bin 'Ali bin Su'id; 'Ubaidullah bin Muhammad Joshini
  • Famous students: Abu Bakr Ahmad bin 'Ali bin Thabit Khatib al-Baghdadi (famous hadith scholar and author); Sahib al-Tariq
  • Why "al-Quduri": Either from his village name Qudur, or from his association with the trade of large cooking vessels (qudur = large pots)
  • Miracle of Hajj: After completing the Mukhtasar, he carried the full manuscript to Makkah, raised it at the Mataf after Tawaf, made du'a for Allah to allow him to correct any errors, then reviewed all 12,000 masa'il page by page — finding only 5–6 mistakes.

docs.title: Imam al-Quduri's Works
docs.text: Book Description Mukhtasar al-Quduri Primary text; ~12,000 masa'il; 62 Kitabs and 61 Abwab; taught globally in Hanafi madrasas Al-Tajrid 7 volumes on ikhtilafi masa'il between Hanafi and Shafi'i, with dalail of both sides Masa'il al-Khilaf Ikhtilaf masa'il within the Hanafi madhab Al-Tartib — Sharh Mukhtasar al-Qarkhi Commentary on al-Qarkhi's famous Qawa'id (Hanafi legal maxims) Sharh Adab al-Qadi On the etiquette and rulings of the Islamic judiciary

docs.title: Key Terminology Reference — Hanafi Scholar Groupings
docs.text: Term Refers To Ayimma Arba'ah All four Imams: Abu Hanifa, Shafi'i, Ahmed, Malik Ayimma Thalatha Three Imams: Shafi'i, Ahmed, Malik (used in certain ikhtilaf discussions) Shaykhain Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Abu Yusuf Sahibain Imam Abu Yusuf + Imam Muhammad Tarafain Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Muhammad Salaf (of Fuqaha) Period from Imam Abu Hanifa to Imam Muhammad Khalaf Period after Imam Muhammad (through figures like Imam Shamsul Islam al-Halwani)

docs.title: Lessons & Practical Application
docs.text:
1. Know the dalil, not just the ruling. Every mas'ala should be known alongside its source: which ayah, which hadith, and which category of evidence. This is what distinguishes real understanding from surface memorisation.

  2. The Fard/Wajib distinction is uniquely Hanafi — other madhabs largely use "Wajib" to mean what Ahnaf call "Fard." When reading cross-madhab discussions, be aware of this difference in terminology.

  3. Makruh Tahrimi should be treated practically like Haram — the difference is at the level of i'tiqad (belief): denying a Makruh Tahrimi does not make one a kafir, but in practice it must be avoided with the same seriousness.

  4. Never issue a ruling without thorough investigation. Imam Malik said "I don't know" to most of ~70 masa'il put to him. Students of fiqh must be honest about the limits of their knowledge, especially while still studying. If in doubt, say: "Give me time to look into it" and consult a local 'alim.

  5. Never label something Haram without absolute certainty — saying "haram" without a thorough analysis is a gravely serious matter. Avoid either extreme: knowing and hiding, or not knowing and speaking anyway.

  6. Kitab al-Buyu' will have masa'il that differ from the earliest Hanafi books — this is expected and deliberate. Imam al-Quduri and Sahibi Hidayah applied the same usul to changed circumstances; this is not innovation but proper application of the principles.

  7. Studying method for this class: After each session, write out all masa'il from the text (Mukhtasar al-Quduri) from memory, then check against the book. Post questions to the class WhatsApp group immediately — they benefit all students.

  8. The value of this knowledge: Learning one mas'ala of deen is reported to be better than months of nafl worship. Completing Mukhtasar al-Quduri means learning approximately 12,000 masa'il — an immense treasure.

  9. Connection to one's teacher (isnad) matters. Imam al-Quduri's chain back to Imam Abu Hanifa through 6–7 scholars is a sign of the authenticity and continuity of this knowledge. The sanad in fiqh, like in hadith, is a guarantee of transmission.

  10. Next class (Wednesday): Begin Kitab al-Taharah (the book of purification) — read ahead in the Quduri text and prepare to discuss the masa'il.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session opened Kitab al-Tahara (Book of Purification) from Imam al-Quduri's Mukhtasar, beginning with a review of the seven categories of Shari'a rulings, an explanation of how Islamic texts are organized (Kitab, Bab, Fasl), and a detailed study of the four fara'id (obligations) of wudu. The primary Qur'anic dalil for wudu was established (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:6), followed by discussion of two key masail: (1) whether the elbow and ankle bone are included in the washing, and (2) the minimum required area for masa of the head. Scholarly differences between the Ahnaf's three Imams and Imam Zufar, as well as between the four madhhabs on masa al-ra's, were covered in detail.

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
1. The seven categories of Shari'a rulings — review and application before opening the kitab
  2. Structure of Islamic legal texts — Kitab, Bab, and Fasl explained
  3. Opening of Kitab al-Tahara — why Imam Quduri begins here; linguistic vs. legal definition of tahara
  4. The four fara'id of wudu — derived from Qur'an and Sunnah
  5. Inclusion of the elbow and ankle bone — ikhtilaf between Aima Thalasa of Ahnaf and Imam Zufar Rahimullah
  6. Minimum masa of the head — three opinions within the Ahnaf and comparison with Imam Shafi'i and Imam Malik
  7. Practical benefits of maintaining wudu — barakah in rizq, ease of good deeds, reward of shahid if one dies in that state

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning Kitab (كِتَاب) Book; highest level of textual organization, covers a major subject area Bab (بَاب) Chapter; groups masail related to a specific topic Fasl (فَصْل) Sub-section;
