docs.title: The Qur'anic Basis for Wudu
docs.text:
Dalil: Surah al-Ma'idah 5:6 "O you who believe, when you stand for prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the two ankle bones."

This single ayah is the foundational dalil for all four fara'id of wudu. The Sharah of Dur al-Mukhtar notes that this ayah points to eight paired matters: two types of tahara (wudu/ghusl), two means (water/tayammum), two obligations (ghusl of limbs/masa of head), two causes making tahara wajib (hadas/janabat), two mubah concessions (sickness/travel), two dalils for ghusl and wudu, two indications toward purpose, and two rewards (forgiveness of sins/completion of ni'mah).

docs.title: The Four Fara'id of Wudu
docs.text:
Per Imam Quduri and the Ahnaf, the obligatory elements of wudu are:

  1. Ghasl al-wajh — Washing the face
  2. Ghasl al-yadayn ila al-murафiq — Washing both arms up to (and including) the elbows
  3. Masa al-ra's — Wiping the head (minimum: one-fourth)
  4. Ghasl al-rijlayn ila al-ka'bayn — Washing both feet up to (and including) the ankle bones

docs.title: Masala 1: Are the Elbows and Ankle Bones Included in the Washing?
docs.text:
Position of Aima Thalasa of Ahnaf (Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad): Yes, they are included. The elbow must be washed as part of the arm; the ankle bone must be washed as part of the foot. If the elbow is not washed, wudu is invalid and salah is not accepted.

Position of Imam Zufar Rahimullah: They are not included. Washing up to the elbow is sufficient without washing the elbow itself.

Dalil of Aima Thalasa: - Hadith in Sahih Muslim (narrated by Nu'aym ibn Abdullah al-Mujmir): Abu Hurairah رضي الله عنه performed wudu, washing his face and arms beyond the elbow, and his legs beyond the ankle bone (into the shank), saying: "This is how I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ perform wudu." He added that the Prophet ﷺ said believers will appear bright on the Day of Resurrection on the limbs washed in wudu, and whoever wishes may increase this brightness. - Principle of genus (jins): the elbow is part of the arm (same genus); the ankle bone is part of the foot (same genus). When a limit falls within the same genus as the thing being washed, it is included. This contrasts with the fast, where day and night are different genera.

Dalil of Imam Zufar: - Qiyas on the Qur'anic ayah about fasting: "Complete the fast until the night" (Surah al-Baqarah). No scholar says the night is included in the fast — i.e., one stops at nightfall, not after it. By the same token, "up to the elbows" means one stops at the elbow.

Answer to Imam Zufar's dalil: The principle of ghaya and mughayyah — day and night are of different genera, so night is excluded. The arm and elbow are of the same genus, so the elbow is included. The fasting analogy does not hold across different-genus boundaries.

Practical ruling: If a person realizes their elbow was not washed, they need only re-wash the elbow and continue — they do not redo the entire wudu, provided no excessive time has elapsed.

docs.title: Masala 2: Minimum Required Area for Masa al-Ra's
docs.text:
Dalil: Hadith of Mughirah ibn Shu'bah رضي الله عنه (in Bukhari and Muslim): On a journey, Mughirah poured water for the Prophet ﷺ after he relieved himself. The Prophet ﷺ washed his face, arms, wiped his head (masaha bi-ra'sihi), and did masa over his two khuf. A version of this hadith uses the word nasiya, indicating he wiped over the forelock/frontal portion.

Three opinions within the Ahnaf on what "nasiya" means:

Opinion Area Required Basis 1st (relied-upon / muftabih) One-fourth of the head The usul: performing one-fourth of a thing equals performing the whole; Hadith mentions "nasiya" = forelock area = approximately one-fourth 2nd The forehead only (hairline area) Narrower reading of "nasiya" — only the frontal strip at the hairline 3rd Three fingers' width Narrowest reading; three fingers placed at the hairline

Ahnaf relied-upon position: Wiping the top/frontal quarter of the head fulfills the fard. Wiping the entire head is sunnah.

Usul underpinning the one-fourth principle: "One-fourth of a thing stands for the whole." This same principle applies in: (1) woman's sattar in salah — if less than one-fourth is exposed briefly without completing a full rukun, salah is not invalidated; (2) Hajj — if less than one-fourth of the head is shaved without ihram permission, dam (major penalty) is not incurred (though a lesser penalty remains).

Other madhhabs on masa al-ra's:

Imam Minimum Required Imam Shafi'i Three hairs (from any part of the head) Imam Malik Entire head must be wiped (based on hadith where the Prophet ﷺ wiped his full head) Ahnaf One-fourth of the head

docs.title: Masala 3: Wudu After Relieving Oneself
docs.text: Ruling: Going for urination or relieving oneself breaks wudu (it constitutes a hadas). This is established by the same hadith of Mughirah — the Prophet ﷺ went to relieve himself and then made wudu upon returning. It is mustahab to perform wudu after relieving oneself even outside of prayer time.

docs.title: Masala 4: Performing Wudu When Already in a State of Wudu
docs.text: Ruling: If a person already has wudu and wishes to perform wudu again for extra reward (mustahab wudu), they should only perform the fara'id (each limb once), not the sunnan (e.g., washing three times). Reasons: 1. Preservation of water — Islam prohibits wasteful use of water even in a river. 2. Since the fard is not due upon them (wudu is already present), only doing the minimum suffices for the nafl intention.

docs.title: Seven Categories of Shari'a Rulings (Review)
docs.text:
Category Definition Example Fard Obligatory; denier becomes kafir Salah, Sawm, Hajj Wajib Obligatory at a lower level; denier not kafir Answering salam, responding to a sneeze Mustahab Recommended Washing hands before eating Mubah Permissible Traveling by car, plane, or train Haram Prohibited Stealing Makruh Tahrimi Prohibitively disliked (treated as haram in aqidah; not kufr to deny) Hoarding scarce goods to profit from shortage Makruh Tanzihi Mildly disliked Drinking water while standing

Important distinction: Calling something haram requires very solid proof from Qur'an, Sunnah, Ijma, or Qiyas. One should not label things haram arbitrarily.

Wajib vs. Fard (aqidah perspective): In aqidah, treat wajib like fard and makruh tahrimi like haram — but denial of wajib does not constitute kufr, unlike denial of fard.

docs.title: Structure of Islamic Legal Texts
docs.text:
Level Term Equivalent Function Highest Kitab (كِتَاب) Volume/Book Covers an entire major subject area (e.g., Kitab al-Tahara covers all purity-related masail) Middle Bab (بَاب) Chapter Groups related masail under a specific topic (e.g., Bab al-Tayammum) Lowest Fasl (فَصْل) Sub-section Breaks a bab into a very specific subject area

Note: In al-Quduri, the Fasl level appears in some chapters but not all.

docs.title: Linguistic Meanings of Tahara
docs.text:
Vocalization Term Meaning Fatha Tahara (طَهَارَة) Purification / the act of purifying (e.g., zakat = taharat al-mal) Dhamma Tuhur (طُهُور) Water used for purification (leftover wudu water) Kasra Tihara (طِهَارَة) Instrument of purification (the vessel/water itself)

Shari'a definition: Tahara is purification — the removal of ritual impurity (hadas or janabat) through wudu, ghusl, or tayammum.

docs.title: Two Types of Tahara
docs.text: Type Removes Method Wudu Minor impurity (hadas) Water applied to specified limbs Ghusl Major impurity (janabat) Full body washing with water Tayammum Minor or major (when water unavailable) Wiping face and hands with clean earth

docs.title: On the Inclusion of Elbows/Ankles in Wudu
docs.text: Scholar/Group Position Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad (Aima Thalasa of Ahnaf) Elbow and ankle bone are included — must be washed Imam Zufar Rahimullah Elbow and ankle bone not included — washing up to them suffices Imam Shafi'i, Imam Malik, Imam Ahmad (general) Elbow and ankle included (broadly aligned with Aima Thalasa on this)

docs.title: On the Minimum Masa al-Ra's
docs.text: Scholar Minimum Ahnaf (relied-upon) One-fourth of the head Imam Shafi'i Three hairs Imam Malik Entire head

docs.title: On Imam Zufar Rahimullah
docs.text: Imam Zufar رحمه الله was among the forty senior fuqaha selected by Imam Abu Hanifa for his scholarly council (shura). His opinions, while sometimes differing from the Aima Thalasa of Ahnaf, were well-grounded and appear throughout Hanafi fiqh books. His ikhtilaf is respected and studied as part of the tradition.

docs.title: On Mughirah ibn Shu'bah رضي الله عنه
docs.text:
• Accepted Islam at the time of Ghazwah al-Ahzab (5th Hijri — well into the Madinah period)
  • Despite accepting Islam relatively late, narrated approximately 136 ahadith
  • Passed away in Kufa — the city central to the development of Hanafi fiqh
  • Passed away in 50th or 51st Hijri

docs.title: Lessons & Practical Application
docs.text:
1. Maintain wudu as a constant state. The Prophet ﷺ heard Bilal رضي الله عنه walking ahead of him in Jannah; when asked the reason, Bilal said he renews his wudu whenever it breaks and prays two raka'at. Wudu brings barakah in rizq, makes good deeds easier, and distances one from sin.

  2. Sleep in a state of wudu. A hadith states that a person who dies in the state of wudu dies as a shahid. Even if wudu breaks after making the intention to sleep with it, the reward still applies — make the niyyah.

  3. Wudu is not re-obligatory if already in wudu. If your wudu from Asr remains intact at Maghrib, you may pray without renewing. If you choose to renew it for extra reward, perform only the fara'id (each limb once) to avoid water waste.

  4. Do not call things haram without solid proof. One of the most repeated cautions in this session: labeling something haram is a serious matter requiring Qur'an, Sunnah, Ijma, or valid Qiyas. Do not do it arbitrarily.

  5. Start everything with Bismillah. Imam Quduri opens with Bismillah and a Qur'anic ayah — this is a means of barakah and completion. The hadith: anything begun with Bismillah has barakah in it.

  6. The one-fourth principle has wide application. Beyond wudu, it applies to: a woman's sattar in salah (less than one-fourth exposed for less than a full rukun = salah intact), and shaving in Hajj (less than one-fourth = no dam, though a lesser penalty applies).

  7. Invest in physical books. The teacher strongly encouraged students to purchase physical copies of al-Quduri and reference texts — for use while traveling, for retention, and for lifelong reference.

  8. Next class (Saturday): Will begin the Sunan of Wudu.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered the sunan (recommended acts) and mustahabbat (desirable acts) of wudu, following the completion of the fara'id (obligatory acts) of wudu in the previous session. The session also introduced the opening discussion on nawaqid al-wudu (acts that break wudu), covering the categories of things that nullify wudu — specifically what exits the body, what enters the body, and states related to the body. The class used Mukhtasar al-Quduri as the primary text, with discussion referencing Hidayah and other classical sources.

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
1. Linguistic and legal definitions of Sunnah — distinguishing Sunnah al-Huda from Sunnah al-Zawa'id
  2. Sunan of wudu — nine acts the Prophet ﷺ performed consistently in wudu
  3. Mustahabbat of wudu — six additional desirable acts, with some scholarly disagreement on categorisation
  4. Absence of wajibat in wudu — unlike other acts of worship, wudu has no intermediate wajib category; it is either fard, sunnah, or mustahab
  5. Nawaqid al-wudu — three categories of nullifiers: what exits the body, what enters the body, and states of the body
  6. Blood and pus — detailed rulings on when flowing blood breaks wudu and the concept of the mazur
  7. Scholarly differences — how Hanafi, Shafi'i, and Maliki positions diverge on multiple masail

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning سُنَن (Sunan) Plural of Sunnah — recommended acts the Prophet ﷺ performed as a matter of worship سُنَّةُ الْهُدَى (Sunnah al-Huda) Acts done by the Prophet ﷺ as part of worship/ibadah — carrying religious significance سُنَّةُ الزَّوَائِد (Sunnah al-Zawa'id) Acts done by the Prophet ﷺ as personal habit (e.g., manner of walking, dressing) مُسْتَحَبَّات (Mustahabbat) Desirable/commendable acts; rewarded if done, no sin for omission فَرَائِض (Fara'id) Obligatory acts of wudu; established by explicit Quranic text وَاجِبَات (Wajibat) Obligatory acts (in other ibadah contexts) — notably absent as a category in wudu غَسْل (Ghasl) Washing — used for limbs in wudu مَسْح (Masah) Wiping — used for head and ears; distinct from ghasl إِنَاء (Ina') Container/vessel for storing water تَسْمِيَة (Tasmiyah) Saying "Bismillah" at the start of wudu سِوَاك (Siwak) Tooth-stick (miswak) used for oral hygiene مَضْمَضَة (Madmada) Rinsing of the mouth اسْتِنْشَاق (Istinshaq) Drawing water into the nostrils to clean them تَخْلِيل (Takhlil) Interlacing/running fingers through beard or between fingers to ensure water coverage تَرْتِيب (Tartib) Performing the acts of wudu in the prescribed order نِيَّة (Niyyah) Intention — made in the heart; saying it aloud is better but not required مَعْذُور (Mazur) A person with a chronic excuse (e.g., continuous bleeding) who is given a concession to pray نَوَاقِض (Nawaqid) Acts/states that break/nullify wudu مَذْي (Mazi) Pre-sexual fluid — exits the frontal passage, breaks wudu وَدْي (Wadi) Thick white fluid exiting after urination — breaks wudu مَنْي (Mani) Semen — requires ghusl, not merely wudu حَيْض (Hayd) Menstrual bleeding نِفَاس (Nifas) Post-natal bleeding اسْتِحَاضَة (Istihada) Irregular/abnormal vaginal bleeding outside of hayd and nifas قَدِيد (Qadid / Sadid) Pus from a wound أَرْكَان الْوُضُوء (Arkan al-Wudu) The pillars/obligatory elements of wudu وُضُوءٌ كَامِل (Wudu Kamil) A complete and perfect wudu — one that fulfils all fara'id, sunan, and mustahabbat أُصُول / قَوَاعِد (Usul / Qawa'id) Foundational legal principles and methodological rules used by the fuqaha قَضَاء (Qada') Making up a missed obligatory prayer دَلِيل (Dalil) Legal evidence/proof from Quran, Hadith, or scholarly consensus

docs.title: Sunan of Wudu
docs.text:
1. Washing the hands three times before placing them into a vessel (upon waking) - Only applies when waking from sleep; at other times this rule does not apply - Reason: a person does not know what their hands may have touched while asleep — if placed directly into a water vessel, the water could become impure - If a person is certain their hands are clean, they may place them directly into the vessel - Dalil: Various ahadith; Hadith of Mughirah ibn Shu'ba (radiAllahu anhu) among the supporting evidences

2. Saying Bismillah at the beginning of wudu (Tasmiyah) - Imam Quduri (rahimahullah): Sunnah mu'akkadah - Sahibi Hidayah: Mustahab - 'Allama (rahimahullah): Sunnah (without specifying subcategory) - Third opinion (some scholars): Wajib — based on a hadith in Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah: "The one who does not say Bismillah at the start of wudu, his wudu is not complete." - Hanafi position: Sunnah — the hadith evidence is considered but does not meet the threshold for establishing a wajib ruling in isolation - If a person enters the bathroom where saying Bismillah aloud is discouraged, and they had already made the intention before entering, they may continue without repeating it

3. Using the Siwak (Miswak) - Using siwak increases the reward of salah 70 times over salah without it - If siwak is unavailable: use fingers with the intention of siwak (same reward applies); alternatively use a toothbrush with the same intention - Key scholarly difference: - Ahnaf (Hanafi): Siwak is a sunnah of wudu (performed at time of wudu) — this is the mu'tamad (relied-upon) opinion - Shafi'i: Siwak is a sunnah of salah (performed just before beginning salah) — hence some worshippers are seen using siwak right before salah begins

4. Rinsing the mouth (Madmada) - Done three times, with new water each time - Important: Madmada should be avoided or done very carefully during fasting (do not gargle deeply) - Dalil: Hadith in Abu Dawud and a variant wording in Sahih Muslim specifying three times with new water each time - Imam Malik: Considers madmada a fard of wudu — if omitted, wudu is incomplete - Ahnaf and Shafi'i: Sunnah

5. Cleaning the nostrils (Istinshaq) - Water is drawn into the soft part of the nose - Done three times with new water each time (Hanafi position) - Shafi'i: Madmada and istinshaq are done together three times — the water from the mouth is used for the nostrils in the same scoop (i.e., six actions become three) - Dalil: Same hadith as madmada (Abu Dawud, Muslim) - Imam Malik: Considers istinshaq a fard of wudu as well

6. Wiping the ears (Masah of ears) - Done after wiping the head; no need to wet hands again — use the remaining moisture from the masah of the head - Both the outer (upper) and inner (lower) parts of the ears are wiped - Imam Shafi'i: New water should be taken for the masah of the ears (separate from the head masah)

7. Interlacing the beard (Takhlil al-lihyah) - Wet hand is run through the beard to ensure water reaches the skin beneath - If the beard is very thick and it is not physically possible to reach the skin, one does as much as possible without pulling or breaking hairs — the hair itself stands in place of the skin in this case - If beard is sparse and skin is visible, one should wash that area properly to ensure water reaches the skin - Running fingers from underneath (back of hand going inward) may allow better penetration - Dalil: Hadith in Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud

8. Interlacing the fingers (Takhlil al-asabi') - Done after masah of head, ears, and beard — using remaining moisture on the hands (no need to re-wet) - Fingers are spread wide and the fingers of one hand are run between the fingers of the other - Purpose: ensures water reaches the gaps between fingers that may have been missed when fingers were held together during washing - Dalil: Hadith in Tirmidhi and Nasa'i - Note: In Imam Quduri's text, takhlil of beard and fingers are listed together as one item, but they can be counted separately

9. Washing each limb three times (Tikrar al-ghasl) - Washing each limb once is the fard (established by the Quranic ayah); three times is the sunnah - The basis for "three times" comes from hadith, not the Quran - Dalil: Hadith in Bukhari and a variant in Abu Dawud - Important distinction: masah (wiping) of the head is NOT included here — the Quranic word used for the head is masah, not ghasl. Masah of the head is done once (see mustahabbat below)

docs.title: Mustahabbat of Wudu
docs.text:
1. Making intention (Niyyah) - Intention is made in the heart; saying it aloud is better - Intention can be made before entering the bathroom (e.g., "I intend to perform wudu and pray Isha") - Hanafi position (Imam Quduri): Niyyah in wudu is mustahab — wudu is valid without it, though the person misses reward - Imam Shafi'i: Niyyah is fard in wudu — wudu is not valid without it - Dalil: Hadith in Bukhari: "Actions are by intentions" — basis of Shafi'i position; Hanafis accept the hadith but classify niyyah as mustahab in this specific context - Contrast with zakat: intention at the time of payment is essential for the zakat to count — the ruling varies by act of worship

2. Wiping the entire head (Masah of full head) - The fard of masah (from the Hanafi Usul) is wiping one-quarter of the head — this fulfils the obligation - Wiping the entire head is mustahab — rewarded but not obligatory - Basis: The Prophet ﷺ wiped the entire head in some narrations and one-quarter in others; Hanafi usul reconciles both by making full head masah mustahab - Masah of the head is done once — the word in the Quran is masah, not ghasl (washing), so the rule of "three times" for limbs does not apply - Dalil: Hadith in Bukhari and Abu Dawud - Imam Shafi'i: Masah should be done three times with new water each time; also holds that masah of even three hairs suffices for the obligatory masah

3. Performing wudu in order (Tartib) - The Quranic sequence: face → hands (to elbows) → head → feet (to ankles) - Hanafi position: Tartib is mustahab — if someone accidentally washed out of order, the wudu is valid; they do not need to restart, but should not do this habitually or deliberately - Imam Shafi'i: Tartib is fard — departing from the Quranic order invalidates the wudu

4. Washing limbs consecutively without long gaps (Muwalaah) - Ideal: proceed from one limb to the next without interruption - If interrupted briefly and the limb has not fully dried: continue from where one left off - If a long time has passed and the limbs have dried without a valid excuse: restart wudu from the beginning - The distinction is between unavoidable urgent interruptions and casual negligence

5. Starting from the right side (Bada' bil-yamin) - The Prophet ﷺ always began actions from his right side — distributing food, wearing shoes, etc. - Applied in wudu: right hand before left hand, right foot before left foot - Dalil: Hadith in Bukhari - Some fuqaha consider this the only true mustahab of wudu, classifying all others as sunan

6. Wiping the neck (Masah of neck) - Not mentioned in Imam Quduri's text but established by other fuqaha - Dalil: Mentioned in 'Ala' al-Sunan and Musnad Ahmad - Included as an additional mustahab making the total six (or seven depending on counting)

docs.title: Nawaqid al-Wudu — Acts That Break Wudu
docs.text:
Three categories framework:

Category Examples What exits the body Blood, pus, urine, stool, gas, mazi, wadi, mani, hayd, nifas, istihada, stomach worms What enters the body Food, drink, intravenous fluids, suppositories — generally do NOT break wudu States of the body Sleep, loss of consciousness/insanity — break wudu

From the two passages (frontal and back): - Anything exiting from either passage breaks wudu - This includes: gas, liquid, solid, semi-solid, and even stomach worms - Dalil: Quranic ayah (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:6) mentioning going to relieve oneself; Hadith in Tirmidhi and Nasa'i

Seven things from the frontal passage: 1. Urine (men and women) 2. Mazi (pre-sexual fluid) 3. Wadi (thick white fluid after urination) 4. Mani (semen — requires ghusl) 5. Hayd (menstrual blood — women) 6. Nifas (post-natal blood — women) 7. Istihada (irregular bleeding — women)

Three things from the back passage: 1. Defecation 2. Gas/wind 3. Stomach worm

Ruling on stomach worm: - Ahnaf, Shafi'i, Hanbali: Breaks wudu - Maliki: Does not break wudu

Blood and pus from the skin (not from the passages): - Blood/pus that oozes out of a wound but does not flow from its original location does NOT break wudu - Once blood/pus begins to flow from its original location, wudu is broken - Wiping it multiple times: if the combined amount across multiple wipes exceeds the threshold, wudu is broken - If blood is visible on clothing or spreads beyond the wound site, wudu is likely broken and must be remade - A band-aid that shows no external sign of bleeding: wudu remains intact; do not open unnecessarily - The exact size threshold (possibly the size of a dirham or a chickpea) — to be confirmed in a subsequent class - Dalil: Specific hadith on this; Quranic ayah (5:6) provides the general framework

Imam Malik and Imam Shafi'i on blood/pus: even if it flows from the wound, wudu is not broken — their own dalail support this position

Sleep and insanity: - Neither sleep nor insanity inherently produces an impurity - They break wudu because the person's rational faculty ('aql) is suspended — they have no awareness of what their body may have done (passed wind, touched impurity, etc.)

docs.title: The Mazur (Person with a Chronic Excuse)
docs.text:
• If blood or another nullifier flows continuously for a full day and night (24 hours) without stopping, the person enters the status of mazur
  • A mazur may make wudu and pray even while the blood continues to flow — the wudu is not considered broken by the ongoing condition
  • If the condition lasts less than 24 hours: the person waits; salah becomes qada' (to be made up) during the period of unbroken flow
  • If flow stops before a prayer time ends: that salah should be prayed in its time
  • If five prayers accumulate as missed, the person transitions to mazur status and may then pray qada' with wudu despite ongoing flow

Practical guidance during the waiting period: - Some Hanafi scholars say one may pray anyway with the intention to repeat later; others say to wait and make qada' — to be confirmed

docs.title: Summary Count of Sunan and Mustahabbat
docs.text:
Category Acts Count Sunan of Wudu Washing hands 3×; Bismillah; Siwak; Madmada; Istinshaq; Masah of ears; Takhlil of beard; Takhlil of fingers; Washing limbs 3× 9 Mustahabbat of Wudu Niyyah; Full masah of head; Tartib (order); Muwalaah (consecutiveness); Starting from right; Masah of neck 6 Total 15

Note: Imam Quduri lists 13 (combining beard and finger takhlil, and omitting masah of neck). Some fuqaha classify all but one as sunan, with only "starting from the right" as mustahab.

docs.title: Distinction: Sunnah vs Mustahab in Hanafi Usul
docs.text: Sunnah Mustahab Source Prophet ﷺ did it consistently as part of ibadah Prophet ﷺ did it as a general habit Omission May incur blame/rebuke (if sunnah mu'akkadah) No blame; only missed reward Example in wudu Madmada, Siwak Niyyah, Tartib

docs.title: Wudu Rulings by Category
docs.text: Act Hanafi Shafi'i Maliki Wajibat in wudu None (no wajib category exists in wudu) N/A N/A Madmada / Istinshaq Sunnah Sunnah (combined in 3 scoops) Fard Siwak Sunnah of wudu Sunnah of salah — Masah of entire head Mustahab Done 3× with new water each time; 3 hairs suffice for fard — Tartib (order) Mustahab Fard — Niyyah in wudu Mustahab Fard — Blood/pus flowing from skin Breaks wudu Does not break wudu Does not break wudu Worm from back passage Breaks wudu (3 mazahib) Breaks wudu Does not break wudu

docs.title: Scholarly Opinions
docs.text:
Imam Abu Hanifa (Rahimahullah): - No wajibat exist in wudu — only fara'id, sunan, and mustahabbat - Siwak is sunnah of wudu - Niyyah is mustahab (not fard) - Tartib is mustahab - Masah of one-quarter of head fulfils the fard; full head is mustahab - Blood that flows from its location breaks wudu

Imam Shafi'i (Rahimahullah): - Niyyah is fard in wudu - Tartib is fard - Masah of the head: done three times with new water; even three hairs are sufficient for the fard portion - Siwak is sunnah of salah (not of wudu) - Madmada and istinshaq combined in one scoop (three times total, not six) - Blood/pus flowing from the skin does NOT break wudu

Imam Malik (Rahimahullah): - Madmada and istinshaq are fard in wudu - Blood/pus flowing from the skin does NOT break wudu - Worm exiting the back passage does NOT break wudu

Sahibi Hidayah: - Classifies Bismillah (tasmiyah) as mustahab (vs. Imam Quduri's classification as sunnah mu'akkadah)

'Allama (rahimahullah) mentioned in class: - Classifies Bismillah as sunnah without specifying subcategory

docs.title: Lessons & Practical Application
docs.text:
On performing wudu: - When waking from sleep, always wash hands before placing them into a water vessel — do not assume cleanliness - Say Bismillah at the start of wudu; if entering the bathroom before having said it, make the intention beforehand - Use siwak (or fingers/toothbrush with the intention of siwak) — the 70× reward for salah is significant - Rinse mouth and clean nostrils three times each, with fresh water each time (Hanafi method), noting this should be avoided during fasting - When wiping ears, use the remaining moisture from the masah of the head — no need to re-wet - For thick beards: do takhlil as deeply as possible without causing pain; the hair replaces the skin - For sparse beards/goatees: wash the visible skin directly to ensure water reaches it - Spread fingers during takhlil to guarantee water reaches between the joints - Wash each limb three times — once is fard, three times is sunnah

On achieving Wudu Kamil (complete/perfect wudu): - Fulfilling all fara'id, sunan, and mustahabbat together constitutes a "kamil wudu" - Praying with kamil wudu gradually changes the quality of salah — the nur of it affects the heart over time, though this may not be felt immediately - Comparison: just as perfecting a skill in worldly pursuits (sport, study) transforms performance, perfecting wudu transforms the quality of prayer

On blood and wounds: - Monitor wounds during salah time: if blood stays at the wound site and does not flow, wudu is intact - If blood seeps through clothing, wudu is likely broken — remake it - A band-aid with no visible blood seeping through: assume wudu is intact; do not open the wound to check unnecessarily - For continuous bleeding: consult a scholar about the mazur ruling for one's specific situation - Approximate size threshold for when flowing blood breaks wudu: to be confirmed (possibly size of a dirham or chickpea)

On asking questions: - Asking genuine questions of scholars and teachers is an act of honour toward them and a means of one's own learning - The Sahaba would wait for Bedouins to ask direct questions to the Prophet ﷺ because their blunt, clear questions produced detailed beneficial explanations - One category of question — asked with sincere intention to learn — is of great benefit in this world and the next - Excessive or purposeless questioning should be avoided (established in hadith in Bukhari and Muslim) - Students are encouraged to post questions to the class chat if the teacher does not follow up

On memorising ahadith: - Students encouraged to begin memorising short ahadith in Arabic — starting with 10–20 smaller narrations - Rationale: all of fiqh and deen rests on the ahadith of the Prophet ﷺ; being able to cite them strengthens conviction and enables one to share knowledge with family, friends, and community - The teacher offered to curate a short list of relevant ahadith to share with the class

Next session: Continuation from the masala of vomiting/throwing up (qay') — next nawaqid of wudu

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered two major topics: (1) a brief completion of the previous session's discussion on types of ghusl and bodily fluids, and (2) an extended treatment of water (maa') — its categories, what renders it permissible or impermissible for tahara, the rules of stagnant versus flowing water, animals that die in water, and the concept of maa' musta'mal (used water). Primary text used is Imam Quduri's Mukhtasar, with supporting evidence from Qur'an, hadith, and the opinions of the four Imams.

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
1. Completing the categories of ghusl (fard, sunnah, wajib, mustahab) from the previous session
  2. The three bodily fluids (mani, madhi, wadi) and their effect on wudu and ghusl
  3. Sources of water permissible for tahara vs. impermissible sources
  4. The three qualities of water (color, taste, smell) and how their alteration affects permissibility
  5. Stagnant water (maa' raakin): small body vs. large body and the effect of najasa
  6. Flowing water (maa' jaar) and its ruling when najasa enters it
  7. Animals without blood dying in water
  8. Maa' musta'mal — its definition, categories, and what may or may not be done with it

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning Tahara Purification / ritual cleanliness Tahur Water that is pure in itself AND capable of purifying others Tahir Pure in itself, but does NOT have the ability to purify others Mutahhar That which purifies other things Hadath Ritual impurity (minor or major) Najasa Physical filth / impurity Najasat-e-Ghaliza Major/heavy impurity Najasat-e-Khafifa Minor/light impurity Mani Seminal fluid — its discharge necessitates ghusl Madhi Pre-seminal fluid during foreplay — breaks wudu only, not ghusl Wadi Thick fluid sometimes exiting after urination — breaks wudu only Maa' musta'mal Used water — water that has already been used to remove a hadath Maa' jaar Flowing water (river, stream) Maa' raakin Stagnant / standing water Ma-e-Kalil Small body of water Ma-e-Kasir Large body of water Ghadir al-Azim A large pond / large stagnant body of water Awdiya Pl. of wadi — valleys; water collected between mountains Uyun Springs / smaller streams Abar Wells (pl. of bir) Bihar Seas / oceans Nabiz Water in which dates have been soaked (not yet fermented to alcohol) Ishnan A type of herb/grass historically added to water to enhance cleansing ability Zafran Saffron Orf Custom / local convention (used in deriving rulings) Shaykhain Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Abu Yusuf Sahibain Imam Abu Yusuf + Imam Muhammad Tarafain Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Muhammad Ibara The textual passage from the primary Fiqh text Dalil / Dalail Evidence / proofs (Qur'an, hadith, ijma', qiyas) Masnoon Related to the Sunnah Mayyat Deceased person Ghusl Janabat Ritual bath due to major impurity (janaba) Laylat al-Jinn The night the Prophet ﷺ met the Jinn (narrated in hadith)

docs.title: 1. Completing Previous Session — Categories of Ghusl
docs.text:
Category Ruling Examples Fard Obligatory Janaba, menstruation, post-natal bleeding Sunnah/Masnoon Sunnah Jumu'ah, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha Wajib Necessary Person who gave ghusl to the deceased (mayyat) must make ghusl for themselves — because droplets fall on the body and one does not know the condition of the deceased Mustahab Recommended (1) When someone accepts Islam; (2) When a child reaches adulthood; (3) When an insane person regains sanity

Note: The Wajib and Mustahab categories are not explicitly in Imam Quduri's text; they were added supplementally in class.

docs.title: 2. The Three Bodily Fluids
docs.text:
Fluid Description Effect on Wudu Effect on Ghusl Mani Seminal discharge with shahwa (desire) Breaks wudu Ghusl becomes obligatory Madhi Pre-seminal fluid during foreplay Breaks wudu Ghusl NOT required — wash and make wudu Wadi Slightly thicker fluid sometimes seen after urination Breaks wudu Ghusl NOT required

Ruling on wadi: If wudu was already performed and wadi appears afterward, wudu must be repeated. Also related: if urine drops appear on clothing, check the size — if larger than roughly a quarter of a coin, wudu is required; if less, it is excused. (Detailed rulings on this topic are in a forthcoming chapter.)

docs.title: 3. Water Permissible for Tahara
docs.text:
Imam Quduri states: "Tahara from hadath is permissible with water from the sky, valleys (awdiya), springs (uyun), wells (abar), and seas (bihar)."

Dalil: Qur'an, Surah al-Furqan (25:48) — Allah sent down purifying water (maa'an tahura) from the heavens. The origin of all these sources ultimately traces back to rainwater.

docs.title: 4. Water IMPERMISSIBLE for Tahara
docs.text:
Source Reason Juice/extract squeezed from fruits or trees (e.g., maple syrup, carrot juice) No longer called "water"; qualities of water (color, taste, smell) have changed Water in which another substance has dominated (ghalaba) — e.g., vinegar, rose water, soup, Gatorade, Rooh Afza, saffron water The name and qualities have changed — it is no longer maa'

Key Principle: Water has three qualities — color, taste, and smell. If all three (or two, per Imam Quduri's text) are altered by a foreign substance, the water cannot be used for tahara.

Hadith Dalil (Ibn Majah): "Water is not made impure by anything except that which changes its smell, taste, and color."

Exception (Sahib al-Hidaya's view): If juice has not been forcibly extracted but has naturally seeped from a fruit, and the consistency still resembles water (not pulp), it may be permissible to perform wudu with it.

docs.title: 5. Water Permissible Despite Additives (One Quality Changed)
docs.text:
If only one of the three qualities is altered, tahara remains permissible. Imam Quduri mentions: - Ishnan (cleansing herb/grass) - Sabun (soap — as used in that era) - Zafran (saffron)

Imam Shafi'i's objection: If saffron is mixed, the water is now called "saffron water," not water — so wudu should not be performed.

Ahnaf's response: Just as water stored in a well is called "well water" but retains its tahur status, calling it "saffron water" does not strip it of that status.

Dalil (Hadith in Sahih Muslim): When washing a deceased person, ishnan and other cleansing substances should be added to the water. If this invalidated the water, the ghusl of the deceased would be invalid — yet the hadith commands this practice, confirming these additives do not negate the water's purity.

Practical modern analogy: Flood water — even though color, taste, and smell may all be affected by soil and debris, the fuqaha permit tahara from it because it is a large, natural body of water. Similarly, autumn lake water with fallen leaves remains permissible.

docs.title: 6. Stagnant Water (Maa' Raakin) — Small Body
docs.text:
Ruling: If any amount of najasa falls into a small, stagnant body of water, the water becomes impure and may not be used for wudu or ghusl.

Dalil: The Prophet ﷺ commanded that stagnant water be protected. He forbade: - Urinating into or near stagnant water (such that splashes could enter) - Performing ghusl al-janaba in or near it

Also established: A person waking from sleep should not put their hands directly into a larger vessel of water before washing them three times, because they do not know what their hands did during the night. (This ruling is specific to waking from sleep; during the day, one washes hands as part of wudu normally.)

Question (addressed in class): Does washing hands three times at the start of wudu satisfy this sunnah? — Yes, if a person wakes up and then uses the restroom before wudu, the three-time hand wash at the start of wudu suffices. However, to specifically fulfill the sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ, one should wash hands three times before placing them into any water vessel.

docs.title: 7. Stagnant Water — Imam Malik's Opinion
docs.text:
Imam Malik (Rahimullah): If najasa falls into a small stagnant body and is so small that none of the three qualities (color, taste, smell) of the water change, the water remains clean.

His dalil (Tirmidhi): Someone asked the Prophet ﷺ about Bi'r Budha'a — a well in Medina into which menstrual rags, dog flesh, and refuse were thrown. The Prophet ﷺ replied: "Indeed, water is pure; nothing makes it impure."

Ahnaf's response to this hadith: Bi'r Budha'a had an underground stream replenishing it — it was effectively flowing water, not truly stagnant. Flowing replenishment changes the ruling. This does not override the general principle for genuinely stagnant small bodies.

docs.title: 8. Defining "Small" vs. "Large" Body of Stagnant Water
docs.text:
School Definition of Small Body Definition of Large Body Ahnaf (opinion of Imam Muhammad, adopted by the madhhab) Less than 10 hand-spans × 10 hand-spans (roughly 10 ft × 10 ft) 10 × 10 hand-spans or more, with enough depth that the bottom is not exposed when water is scooped Imam Shafi'i Less than two large jars/jugs of water Two jars or more

Ahnaf's large body test (ripple test): If movement (e.g., someone taking a ghusl) on one side does not immediately cause perceptible movement on the other side, it is a large body. - Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Abu Yusuf (Shaykhain): the benchmark action is a full ghusl on one side - Imam Muhammad: the benchmark is scooping water with the hands on one side

Ruling for a large stagnant body: Najasa falling in does not automatically render it impure — it only becomes impure if one of the three qualities (color, taste, smell) is visibly changed. This is why the large hawd (water tanks) in South Asian masajid are ruled permissible even when many people perform wudu from them.

docs.title: 9. Flowing Water (Maa' Jaar)
docs.text:
Ruling: Najasa falling into flowing water does not render it impure, as long as no athar (trace/effect) of the najasa remains.

Reason (Imam Quduri): "The najasa cannot settle or remain because of the flow of the water" — it disperses and is carried away.

Three definitions of "flowing water" in Shariah: 1. Orf (local custom) — if the people of that locality consider it flowing water, it is treated as such 2. If dry leaves or grass stems placed on the surface flow away with the current 3. If you scoop water and immediately a new quantity fills your hand from upstream — it is flowing

docs.title: 10. Animals Dying in Water
docs.text:
Ruling (Ahnaf and one opinion of Imam Shafi'i): If an animal that has no flowing blood dies in water, the water does NOT become impure.

Examples: Fish, frogs, crabs, mosquitoes, flies, scorpions, ticks (zanaabir, aqarib)

Dalil: Qur'an, Surah al-An'am — flowing blood is najis. Therefore, if an animal has no flowing blood to begin with, its death in water does not introduce najasa.

Extension of this principle: If a fly or mosquito falls into food or drink, it can be removed and the food/drink remains permissible. (Dalil: the famous hadith about dipping the fly fully and then drinking.)

Imam Shafi'i's nuance: Fish — agrees with Ahnaf. Other water-dwelling animals — does not fully agree.

If an animal WITH blood dies in stagnant water: Rulings differ based on the size of the body of water and whether the carcass decomposes (if it decomposes in a small body, the entire body of water is rendered impure). Details forthcoming in a dedicated chapter.

docs.title: 11. Maa' Musta'mal (Used Water)
docs.text:
Definition: Water that has been used to remove a hadath (ritual impurity), whether: - To perform a new wudu (after hadath occurred), OR - To perform wudu over wudu (i.e., renewing wudu when existing wudu was intact)

When does water become musta'mal? — All four madhhabs agree: the moment the water leaves the body (i.e., drips off), it becomes maa' musta'mal. While still on the body, it retains its tahur status.

docs.title: Opinions on the Status of Maa' Musta'mal:
docs.text:
Scholar Status Imam Abu Yusuf (Rahimullah) Najasat-e-Khafifa (minor impurity) One opinion of Imam Abu Hanifa (Rahimullah) Najasat-e-Ghaliza (major impurity) Imam Muhammad (Rahimullah) Still Tahir (pure), but not Mutahhar Muftabi (operative fatwa) — Ahnaf Tahir but not Mutahhar (in line with Imam Abu Hanifa's other opinion and Imam Muhammad)

This is also one of the opinions of Imam Malik, Imam Shafi'i, and Imam Ahmad (Rahimahumullah).

docs.title: What can Maa' Musta'mal be used for?
docs.text:
Use Permissibility Cleaning after using the restroom (istinja) Permitted Irrigation, cooking, general use Permitted Making wudu NOT permitted Making ghusl NOT permitted

Dalil (two proofs): 1. The Prophet ﷺ used to give leftover wudu water to the sick for baraka and cure. If it were najis, he would not have given it to others. 2. Leftover wudu water splashed onto the bodies and clothes of Sahaba, yet no narration exists of them changing their clothes before prayer because of this — confirming the water is tahir in itself.

docs.title: Summary: Types of Water and Their Rulings
docs.text: Water Type Tahara Permissible? Rainwater, valley water, springs, wells, oceans Yes — tahur Squeezed fruit juice / tree extracts No Water in which one quality has changed due to additives (soap, ishnan, saffron) Yes Water in which two or three qualities changed (vinegar, rose water, soup, Gatorade) No Small stagnant body (< 10×10 spans) with najasa in it No Large stagnant body (≥ 10×10 spans) with najasa in it, qualities unchanged Yes Flowing water with najasa, no visible trace/effect remaining Yes Maa' musta'mal No (wudu/ghusl); Yes (other cleaning) Water in which a bloodless animal dies Yes Water in which a blooded animal dies Depends on body size and decomposition

docs.title: Scholarly Opinions
docs.text:
Issue Imam Abu Hanifa Imam Abu Yusuf Imam Muhammad Imam Shafi'i Imam Malik Imam Zufar Maa' musta'mal from wudu-over-wudu Becomes musta'mal Becomes musta'mal Becomes musta'mal — — Does NOT become musta'mal Status of maa' musta'mal Najasat-e-Ghaliza (one opinion) / Tahir (operative opinion) Najasat-e-Khafifa Tahir Tahir, not mutahhar (one opinion) Tahir, not mutahhar — Large body definition Ripple test via ghusl Ripple test via ghusl Ripple test via hand-scooping (adopted by madhhab) Two jars — — Bloodless animal dying in water Does not make water impure — — Fish: agrees; others: disagrees — — Saffron water for wudu Permissible (name does not change essence) — — Impermissible (name has changed) — — Najasa in small stagnant body, qualities unchanged Water is impure regardless — — — Water remains pure —

Terminology reminder: - Shaykhain = Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Abu Yusuf - Sahibain = Imam Abu Yusuf + Imam Muhammad - Tarafain = Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Muhammad

docs.title: Lessons & Practical Application
docs.text:
1. Know your water source: Islam places enormous emphasis on the purity of water used for tahara. Understanding the categories of water equips a Muslim to make correct decisions in any environment.

  2. The three qualities test: When in doubt about water's suitability for wudu, check color, taste, and smell. If one is altered by a permissible additive (soap, ishnan), you may proceed. If two or more are altered, do not use it for tahara.

  3. Flood and outdoor situations: Even flood water or autumn lake water with leaves and discoloration is generally permissible for tahara due to the large volume and natural origin — a relevant ruling for disaster situations.

  4. Stagnant water near najasa: If someone urinates near a small pond or visible najasa has entered it, do not make wudu from it, regardless of how small the najasa appeared. The ruling for ma-e-kalil is strict.

  5. Washing hands before submerging in a shared vessel (after sleep): When waking, do not plunge hands into a shared water container before washing them three times. This sunnah is fulfilled if you wash hands three times at the start of wudu after using the restroom.

  6. Conservation of water: Even in wudu, water should not be wasted. The Prophet ﷺ was described as making wudu conservatively even when standing in a river. Excessive water use is israf (extravagance) and is impermissible.

  7. Donating leftover wudu water: The Prophet ﷺ gave his leftover wudu water for healing — a beautiful sunnah that also demonstrates the tahir status of maa' musta'mal.

  8. Large hawd (water tank) in masajid: The collective ruling of South Asian scholars is that large hawd tanks used for communal wudu are permissible, as they meet the criteria of ma-e-kasir. This is a real-world application of the 10×10 rule.

  9. Coming next session (Wednesday): The topic of tanning (dabagha) — the ruling on the skin of a dead animal after it has been tanned, and whether it may be used.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered two major topics in Kitab al-Tahara: (1) the purification of animal skins through tanning (dabaghat) and the permissibility of using parts of dead animals, and (2) the rulings on wells (bi'r) that have been contaminated by najasa — specifically what quantity of water must be removed depending on what fell in, and what actions must be repeated by those who unknowingly used the contaminated water.

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
• Dabaghat (tanning) purifies animal hides, making them usable for prayer mats, vessels, and containers — with two exceptions: pig skin and human skin.
  • Eight parts of a dead animal are inherently pure and do not require tanning — a position unique to the Hanafi school.
  • Well contamination (bi'r) rulings are categorized by the size/type of animal that fell in and whether the animal died, decomposed, or swelled.
  • Quantity of water to remove varies by animal category, with six distinct opinions among Hanafi jurists for wells with a constant water source.
  • Repeating salah and ghusl is required for those who unknowingly used contaminated well water, with differing opinions on how many days' worth of salah must be repeated.
  • Shari'ah concession (rukhsa) applies when strict enforcement would cause undue hardship — e.g., small quantities of dried droppings blown into a well.

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning دِبَاغَة (Dibagha/Dabaghat) Tanning — the process that purifies animal hide الدِّبَاغَة الحَقِيقِيَّة (Hakiki Dibagha) Actual/physical tanning — using chemicals, salt, spices, etc. applied to the hide الدِّبَاغَة الحُكُمِيَّة (Hukmi Dibagha) Constructive tanning — natural drying in open air, sun, and soil without any substance applied نَجَس / نَجَاسَة (Najis/Najasa) Impure / ritual impurity الخِنْزِير (al-Khinzir) Swine/pig الآدَمِي (al-Adami) A human being شَعْر (Sha'r) Hair عَظْم (Azm) Bone حَافِر (Hafir) Hoof قَرْن (Qarn) Horn صُوف (Suf) Wool ظُفْر (Zufr) Nail/claw رِيش (Rish) Feather مِنْقَار (Minqar) Beak البِئْر (al-Bi'r) Well نَزَحَ / النُّزُوح (Nazaha/al-Nuzuh) To remove/draw out water from a well الدَّلْو (al-Dalw) Bucket/pail used to draw water from a well الفَأْرَة (al-Fa'ra) Mouse/small rodent العُصْفُورَة (al-Usfura) Small bird (sparrow-type) السَّعْوَة (al-Sa'wa) A small/medium animal (wagtail — small bird, per the Matammim translation) السُّودَانِيَّة (al-Sudaniyya) King crow (from the root of blackness); a larger bird المَعِين (al-Ma'in) A well with a constantly flowing/replenishing water source الحَدَث (al-Hadath) Ritual impurity requiring wudu or ghusl for removal إِزَالَةُ النَّجَاسَة (Izalat al-Najasa) Removal of physical impurity (najasa) الرُّخْصَة (al-Rukhsa) Shari'ah concession/dispensation العُرْف (al-Urf) Local custom; used to determine standard bucket size التَّفَسُّخ (al-Tafassukh) Decomposition; body beginning to crack open الانْتِفَاخ (al-Intifakh) Swelling of a dead body الصَّاحِبَان (al-Sahibaan) "The Two Companions" — Imam Abu Yusuf and Imam Muhammad (al-Shaybani)

docs.title: Ruling 1: Tanning Purifies Animal Hides
docs.text:
Every animal skin — whether from a zabihah or non-zabihah animal — becomes pure once it undergoes dabaghat (tanning), except: - The skin of swine (khinzir) — najis in its essence, no process purifies it - The skin of a human being — impermissible to use out of respect for human dignity (karamat/azmat al-adam)

Once tanned, the leather may be used for: - Praying upon (salah on it is valid — detailed ruling deferred to Kitab al-Salah) - Making wudu with water carried in it - Constructing vessels/sacks for water transport

Evidences: - Hadith in al-Nasa'i: "Every skin that is tanned becomes pure." - Hadith of A'isha (r.a.) in al-Nasa'i on the purification of dead skin through tanning. - Surah al-An'am (6:145) — cited as dalil for the impermissibility of swine skin.

docs.title: Ruling 2: Eight Parts of a Dead Animal Are Inherently Pure (Hanafi Position)
docs.text:
The following eight parts of a dead animal (mayta) do not require tanning and are usable:

  1. Hair (sha'r)
  2. Bone (azm)
  3. Hoof (hafir)
  4. Horn (qarn)
  5. Wool (suf)
  6. Nail/claw (zufr)
  7. Feather (rish)
  8. Beak (minqar)

Hanafi Principle: Any part of an animal that does not contain life (i.e., has no blood, no sensation) remains pure even after the animal's death.

Exception: None of these eight are permissible if they come from swine.

Evidence: The Prophet ﷺ gave Fatima (r.a.) a bracelet made from ivory (elephant tusk) — used as dalil that bones/tusks of non-slaughtered animals are permissible.

Opposing Opinion (Imam al-Shafi'i): All eight parts are najis. None may be used from a dead animal.

docs.title: Ruling 3: Contamination of Wells — Water Removal by Animal Category
docs.text:
Animal/Scenario Water to Remove Small mouse, small bird (usfura), sa'wa, sudaniyya 20–30 buckets (20 = minimum/sufficient; 30 = mustahab) Pigeon, chicken, cat, or similarly-sized animal 40–50 buckets (40 = sufficient; 50 = mustahab) Dog, goat, human being Entire well must be emptied Any animal whose body has swollen and begun to crack (regardless of size) Entire well must be emptied

Note: The condition in Imam Quduri's text for the third category (dog/goat/human) is that the animal died in the well. However, some fuqaha hold that for inherently najis animals (e.g., dog), the entire water must be removed even if the animal came out alive.

Dalil for removing entire well: 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (r.a.) was asked about a person who died in the well of Zamzam and ruled that the entire well must be drained. This athar is recorded in al-Tahawi and is taken as a dalil.

docs.title: Ruling 4: Wells with a Constant Water Source (Ma'in Well)
docs.text:
If a well has a constantly replenishing underground source (ma'in), draining it entirely is impractical. Six opinions exist among Hanafi jurists:

# Opinion Method Source 1 Consult well-digging experts in the locality who can estimate when the well is effectively drained Expert testimony — 2 Lower two knowledgeable people into the well; they ascertain sufficiency Two expert witnesses in the well Imam Abu Hanifa; Sahib al-Hidaya 3 Dig a second identical-sized well nearby; transfer water until new well is full Parallel well method — 4 Insert a measuring stick; remove buckets incrementally and measure water-level drop per bucket; extrapolate total Stick/measurement method Imam Abu Yusuf 5 Remove 200–300 buckets Fixed quantity Imam Muhammad (preferred; agreed upon by Hanafi fuqaha — mu'tamad) 6 Remove 250–300 buckets Fixed quantity (variant) Imam Muhammad (second narration)

Mu'tamad (relied-upon) position: Opinion #5 — 200 to 300 buckets (average local size).

docs.title: Ruling 5: Repeating Salah After Unknowing Use of Contaminated Well Water
docs.text:
Scenario A — Animal found dead, body NOT swollen (time of fall unknown): - Remove water as per the animal's category. - All who used the water must repeat salah of one full day and night = 5 prayers. - Clothes/utensils washed with it should be re-washed.

Scenario B — Animal found dead AND body has swollen and cracked (time of fall unknown):

Position Ruling Imam Abu Hanifa (mu'tamad) Repeat salah of 3 days and 3 nights = 15 prayers Sahiban (Abu Yusuf & Muhammad) No repetition is required until investigation confirms how long ago the animal fell; only repeat for the confirmed period

docs.title: Ruling 6: Concession for Small Quantities of Dried Droppings
docs.text:
If dried animal droppings (e.g., from goats grazing nearby) are blown by wind into a well in small quantities — not enough to visibly dirty or alter the water — the Hanafi school grants a rukhsa: the water remains usable for wudu and tahara. This is based on the principle that hardship lifts restriction (al-mashaqqah tajlib al-taysir).

Exception: Chicken droppings — even a small quantity is considered najis by consensus of all four madhabs.

Note on pigeon droppings: Not considered najis. Dalil: Pigeons were present in Masjid al-Nabawi at the time of the Prophet ﷺ and no instruction was given to clean the masjid on their account.

docs.title: Ruling 7: Using Contaminated Water for Izalat al-Najasa
docs.text: Musta'mal water (used water) that has lost its capacity to remove hadath (ritual impurity) may still be used for izalat al-najasa (removing physical najasa from a surface or garment).

docs.title: Conditions for Tanning to Purify Hide
docs.text:
• Must undergo either hakiki or hukmi dabagha
  • Must not be from swine or human

docs.title: Conditions for Well Contamination Ruling to Apply
docs.text:
1. Animal must have died in the well (per Imam Quduri's text) — for dog/goat/human category; some fuqaha differ
  2. If animal swam out alive: rulings on full drainage may still apply for inherently najis animals
  3. If two animals die simultaneously: remove water quantity corresponding to the larger animal — one cleaning suffices for both

docs.title: Conditions for Salah Repetition
docs.text:
• Person must have had no valid prior wudu before using the contaminated water
  • If person had performed wudu at another source and only used this well for another wudu on top of it, their salah does not need to be repeated
  • Ghusl performed with contaminated water: must be repeated
  • Ghusl performed elsewhere; contaminated water used only for other purposes: nothing to repeat

docs.title: Bucket Size Determination
docs.text:
• Determined by local custom ('urf); whichever size is the average in that locality
  • Approximate average bucket: ~3.5 liters
  • Approximate large bucket: ~60–70 liters (≈ 20× average)
  • Large buckets may be used and converted proportionally to the equivalent number of average-sized buckets

docs.title: Scholarly Opinions
docs.text: Issue Imam Abu Hanifa Imam Abu Yusuf Imam Muhammad Imam al-Shafi'i Eight parts of dead animal Pure; permissible to use Pure; permissible to use Pure; permissible to use All najis; none permissible Water removal (ma'in well) Two expert witnesses in well Stick measurement method 200–300 buckets (mu'tamad) — Salah repetition (swollen animal, unknown time) 3 days & nights (15 prayers) No repetition until time confirmed No repetition until time confirmed — Salah repetition (dead, not swollen, unknown time) 1 day & night (5 prayers) — — —

docs.title: Lessons & Practical Application
docs.text:
1. Rukhsa and hardship: Shari'ah consistently provides concessions where strict enforcement creates undue difficulty. The well-contamination rulings are calibrated to real-world practicality — small droppings blown by wind, the ability to use locally-sized buckets, and the use of expert judgment are all accommodations for daily life in rural/agrarian contexts. The same principle underpins tayammum (dry ablution when water would cause harm).

  2. 'Urf (custom) as a legal tool: The bucket size ruling is a clear example of how Hanafi fiqh integrates local custom into its rulings. There is no fixed universal measurement; what counts is the standard of the community. This is a foundational Hanafi usul principle applicable across many chapters of fiqh.

  3. Studying historical masail builds legal reasoning: These well-water rulings may rarely arise today due to indoor plumbing, but studying them teaches how fuqaha derive rulings, apply qiyas, weigh conflicting evidences, and accommodate necessity — skills transferable to contemporary masail.

  4. Zamzam as a living example: The discussion of ma'in wells becomes vivid through the example of Zamzam, whose level never diminishes despite continuous heavy pumping — a contemporary miracle that connects directly to the historical fiqh scenario of a well with a constant source.

  5. Comparative madhab awareness: The Shafi'i position on the eight animal parts being najis versus the Hanafi position of them being pure illustrates how the same hadith evidence can be weighted differently, and why knowing the dalil behind a ruling matters for proper application and scholarly dialogue.

  6. Topics deferred to later chapters:

  7. Exact process/method of dabaghat → Kitab al-Sayd (Hunting)
  8. Ruling on praying on tanned leather in detail → Kitab al-Salah
  9. Leftover water (musta'mal water) rulings → next session (Saturday)
  10. Tayammum → upcoming chapter

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered two major topics: (1) the final categories of leftover water (su'r) from animals and their rulings for purification, and (2) an introduction to Tayammum — its linguistic and legal definition, historical origin, conditions, obligatory elements (arkan), and sunnahs. The session was primarily based on Imam al-Quduri's Mukhtasar (p. 29 onwards), with supporting hadith from Bukhari, Abu Dawud, Bayhaqi, and Dar al-Qutni, and comparative opinions from the four madhabs.

docs.title: Key Themes
docs.text:
• Completing the chapter on water: which animals' leftover water (su'r) is pure, impure, makruh, or doubtful
  • The five categories of su'r and where the four madhabs agree or differ
  • Introduction to Tayammum: its linguistic origin, shar'i definition, historical context (Ghazwah Zat al-Riqa'), and the role of Aisha (RA) in its revelation
  • The arkan (obligatory elements) and sunnah acts of Tayammum
  • What breaks Tayammum, including the special case of sighting water
  • Comparative opinion: Imam Abu Hanifa/Imam Muhammad vs. Imam Abu Yusuf on valid substances for Tayammum

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning سُؤْر (su'r) Leftover water/remnant from drinking طَاهِر (tahir) Pure / legally clean نَجِس (najis) Impure / legally unclean مَكْرُوه (makruh) Disliked / reprehensible (not forbidden) مَشْكُوك (mashkuk) Doubtful / uncertain مُتَّفَق عليه (muttafaq 'alayh) Agreed upon (by all four madhabs) اِخْتِلَاف (ikhtilaf) Scholarly disagreement تَيَمُّم (tayammum) Dry ablution using earth/dust as a substitute for water صَعِيد (sa'id) Clean earth/ground used for tayammum الْقَصْد (al-qasd) Intention / to aim — the linguistic root meaning of tayammum حَدَث (hadath) State of ritual impurity (minor) جَنَابَة (janabah) State of major ritual impurity requiring ghusl بَهِيمَة (bahimah) Four-legged animal مُخَلَّاة (mukhallaah) Free-roaming domestic animal تَرْتِيب (tarteeb) Sequential order (face → right hand → left hand in tayammum) رُكْن (rukn) Obligatory pillar/element فَرْض (fard) Obligatory مُسْتَحَب (mustahab) Recommended سَبِيلَان (sabilaan) The two passages (front and back) — relevant to what breaks wudu مُسَافِر (musafir) Traveler نَهَر (nahr) River حَجَر (hajar) Stone / rock كُحْل (kuhl) Antimony (kohl) زَرْنِيخ (zarnikh) Arsenic sulphide / a mineral (meaning to be provided later by ustadh) نُوْرَة (nurah) Limestone / calcium oxide دِبَاغَة (dibaghat) Tanning (of animal skin) أُمَّهَات الْمُؤْمِنِين (Ummahaat al-Mu'mineen) Mothers of the Believers (wives of the Prophet ﷺ) مُفْتَى بِه (muftaa bihi) The position adopted for fatwa

docs.title: Su'r of Halal Animals and Humans
docs.text:
• Ruling: Pure (tahir); permissible to use for wudu and ghusl.
  • Dalil: Hadith of the Prophet ﷺ sharing his leftover water with the Sahabah.
  • Scope: No restriction on whether the human is Muslim or non-Muslim, male or female, in a state of janabah or hayd.
  • Aisha (RA) narrated she gave her leftover water to the Prophet ﷺ while she was in a state of janabah and he drank from the same vessel.
  • Thumamah ibn Uthal (RA) was kept in Masjid al-Nabawi before accepting Islam — proof that a kafir is not physically najis in his person.
  • Abu Hurayrah (RA) hadith: he was in janabah and walked with the Prophet ﷺ — no prohibition issued.
  • Hadith in Bayhaqi confirms no restriction on the person's state.

docs.title: Su'r of Dogs and Swine
docs.text:
• Ruling: Najis (impure); forbidden for use in purification. Agreed upon by all four madhabs.
  • Dalil: Hadith in Bukhari — a vessel from which a dog has drunk must be washed.
  • Ahnaf: 3 washings suffice.
  • Imam al-Shafi'i: 7 washings required.
  • Swine is najis in all circumstances.

docs.title: Su'r of Wild Hunting Animals (other than dogs/swine)
docs.text:
• Ahnaf ruling: Najis — the saliva of wild hunting animals contaminates the water.
  • Imam al-Shafi'i's ruling: Pure — he uses as dalil a hadith where the Prophet ﷺ was asked about a pond where wild animals drank and he replied: "What they drank is in their stomachs; what remains is for us."
  • Key distinction: Ahnaf hold that these animals' mouths carry impurity from hunting/eating carrion, making their saliva najis.

docs.title: Su'r of Domestic/Free-Roaming Animals (Cat, Chicken, House Mouse, Snake)
docs.text:
• Ruling (Ahnaf): Makruh — disliked but not forbidden; wudu performed with it is valid.
  • Dalil: Hadith in Dar al-Qutni — the Prophet ﷺ placed water before a cat to drink, then performed wudu from the leftover water.
  • Reason cats are not classified with wild animals: They are so thoroughly domesticated that excluding them from households is practically impossible.
  • Imam al-Shafi'i and Imam Abu Yusuf (Ahnaf): Consider cat's su'r pure — no issue with using it.

docs.title: Su'r of Donkeys and Mules
docs.text:
• Ruling (Ahnaf): Mashkuk (doubtful).
  • Reason for doubt: Donkey meat was initially permissible, then prohibited (around the time of Fatih Makkah or Khaybar). Ikhtilaf existed among Sahabah: Ibn Umar (RA) held it impermissible; Ibn Abbas (RA) held it pure.
  • Practical ruling: If no other water is available, perform both wudu and tayammum (in any order), then proceed with salah.
  • Imam al-Shafi'i: Su'r of donkey is fully pure.
  • Note: Horse su'r falls into the halal-meat category (pure) and is not in this doubtful group.

docs.title: Hunting Dogs Used in Halal Hunting
docs.text: • The general ruling on dogs' su'r being najis does not automatically render the hunted animal haram — this topic has its own chapter (Kitab al-Sayd) with specific conditions.

docs.title: Five Categories of Su'r (Summary)
docs.text: Category Animals Ruling Agreement 1 Humans + all halal-meat animals Pure (tahir) Muttafaq 'alayh (all 4 madhabs) 2 Dogs + swine Najis (impure) Muttafaq 'alayh (all 4 madhabs) 3 Wild hunting animals (other than dog/swine) Najis (Ahnaf) / Pure (Shafi'i) Ikhtilafi masala 4 Domestic free-roaming animals (cat, chicken, house animals) Makruh Ahnaf position; Shafi'i & Abu Yusuf say pure 5 Donkeys and mules Mashkuk (doubtful) Ikhtilafi masala

docs.title: Conditions Permitting Tayammum
docs.text:
1. Traveling and water is unavailable (no water within approximately one mile).
  2. Water is present but one fears sickness will worsen if used.
  3. Healthy person fears cold water will cause fatal illness.
  4. Time of salah is imminent and reaching water would cause the prayer time to lapse.

docs.title: Valid Substances for Tayammum
docs.text:
• Imam Abu Hanifa and Imam Muhammad: Anything from the genus of earth — soil, sand, stone (hajar), limestone (nurah), antimony (kuhl), zarnikh, and similar minerals.
  • Imam Abu Yusuf: Only soil or sand; solid rock with no dust does not suffice.
  • Muftaa bihi (operative fatwa): Imam Abu Hanifa's opinion — rock and stone are valid.
  • Practical note: Even dust collected on shelves may suffice if enough is present to wipe the face and hands.
  • The earth must be clean (free of najasah).

docs.title: Arkan (Obligatory Elements) of Tayammum — 2
docs.text:
1. Striking the hands on the earth.
  2. Wiping the face and both hands (up to and including the elbows).

docs.title: Six Conditions (Shurut) of Tayammum
docs.text:
1. Making niyyah (intention) — fard in tayammum (unlike wudu where it is only mustahab).
  2. Wiping the face and hands completely with dust.
  3. Minimum three fingers must be used.
  4. The substance must be from the genus of earth.
  5. The earth must be free of najasah.
  6. Water must be either unavailable or harmful to use.

docs.title: Eight Sunnahs of Tayammum
docs.text:
1. Saying Bismillah before starting.
  2. Striking with the inner (soft) portion of the palms.
  3. Striking with fingers spread apart and palms laid firmly on the surface.
  4. Moving the hands slightly forward after striking.
  5. Drawing the hands back to their original position.
  6. Shaking off excess dust by clapping the hands lightly.
  7. Observing Tarteeb: face first, then right hand, then left hand.
  8. Continuity — not allowing too long a pause between wiping the face and wiping the hands.

docs.title: What Breaks Tayammum
docs.text:
Everything that breaks wudu also breaks tayammum: - Anything exiting from the sabilaan (front/back passages). - Blood, pus, or any discharge exiting through the skin. - Vomiting (when mouthful). - Laughing aloud during salah. - Loss of consciousness or sleep. - Insanity.

Additional breaker specific to tayammum: - Sighting water one is able to use — tayammum is immediately invalidated. If water is seen but is inaccessible (e.g., at the bottom of a dangerous ravine, surrounded by crocodiles, or a full day's journey away), the tayammum remains intact.

docs.title: Tayammum: Salah Already Performed vs. Mid-Salah
docs.text: Scenario Ruling Sees water during salah Both tayammum and salah are invalidated; must redo both. Sees water after completing salah (after salam) Tayammum invalidated; wudu must be renewed — but the completed salah stands and need not be repeated.

docs.title: Scholarly Opinions
docs.text: Issue Ahnaf (Abu Hanifa + Muhammad) Imam Abu Yusuf Imam al-Shafi'i Su'r of wild hunting animals Najis Najis Pure Su'r of cat Makruh Pure Pure Su'r of donkey Mashkuk (doubtful) — Pure Valid substances for tayammum All earth-genus substances (stone, sand, minerals) Only soil or sand — Vessel washed after dog drinks 3 times — 7 times Niyyah in wudu Mustahab — Fard (obligatory) Niyyah in tayammum Fard Fard Fard

docs.title: Tayammum for Janabah vs. Hadath
docs.text: • Ahnaf ruling: The method of tayammum is identical regardless of whether one is purifying from major (janabah) or minor (hadath) impurity — two strikes, wipe face then hands. The body is not wiped entirely.

docs.title: Tayammum as a Divine Gift to This Ummah
docs.text:
• Tayammum is exclusive to the Ummah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — no previous nation was given this concession.
  • Hadith (Bukhari): "The entire earth has been made a masjid for me and a means of purification." — The earth serves a dual function: a place of prayer and an instrument of purification.

docs.title: Historical Origin of Tayammum
docs.text:
• The ayah of tayammum (Surah al-Ma'idah) was revealed during Ghazwah Zat al-Riqa' (dominant opinion; Imam al-Kasani, author of Bada'i' al-Sana'i, supports this).
  • Imam al-Bukhari placed it after Ghazwah Khaybar.
  • The incident: Aisha (RA)'s necklace (belonging to Asma) went missing; Sahabah stayed searching; water ran out by Fajr time — prompting the revelation.
  • The Sahabi Usaid ibn Hudayr (RA) said to Aisha (RA) after the revelation: "May Allah have mercy on you — never were you beset with a difficulty but Allah made a way out for you and for the Muslims."

docs.title: The Role of Aisha (RA) in Fiqh
docs.text:
• Numerous masail in Islamic law were clarified through Aisha (RA). A dedicated book exists compiling the fiqhi masail she derived and resolved.
  • Even senior Sahabah such as Abu Bakr and Uthman (RA) would refer masail to her when they could not reach a conclusion.
  • She is considered a muftia among the Sahabah, and her verdicts carried the highest authority.

docs.title: Practical Scenarios for Modern Travelers
docs.text:
• If the end of salah time is near and the next rest stop is too far to make wudu and still pray on time — tayammum is valid.
  • Dust on shelves or surfaces can suffice for tayammum if there is enough to visibly cover the face and hands; no exact quantity is stipulated.
  • Using rock or stone (as per Imam Abu Hanifa — the operative fatwa) is valid even if no loose soil is present.
  • For mashkuk (doubtful) water like donkey/mule su'r: perform both wudu and tayammum, then pray — order does not matter.

docs.title: Key Reference Works Mentioned
docs.text:
• Bada'i' al-Sana'i' (Imam al-Kasani) — primary Hanafi reference; cited in modern fatawa.
  • Dur al-Mukhtar / Radd al-Muhtar — later Hanafi fatawa compilation.
  • Al-Mabsut, Jami' al-Saghir, Jami' al-Kabir (Imam Muhammad al-Shaybani) — Zahir al-Riwayah: the six core books of Hanafi fiqh.
  • Modern fatawa always trace back through these works to the Zahir al-Riwayah as ultimate authority.
