docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This was the opening session of Nahw 201, covering the Muqaddimah (introduction) of Hidayat al-Nahw by its Musannif (author). The teacher began with motivational remarks about the importance of Nahw and Sarf as foundational sciences, then introduced the first Fasl (chapter) of the Muqaddimah: the definition and purpose of Nahw. The session also included Q&A about class preparation and an overview of what the book covers.

docs.title: Definition of Nahw (علم النحو)
docs.text:
From the text of Hidayat al-Nahw:

فَصِيعَةٌ: النَّحْوُ عِلْمٌ بِأُصُولٍ يُعْرَفُ بِهَا أَحْوَالُ أَوَاخِرِ الْكَلِمِ الثَّلَاثِ مِنْ حَيْثُ الْإِعْرَابِ وَالْبِنَاءِ وَكَيْفِيَّةُ تَرْكِيبِ بَعْضِهَا مَعَ بَعْضٍ

Translation: Nahw is a science of foundational principles (usool/qawanin — grammatical rules) by which one knows: 1. The ahwal (states/conditions) of the endings (awakhir) of the three parts of speech 2. From the standpoint of i'rab and bina 3. And how words are constructed together (kayfiyyat al-tarkib)

Key point: Nahw deals specifically with the last letter (harf akhir) of a word — not the first or middle letters. For example, in جَاءَ زَيْدٌ, Nahw determines what haraka goes on the Daal of Zaid.

docs.title: The Three Parts of Speech (الكلم الثلاث)
docs.text:
1. الاسم (Ism) — Noun
  2. الفعل (Fi'l) — Verb
  3. الحرف (Harf) — Particle/Preposition

Nahw governs the endings of all three.

docs.title: Purpose of Nahw (الغرض منه)
docs.text:
وَالْغَرَضُ مِنْهُ صِيَانَةُ الذِّهْنِ عَنِ الْخَطَإِ اللَّفْظِيِّ

Translation: The purpose of Nahw is to protect the mind from verbal/linguistic error.

Important clarification from the teacher: The Musannif said "mind" (ذهن/zihan), not tongue. This is because errors originate in the mind before they reach the tongue. If the mind is protected from error, the tongue follows correctly.

Practical example: - Without Nahw, one might say: جَاءَ زَيْدًا / جَاءَ زَيْدٍ / جَاءَ زَيْد (incorrect) - With Nahw, one says confidently: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ (correct — Zaid is the Fa'il, so Marfu', hence Dhamma)

docs.title: Mu'rab vs. Mabni — Introductory Distinction
docs.text:
This was introduced through Q&A at the end of the session:

Mabni (مبني): A word whose ending does not change regardless of its position in a sentence.

  • Example: هَذَا (hatha — this)
  • جَاءَ هَذَا (Hatha came)
  • رَأَيْتُ هَذَا (I saw Hatha)
  • مَرَرْتُ بِهَذَا (I passed by Hatha)
  • → The word هَذَا remains unchanged in all three cases.

Mu'rab (معرب): A word whose ending changes according to its grammatical role.

  • Example: زَيْد
  • جَاءَ زَيْدٌ (Zaidun — Marfu', Dhamma — subject)
  • رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا (Zaidan — Mansub, Fathah — object)
  • مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ (Zaidin — Majrur, Kasra — after preposition)
  • → The ending of Zaid changes in each case.

docs.title: I'rab — Primary vs. Secondary (Asl vs. Niyabi)
docs.text:
Briefly introduced; to be covered in detail later:

  • Primary (Asl) I'rab: The word takes the actual haraka — e.g., جَاءَ زَيْدٌ (Dhamma directly on Daal)
  • Secondary/Representative (Niyabi) I'rab: A letter represents the haraka instead of an actual haraka:
  • Waw (و) represents Dhamma (Raf')
  • Alif (ا) represents Fathah or sometimes Dhamma (Nasb/Raf')
  • Ya (ي) represents Kasra (Jarr/Nasb)

docs.title: Book Structure — Muqaddimah Overview
docs.text: The Muqaddimah of Hidayat al-Nahw has three Fusool (chapters): 1. Fasl al-Awwal: Definition and purpose of Nahw (covered this session) 2. Fasl al-Thani: Al-Kalima wal-Kalam (next session) 3. Fasl al-Thalith: (to be covered)

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning النَّحْو (Al-Nahw) Arabic grammar science — governs word endings الصَّرْف (Al-Sarf) Arabic morphology — governs internal word structure الْبَلَاغَة (Al-Balagha) Arabic rhetoric عُلُوم شَرْعِيَّة (Uloom Shar'iyya) Religious sciences (Tafsir, Hadith, Fiqh) عُلُوم آلِيَّة (Uloom Aliyya) Instrumental sciences (Nahw, Sarf, Balagha — tools for understanding) الْمُقَدِّمَة (Al-Muqaddimah) Foreword/introduction of a book الْفَصْل (Al-Fasl) / فُصُول (Fusool) Chapter(s) الْمُصَنِّف (Al-Musannif) Author of the book مُخْتَصَر (Mukhtasar) Concise/brief جَامِعَة (Jami'a) Comprehensive أُصُول (Usool) Principles/foundations; here: grammatical rules قَوَانِين (Qawanin) Laws/rules (synonym for Usool in this context) أَحْوَال (Ahwal) States/conditions أَوَاخِر (Awakhir) Endings (of words) الْكَلِم الثَّلَاث (Al-Kalim al-Thalath) The three parts of speech (Ism, Fi'l, Harf) الِاسْم (Al-Ism) Noun الْفِعْل (Al-Fi'l) Verb الْحَرْف (Al-Harf) Particle/preposition الْإِعْرَاب (Al-I'rab) Inflection — the changing of word endings الْبِنَاء (Al-Bina) Indeclinability — fixed endings that do not change التَّرْكِيب (Al-Tarkib) Construction/composition of sentences الْغَرَض (Al-Gharad) Purpose/aim صِيَانَة (Siyāna) Protection/preservation الذِّهْن (Al-Zihan) The mind/intellect الْخَطَأ اللَّفْظِيّ (Al-Khata al-Lafzi) Verbal/linguistic error مَبْنِي (Mabni) Indeclinable — word with fixed, unchanging ending مُعْرَب (Mu'rab) Declinable — word whose ending changes with grammatical role مَرْفُوع (Marfu') Nominative case — typically Dhamma (ـُ) مَنْصُوب (Mansub) Accusative case — typically Fathah (ـَ) مَجْرُور (Majrur) Genitive case — typically Kasra (ـِ) مَجْزُوم (Majzum) Jussive — typically Sukoon (ـْ), applies to verbs حَرَكَة (Haraka) / حَرَكَات (Harakat) Vowel diacritic(s) الضَّمَّة (Al-Dhamma) The "u" vowel (ـُ) الْفَتْحَة (Al-Fathah) The "a" vowel (ـَ) الْكَسْرَة (Al-Kasra) The "i" vowel (ـِ) السُّكُون (Al-Sukoon) Absence of vowel (ـْ) هَذَا (Hatha) This (demonstrative pronoun — example of Mabni) الْمُطَالَعَة (Al-Mutala'a) Pre-class preparation/reading الْمُذَاكَرَة / التَّكْرَار (Al-Mudhakara / Al-Takrar) Revision/review after class شُرُوحَات (Shuruhaat) Explanatory commentaries on texts

docs.title: Example 1: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ
docs.text: Word I'rab Reason جَاءَ (Ja'a) Fi'l Madi, Mabni 'ala al-Fathah Verb — ends in Fathah, fixed زَيْدٌ (Zaidun) Ism, Fa'il, Marfu', 'alamatuhu al-Dhamma Subject of the verb; Mu'rab, takes Dhamma

docs.title: Example 2: رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا
docs.text: Word I'rab Reason رَأَيْتُ (Ra'aytu) Fi'l Madi + Fa'il (Tu) Verb with attached subject pronoun زَيْدًا (Zaidan) Ism, Maf'ul bih, Mansub, 'alamatuhu al-Fathah Direct object; takes Fathah

docs.title: Example 3: مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ
docs.text: Word I'rab Reason مَرَرْتُ (Marartu) Fi'l Madi + Fa'il Verb with attached subject بِ (Bi) Harf Jarr Preposition زَيْدٍ (Zaidin) Ism, Majrur by Bi, 'alamatuhu al-Kasra Governed by preposition; takes Kasra

docs.title: Example 4: Mabni — هَذَا across positions
docs.text:
Sentence Role of هَذَا Ending جَاءَ هَذَا Subject (Fa'il) هَذَا — unchanged رَأَيْتُ هَذَا Object (Maf'ul bih) هَذَا — unchanged مَرَرْتُ بِهَذَا Majrur (after preposition) هَذَا — unchanged

Conclusion: هَذَا is Mabni — its ending never changes regardless of grammatical role.

docs.title: Practice Examples
docs.text:
1. Identify Mabni vs. Mu'rab: Take the word زَيْد and place it in three sentences (as subject, object, and after a preposition). Note how the ending changes each time — this confirms it is Mu'rab.

  2. Identify the ending: In the sentence جَاءَ زَيْدٌ, point to the exact letter Nahw governs — the Daal of Zaid (the last letter). Ask: what haraka is on it, and why?

  3. Prepare pages 8–10 of Hidayat al-Nahw (upper portion of p.10 only; the lower portion is explanatory notes for reference): try to translate and assign proper I'rab before the next class.

  4. Self-test confidence: Read any Arabic text without vowel markings (Arabic without harakat). Assign the harakat yourself based on I'rab. This builds the confidence the teacher described — being unable to be "shaken" by a questioner.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Nahw and Sarf are Uloom Aliyya — instrumental sciences that are prerequisites for mastering Tafsir, Hadith, and Fiqh. Scholars equate their reward with studying the major Islamic sciences because without them, those sciences cannot be understood properly.

  2. Hidayat al-Nahw is both Mukhtasar (concise) and Jami'a (comprehensive) — this dual quality is rare and is why the book is widely used in madrasas, particularly in South Asia.

  3. The definition of Nahw encompasses three things: knowing the states of word endings, distinguishing Mu'rab from Mabni, and knowing how to construct words together in sentences.

  4. The purpose of Nahw is to protect the mind (and consequently the tongue) from committing errors in Arabic expression — enabling confident, grounded I'rab rather than coincidental correctness.

  5. Mabni vs. Mu'rab is the central axis of Nahw: Mabni words have fixed endings regardless of position; Mu'rab words change their endings based on their grammatical role (Raf', Nasb, Jarr, Jazm).

  6. Three habits are mandatory for this course:

  7. Mutala'a — prepare (translate + attempt I'rab) before class; prepare as if you will teach it
  8. Presence in class — attend live; do not let recordings pile up

  9. Takrar/Mudhakara — revise what was taught before the next session

  10. Dependency on Shuruhaat is a weakness — the goal is to reach a level where Arabic texts can be read and understood directly, without relying on Urdu or Arabic commentaries for basic translation.

  11. Next session covers: Al-Kalima wal-Kalam (Fasl al-Thani of the Muqaddimah) — pages 8–10 of Hidayat al-Nahw (upper portion).

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session introduced the foundational concepts of Nahw (Arabic grammar) by covering the definitions of Kalima and Kalam — the two core subjects of the discipline. The ustadh walked through the Musannif's definitions of the three types of Kalima (Ism, Fi'l, Harf) and then focused in depth on Ism: its definition and all its distinguishing Alamat (signs/markers). Fi'l and Harf definitions were introduced but their Alamat will be covered in the next session.

docs.title: 1. Kalima vs. Kalam
docs.text:
• Kalima (كَلِمَة) — a single word. It is a lafz (utterance) designed to denote a specific, singular meaning.
  • Kalam (كَلَام) — two or more words that come together in proper order to form a meaningful sentence/phrase.
  • Example: Zaidun alone = Kalima. Zaidun maridun (Zaid is sick) = Kalam.
  • Kalam is murakkab (compound); Kalima is mufrad (single).
  • The entire discipline of Nahw revolves around rules pertaining to these two things.

docs.title: 2. The Three Types of Kalima
docs.text:
Every single word (Kalima) falls into one of three categories:

Type Arabic Characteristic Ism اِسْم Denotes meaning on its own; no tense Fi'l فِعْل Denotes meaning on its own; tense is embedded Harf حَرْف Does NOT denote meaning on its own; requires support

docs.title: 3. Definition of Harf (حَرْف)
docs.text:
• لِأَنَّهَا إِمَّا أَلَّا تَدُلَّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا وَهُوَ الْحَرْفُ
  • Harf is that which does not convey its meaning on its own — it always requires an accompanying word.
  • Example: Ilā (إِلَى) alone is meaningless. Ilā al-masjid conveys meaning.

docs.title: 4. Definition of Fi'l (فِعْل)
docs.text:
• أَوْ تَدُلَّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا وَيَقْتَرِنُ مَعْنَاهَا بِأَحَدِ الْأَزْمِنَةِ الثَّلَاثَةِ وَهُوَ الْفِعْلُ
  • Fi'l denotes meaning on its own AND carries one of the three tenses embedded within it.
  • Three tenses: Māḍī (past) | Ḥāl (present) | Istiqbāl (future)
  • Examples: Dhahaba (ذَهَبَ) = past | Yadhabu (يَذْهَبُ) = present/future

docs.title: 5. Definition of Ism (اِسْم)
docs.text:
• فَحَدُّ الِاسْمِ أَنَّهُ كَلِمَةٌ تَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا غَيْرُ مُقْتَرِنٍ بِأَحَدِ الْأَزْمِنَةِ الثَّلَاثَةِ
  • Ism is a word that denotes meaning on its own but is not associated with any of the three tenses (past, present, future).
  • It evokes an image or concept in the mind without implying when.
  • Examples: Al-kitāb (book), Al-masjid (mosque), Al-madrasah (school), Al-walad (boy), Al-sayyāra (car)

docs.title: 6. Alamat of Ism (Signs that Identify a Noun)
docs.text:
These are markers — if any one of them is present on a word, it is confirmed to be an Ism. Fi'l and Harf never carry these markers.

# Alamah (Sign) Explanation Example 1 Al-Ikhbār (الإِخْبَار) Can have information given about it (mubtada) OR can itself be information (khabar) Zaidun qā'imun — Zaid = mubtada; qā'im = khabar 2 Iḍāfah (الإِضَافَة) Can serve as Muḍāf (the first word in a possessive construction) Only Ism can be Muḍāf 3 Alif-Lām (ال) The definite article attaches only to Ism Al-rajul, al-kitāb 4 Jarr / Kasra (الجَرّ) Can take kasra (the i-vowel) due to a preposition or iḍāfah Fi'l never takes kasra or tanwīn 5 Tanwīn (التَّنْوِين) The nunation suffix (-un, -an, -in) appears only on Ism Sayyāratun, kitābun 6 Taṣniyah (التَّثْنِيَة) Can be made dual Kitābāni (two books) 7 Jamʿ (الجَمْع) Can be made plural Kutub (books) 8 Ṣifah / Naʿt (الصِّفَة) Can function as or receive an adjective Only Ism can be described 9 Taṣghīr (التَّصْغِير) Can be diminutivized (made to mean "small X") Waladun → Wulaid (little boy); Rajulun → Rujail (small man) 10 Nidāʾ (النِّدَاء) Can be called upon with Yā (يَا) Yā Zaid, Yā Bakr — Yā never precedes Fi'l

Key point: Fi'l never carries jarr, kasra, or tanwīn. You will never read dhahabun, dhahaban, or dhahabin. This alone can confirm a word is Ism.

docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning كَلِمَة (Kalima) A single word كَلَام (Kalām) A meaningful sentence/phrase (two or more words) اِسْم (Ism) Noun فِعْل (Fiʿl) Verb حَرْف (Ḥarf) Particle لَفْظ (Lafẓ) Utterance; a spoken/written form مَعْنَى (Maʿnā) Meaning مُفْرَد (Mufrad) Single; uncompounded مُرَكَّب (Murakkab) Compound; composed of parts مَوْضُوعُهُ (Mawḍūʿuhu) Its subject matter حَدّ / تَعْرِيف (Ḥadd / Taʿrīf) Definition عَلَامَة / أَلَامَات (ʿAlāmah / ʿAlāmāt) Sign(s)/marker(s) for identification مَاضِي (Māḍī) Past tense حَال (Ḥāl) Present tense اِسْتِقْبَال (Istiqbāl) Future tense إِضَافَة (Iḍāfah) Possessive construction (genitive annexation) مُضَاف (Muḍāf) The first word in an iḍāfah تَنْوِين (Tanwīn) Nunation (-un, -an, -in endings) تَثْنِيَة (Taṣniyah) Dual form جَمْع (Jamʿ) Plural صِفَة / نَعْت (Ṣifah / Naʿt) Adjective/descriptive word تَصْغِير (Taṣghīr) Diminutive form ("small/little X") نِدَاء (Nidāʾ) Vocative call (using Yā) مُبْتَدَأ (Mubtadaʾ) Subject (the one information is given about) خَبَر (Khabar) Predicate (the information itself) اِنْحِصَار (Inḥiṣār) Restriction; confinement to specific categories خَوَاصّ (Khawāṣṣ) Characteristics; distinguishing properties

docs.title: Example 1: Kalima vs. Kalam
docs.text:
• Zaidun — Kalima (single word, one unit)
  • Zaidun maridun — Kalām (complete sentence: "Zaid is sick")
  • Zaidun = Mubtadaʾ (subject), marfūʿ, sign: ḍammah
  • Maridun = Khabar (predicate), marfūʿ, sign: ḍammah

docs.title: Example 2: Identifying Ism via Alif-Lām
docs.text: • Al-qiṭār (القِطَار) — has Alif-Lām → confirmed Ism (no further analysis needed)

docs.title: Example 3: Identifying Ism via Kasra and Tanwīn
docs.text:
• Sayyāratun (سَيَّارَةٌ) — has tanwīn → confirmed Ism
  • Sayyāratin (سَيَّارَةٍ) — has kasra → confirmed Ism (Fi'l never takes kasra)

docs.title: Example 4: Ikhbār (information about and with)
docs.text:
• Zaidun qāʾimun (زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ) — "Zaid is standing"
  • Information is given about Zaid → Zaid is Ism (mubtadaʾ)
  • Qāʾimun is the information itself → Qāʾim is also Ism (khabar)

docs.title: Example 5: Harf needing support
docs.text:
• Ilā alone — no meaning conveyed
  • Ilā al-masjid — "to the mosque" — meaning now conveyed with support

docs.title: Practice Examples
docs.text:
Identify whether each word is Ism, Fiʿl, or Ḥarf, and state the evidence:

  1. ذَهَبَ (Dhahaba) — Fiʿl (past tense embedded; conveys meaning alone)
  2. يَذْهَبُ (Yadhabu) — Fiʿl (present/future tense)
  3. إِلَى (Ilā) — Ḥarf (cannot convey meaning alone)
  4. الْكِتَابُ (Al-kitābu) — Ism (has Alif-Lām)
  5. وَلَدٌ (Waladun) — Ism (has tanwīn)
  6. وُلَيْد (Wulaid) — Ism (is a taṣghīr form; only Ism can be diminutivized)
  7. كِتَابَيْنِ (Kitābaini) — Ism (dual form / taṣniyah)
  8. كُتُب (Kutub) — Ism (jamʿ / plural)
  9. يَا زَيْد (Yā Zaid) — Yā is Ḥarf Nidāʾ; Zaid is Ism (Yā only precedes Ism)
  10. سَيَّارَةٍ (Sayyāratin) — Ism (kasra; Fi'l never takes kasra)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Nahw's core subject matter is Kalima and Kalām — every grammatical rule connects back to either a single word or a compound sentence.

  2. Three and only three types of Kalima exist: Ism (noun), Fiʿl (verb), Ḥarf (particle). Every Arabic word belongs to one of these.

  3. The defining difference between Ism and Fiʿl is tense — both convey meaning independently, but Fiʿl carries tense (past/present/future) while Ism does not.

  4. Ḥarf is structurally dependent — it cannot convey meaning without attaching to another word.

  5. Alamāt are your shortcut — you do not need to know a word's dictionary meaning to classify it. Seeing Alif-Lām, tanwīn, kasra, taṣniyah, jamʿ, taṣghīr, or Yā before a word instantly confirms it is Ism. No analysis required.

  6. Fi'l never takes jarr, kasra, or tanwīn — this is an absolute rule. If any of these appear on a word, it is definitively Ism.

  7. Yā (Ḥarf Nidāʾ) only precedes Ism — if you see Yā, the next word is always Ism.

  8. Digestion over speed — the ustadh emphasized reviewing and memorizing these alamāt thoroughly before advancing, as everything in Nahw builds on this foundation.

  9. Coming next session: Definition and Alamāt of Fiʿl, and definition and Alamāt of Ḥarf. Students should also be prepared to read the Arabic text aloud for checking.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered the definitions and distinguishing markers (alamat) of fi'l (verb) and harf (particle), completing the chapter on the three parts of speech (kalima). The session concluded with an introduction to kalam (meaningful sentence), covering the concepts of isnad, musnad, and musnad ilayh, and the distinction between jumlah ismiyyah and jumlah fi'liyyah.

docs.title: 1. Definition of Fi'l (الفعل)
docs.text:
الفعل كلمة تدل على معنى في نفسها

A fi'l is a word that: 1. Denotes a meaning on its own, AND 2. Has a tense (زمان) associated with it

The three tenses of fi'l: - ماضي (past) — e.g. ضَرَبَ - مضارع (present/future) — e.g. يَضْرِبُ - أمر (command) — e.g. اضْرِبْ

docs.title: 2. Alamat (Distinguishing Markers) of Fi'l
docs.text:
A. أن يصح الإخبار به لا عنه A fi'l can only be used as ikhbar bihi (giving information WITH it), never ikhbar anhu (giving information ABOUT it). - Ism can be both: e.g. زَيْدٌ نَائِمٌ (information is given about Zaid) - Fi'l is always information itself: e.g. ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ — here ضَرَبَ conveys the information, it is not what information is being given about

B. دخول قد قد enters only upon fi'l, never upon ism. - قَدْ ذَهَبَ — confirms the word is fi'l - Quranic example: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى (Al-A'la) — قد here adds taqid (emphasis/certainty) - On mudari': قد gives the meaning of sometimes/occasionally (e.g. "Do you visit Hamid every day?" → "Sometimes.")

C. دخول السين وسوف - سَيَعْلَمُ — سين upon a word confirms it is fi'l (future) - سَوْفَ يَعْلَمُ — same function

D. الجزم - Jazm (sukun or deletion of nun) comes only upon fi'l - e.g. لَمْ يَذْهَبْ — jazm confirms the word is fi'l

E. التصريف إلى الماضي والمضارع - The ability to change a word between madhi and mudari' forms is exclusive to fi'l - Ism does not undergo this type of change

F. كونه أمرًا أو نهيًا - Only fi'l becomes amr (command) or nahi (prohibition) - e.g. كُلْ، اذْخُلْ، اسْجُدْ، لَا تَسْجُدْ، لَا تَأْكُلْ

G. اتصال الضمائر البارزة المرفوعة - Attached subject pronouns (تاء المتكلم، تاء المخاطب، etc.) connect only to fi'l - e.g. ضَرَبْتَ، ضَرَبْتُ، ضَرَبْتِ، أَكَلْتَ، أَكَلْتُ

H. تاء التأنيث الساكنة - The silent feminine ta (ـَتْ) attaches only to fi'l - e.g. ضَرَبَتْ، أَكَلَتْ

I. نون التوكيد - Nun of emphasis attaches only to fi'l, adding taqid - Two types: - ثقيلة (heavy/mushaddad): لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ - خفيفة (light): لَيَذْهَبَنْ - Quranic example: لَئِن شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ (Ibrahim:7) — the shadda nun adds certainty to Allah's promise

docs.title: 3. Definition of Harf (الحرف)
docs.text:
الحرف كلمة لا تدل على معنى في نفسها بل تدل على معنى في غيرها

A harf is a word that does not denote a meaning on its own; it only conveys meaning through another word. - e.g. مِن — its meaning is ibtida' (starting point), but this meaning is only realized when the starting point is mentioned: مِنَ البَصْرَةِ

Alamat of Harf: - لا يصح الإخبار عنه ولا به — you cannot give information about it, nor with it - لا يقبل علامات الأسماء — does not accept the markers of ism - لا يقبل علامات الفعل — does not accept the markers of fi'l

Why is it called harf? Harf means tarf (edge/corner) — it is at the periphery of kalam, not a primary pillar. It is not maqsood bidhatihi (independently intended); it supports and connects, but ism and fi'l are the pillars.

Roles of Harf in Arabic (فوائده): 1. الربط بين الاسمين — connecting two nouns: e.g. زَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ (fi connects Zaid and the house) 2. الربط بين الفعلين — connecting two verbs: e.g. with عَطْف particles 3. الربط بين الجملتين — connecting two sentences: e.g. إِن جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ أَكْرَمْتُهُ — without إِن, these are two disconnected statements; with إِن, they form one conditional meaning

docs.title: 4. Definition and Nature of Kalam (الكلام)
docs.text:
Kalam is a meaningful utterance that contains isnad — the attribution of something (musnad) toward someone or something (musnad ilayh).

الإسناد: نسبة يُحدث الكلمتين إلى الأخرى — the connection established between two words whereby one is attributed to the other

Key principle: Simply placing two words together does not form kalam. What makes kalam is isnad.

Musnad (المسند): That which is attributed — the predicate/verb (the information being conveyed)

Musnad Ilayh (المسند إليه): That toward which something is attributed — the subject (the one being spoken about)

Examples: | Sentence | Musnad | Musnad Ilayh | |---|---|---| | ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ | ضَرَبَ | زَيْدٌ | | أَكَلَتْ فَاطِمَةُ | أَكَلَتْ | فَاطِمَةُ | | قَرَأَ حَامِدٌ | قَرَأَ | حَامِدٌ | | زَيْدٌ جَالِسٌ | جَالِسٌ | زَيْدٌ |

Alamat that isnad is present: The listener (mukhatab) receives a complete message (fa'idah tammah) and the speaker's silence afterward is valid (yasihhu as-sukut alayha). If the listener is still waiting for more information, isnad is incomplete.

Counter-example: زَيْدٌ حَامِدٌ — if the speaker goes silent, the listener waits: what about them? No musnad is established → not valid kalam until a khabar is added: زَيْدٌ حَامِدٌ نَائِمٌ.

docs.title: 5. Types of Jumlah (الجملة)
docs.text:
Kalam (meaningful sentence) forms in two ways:

Type Structure Example جملة اسمية ism + ism (musnad ilayh + musnad) زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ جملة فعلية fi'l + ism قَامَ زَيْدٌ

Musnad and musnad ilayh exist only within these two structures. Every valid kalam must contain both.

docs.title: 6. Objection and Response: يا زيد
docs.text:
Objection: "Ya Zayd" (يَا زَيْدُ) is a valid sentence but contains only a harf (يا) and an ism (زيد) — where is musnad and musnad ilayh?"

Answer: حرف النداء قائم مقام الفعل — the harf of nida' stands in the place of a fi'l. يَا زَيْدُ in meaning is: أَدْعُو زَيْدًا or أَطْلُبُ زَيْدًا ("I am calling Zaid" / "I am seeking Zaid"). So by meaning, يَا is a fi'l. The rule is not broken — one fi'l (in meaning) + one ism = valid kalam.

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning الفعل Verb / fi'l (one of the three parts of speech) الاسم Noun / ism الحرف Particle / harf الماضي Past tense verb المضارع Present/future tense verb الأمر Command form (imperative) النهي Prohibition الإخبار به Giving information WITH a word (predicate role) الإخبار عنه Giving information ABOUT a word (subject role) قد Particle of certainty/sometimes (enters fi'l only) تقيد Emphasis, certainty السين / سوف Future tense particles (enter fi'l only) الجزم Jussive state (sukun/deletion) — exclusive to fi'l التصريف Morphological change / conjugation تاء التأنيث الساكنة Silent feminine ta (ـَتْ) — marker of fi'l نون التوكيد الثقيلة Heavy emphatic nun (نَّ) نون التوكيد الخفيفة Light emphatic nun (نْ) الضمائر البارزة المرفوعة Explicit nominative attached pronouns الإسناد Attribution — the link between musnad and musnad ilayh المسند Predicate — that which is attributed المسند إليه Subject — that toward which attribution is made الجملة الاسمية Nominal sentence (ism + ism) الجملة الفعلية Verbal sentence (fi'l + ism) الكلام Meaningful speech / sentence with complete benefit الفائدة التامة Complete benefit conveyed to the listener يصح السكوت عليه The speaker's silence is valid after it حرف النداء Particle of calling/address (e.g. يا) قائم مقام الفعل Standing in place of a verb الابتداء Starting point (the core meaning of مِن) مقصود بذاته Independently intended / primary الخبر Predicate in nominal sentence المبتدأ Subject in nominal sentence

docs.title: I'rab (Sentence Analysis) Examples
docs.text:
1. ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ - ضَرَبَ: fi'l madi, musnad - زَيْدٌ: ism, fa'il (agent), musnad ilayh, marfu' with damm

2. زَيْدٌ جَالِسٌ - زَيْدٌ: ism, mubtada', musnad ilayh, marfu' - جَالِسٌ: khabar, musnad, marfu'

3. قَرَأَ حَامِدٌ - قَرَأَ: fi'l madi, musnad - حَامِدٌ: fa'il, musnad ilayh, marfu'

4. لَمْ يَذْهَبْ - لَمْ: harf jazm (nafi) - يَذْهَبْ: fi'l mudari' majzum — the jazm proves it is fi'l

5. أَكَلَتْ فَاطِمَةُ - أَكَلَتْ: fi'l madi — the ـَتْ (ta ta'nith sakina) confirms it is fi'l; musnad - فَاطِمَةُ: fa'il, musnad ilayh, marfu'

6. قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى (Al-A'la: 14) - قَدْ: harf taqid — confirms أَفْلَحَ is fi'l - أَفْلَحَ: fi'l madi, musnad - مَن: ism mawsul, musnad ilayh, fa'il

7. لَئِن شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ (Ibrahim: 7) - لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ: fi'l mudari' — the nun thaqilah (نَّ) confirms it is fi'l and adds taqid to Allah's promise of increase

8. زَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ - زَيْدٌ: mubtada', musnad ilayh - فِي: harf jar — connects zaid (ism) with the following ism - الدَّارِ: majrur by في — harf playing its role of connecting two nouns

docs.title: Practice Examples
docs.text:
Identifying fi'l by its alamat:

Word Alamat Present Conclusion قَدْ ذَهَبَ قد entered upon it Fi'l confirmed سَيَعْلَمُ سين entered upon it Fi'l confirmed لَمْ يَذْهَبْ Jazm present (sukun) Fi'l confirmed ضَرَبْتُ Damin mutakallim attached Fi'l confirmed ضَرَبَتْ Ta ta'nith sakinah attached Fi'l confirmed لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ Nun tawkid attached Fi'l confirmed

Distinguishing kalam from non-kalam:

Utterance Kalam? Reason زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ Yes Musnad (قائم) + musnad ilayh (زيد) present; silence is valid قَامَ زَيْدٌ Yes Fi'l (musnad) + ism fa'il (musnad ilayh); silence is valid زَيْدٌ حَامِدٌ Incomplete Listener waits — no clear khabar/musnad established without context الكِتَابُ الكَلَامُ No Two musnad ilayh, no musnad يَا زَيْدُ Yes يا = fi'l in meaning (أَدْعُو); zaid = maf'ul/musnad ilayh

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Fi'l is defined by two things: carrying meaning independently AND having an associated tense (madhi, mudari', amr).

  2. Nine alamat of fi'l were covered: ikhbar bihi (not anhu), acceptance of قد/سين/سوف, acceptance of jazm, tasrif between madhi and mudari', becoming amr/nahi, attachment of marfu' pronouns, attachment of ta ta'nith sakinah, and attachment of nun tawkid.

  3. Harf has no independent meaning — it only conveys meaning in relation to other words. It accepts neither the markers of ism nor the markers of fi'l. Despite this, it plays critical structural roles: connecting nouns, connecting verbs, and connecting sentences.

  4. Kalam requires isnad — merely placing words together is not enough. One element must be musnad (predicate) and one must be musnad ilayh (subject). Without this attribution-connection, there is no kalam.

  5. Two and only two structures produce valid kalam: jumlah ismiyyah (ism + ism) and jumlah fi'liyyah (fi'l + ism). Musnad and musnad ilayh are found exclusively in these two.

  6. Soundness of silence (يصح السكوت) is the practical test for kalam — if the listener is satisfied and not waiting for more, isnad is complete.

  7. Harf al-nida' (يا) stands in place of a fi'l — this resolves the apparent objection that يَا زَيْدُ violates the rule, since يا carries the meaning of أَدْعُو/أَطْلُبُ.

  8. The chapter on kalima (the three parts of speech) is now complete. The next session begins the detailed study of ism, which will continue for several months, followed by fi'l, then harf.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered the opening of Baab al-Awwal (the first chapter) on Ism al-Mu'rab from the text. The teacher introduced the definition of Ism al-Mu'rab, its three conditions, the definition and types of I'rab, and which parts of speech receive I'rab. The session concluded with a note that the nine categories of I'rab will be covered over the next two sessions.

docs.title: 1. Classification of Ism
docs.text: Ism (noun) is divided into two categories: - Mu'rab — its ending changes according to the governing factor (Aamil) - Mabni — its ending does not change; it is fixed

docs.title: 2. Definition of Ism al-Mu'rab
docs.text:
Huwa kullu ismin rukkiba ma'a ghairihi wa la yushbihu mabniyya al-asl

Every noun that is compounded with another word and does not resemble Mabniyya al-Asl.

docs.title: 3. Three Conditions for a Word to be Ism al-Mu'rab
docs.text:
# Condition Explanation 1 Must be an Ism Harf is permanently Mabni; Fil Madi and Fil Amr are permanently Mabni — so only Ism qualifies 2 Must be Murakab (compounded) It must appear in a sentence with another word (e.g., with a Fa'il or another noun) 3 Must not resemble Mabniyya al-Asl It must not have similarity to words that are Mabni by nature (i.e., Huruf al-Jar and Asma' al-Ishara)

Example of condition 2 failing: Zaid alone (isolated) — not Murakab, so it is Mabni in that state.

Example of condition 3 failing: Ha'ula'i — it is an Ism and it is Murakab, but it is Mushabih (similar) to Mabniyya al-Asl, so it is Mabni, not Mu'rab.

docs.title: 4. Mabniyya al-Asl — What It Is and Why Asma' al-Ishara Resemble It
docs.text:
Mabniyya al-Asl = that which is Mabni by birth/nature. These are the Huruf: إِلَى، عَلَى، مِن، فِي

Why Asma' al-Ishara are Mushabih to Mabniyya al-Asl: - Huruf al-Jar require another word to convey their meaning (e.g., fi al-dar, ila al-masjid) — they are dependent. - Similarly, Asma' al-Ishara require a Mushaar ilayhi (the thing being pointed at) to convey meaning. If you say ha'ula'i without any context or pointing, the listener does not know who is meant. Just as fi needs a word after it, ha'ula'i needs a physical or contextual gesture. - Because of this dependency/resemblance, all Asma' al-Ishara are Mabni, not Mu'rab.

Asma' al-Ishara (all Mabni):

| هَذَا | هَذِهِ | ذَلِكَ | تِلْكَ | هَؤُلَاءِ | أُولَئِكَ |

docs.title: 5. Hukm (Ruling) of Ism al-Mu'rab
docs.text:
Wa hukmahu an yakhtalifa akhiruhu bikhtilafi al-awamili ikhtilafan lafziyyan aw taqdirayyan

The ending of Ism al-Mu'rab changes as the Awamil (governing factors) change. That change is either:

  • Lafzi (لَفْظِي) — visible/audible; we can see and hear the change
  • Example: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ ← Dammah | رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا ← Fathah | مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ ← Kasrah
  • Taqdiri (تَقْدِيرِي) — hidden/invisible; the change exists grammatically but is not pronounced
  • Categories of Taqdiri I'rab will be covered in upcoming sessions

Lafzi I'rab is the default/original (asl); Taqdiri is the exception (approximately 10–15% of cases).

docs.title: 6. The Three Types of I'rab for Ism
docs.text:
Wa i'rabu al-ismi 'ala thalathati anwa'

  1. Rafa' (رَفْع)
  2. Nasb (نَصْب)
  3. Jarr (جَرّ)

Note: Ism does not have Jazm. Jazm is specific to Fil Mudhari'.

docs.title: 7. Aamil — The Governing Factor
docs.text:
Aamil = that which causes I'rab (Rafa', Nasb, or Jarr) in a word.

Sentence Aamil جَاءَ زَيْدٌ جَاءَ (caused Rafa') رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا رَأَيْتُ (caused Nasb) مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ الْبَاء (caused Jarr)

docs.title: 8. Mahallu al-I'rab — The Site of I'rab
docs.text:
Wa mahall al-i'rabi min al-ismi huwa al-harfu al-akhir

I'rab is located on the last letter of the word.

Example breakdown of جَاءَ زَيْدٌ: - Aamil: جَاءَ - Ism al-Mu'rab: زَيْدٌ - I'rab: الضَّمَّة (Dammah — indicating Rafa') - Mahallu al-I'rab: الدَّال (the Dal, the last letter of زَيْد)

docs.title: 9. Which Words Receive I'rab?
docs.text:
Only two categories in Arabic receive I'rab:

  1. Ism al-Mu'rab (with the exception of Ism that resembles Mabniyya al-Asl)
  2. Fil al-Mudhari' (present/future tense verb)

What does NOT receive I'rab (always Mabni): - Harf — never receives I'rab - Fil Madi (past tense verb) — always Mabni - Fil Amr (command verb) — always Mabni

docs.title: 10. Primary vs. Secondary I'rab Signs
docs.text:
Type Signs Analogy Primary (Asli) ضَمَّة، فَتْحَة، كَسْرَة President Secondary (Niyabi) وَاو، أَلِف، يَاء Vice President — steps in when primary is unavailable

The secondary signs (Waw, Alif, Ya) replace the primary signs in specific grammatical contexts (to be detailed in upcoming sessions on the nine categories of I'rab).

docs.title: 11. The Nine Categories of I'rab (Preview)
docs.text: The three I'rab types (Rafa', Nasb, Jarr) can each appear as either Lafzi or Taqdiri, and in some cases through secondary signs — giving rise to a total of nine categories. These will be covered in the next two sessions.

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning الِاسْمُ الْمُعْرَب A noun whose ending changes according to its grammatical position الِاسْمُ الْمَبْنِي A noun whose ending is fixed and never changes مُرَكَّب Compounded; placed together with another word in a sentence مَبْنِيُّ الْأَصْل That which is Mabni by nature/birth (originally Mabni) — i.e., Huruf مُشَابِه Resembling; similar to الْعَامِل The governing factor that causes I'rab in a word الْإِعْرَاب The grammatical inflection/change at the end of a Mu'rab word الرَّفْع Nominative state — marked by Dammah (or its representatives) النَّصْب Accusative state — marked by Fathah (or its representatives) الْجَرّ Genitive state — marked by Kasrah (or its representatives) لَفْظِي Visible/audible; a change that can be seen and heard تَقْدِيرِي Hidden/estimated; a change that exists grammatically but is not pronounced مَحَلُّ الْإِعْرَاب The site of I'rab; the last letter of the word أَسْمَاء الْإِشَارَة Demonstrative pronouns (هَذَا، ذَلِكَ، هَؤُلَاءِ، etc.) مُشَار إِلَيْه The thing being pointed at/referred to in an Ism Ishara construction الْحَرْف الْأَخِير The last letter (the locus of I'rab) الْفِعْل الْمُضَارِع Present/future tense verb — the only verb form that receives I'rab الْفِعْل الْمَاضِي Past tense verb — always Mabni فِعْل الْأَمْر Command verb — always Mabni أَوَامِل (ج. عَامِل) Plural of Aamil; the governing factors

docs.title: Example 1: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ
docs.text: Word Role I'rab Sign Mahallu al-I'rab جَاءَ Fil Madi / Aamil Mabni (no I'rab) — — زَيْدٌ Fa'il (Ism Mu'rab) Rafa' Dammah (ضَمَّة) الدَّال

docs.title: Example 2: رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا
docs.text: Word Role I'rab Sign Mahallu al-I'rab رَأَيْتُ Fil Madi / Aamil Mabni — — زَيْدًا Maf'ul bih (Ism Mu'rab) Nasb Fathah (فَتْحَة) الدَّال

docs.title: Example 3: مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ
docs.text: Word Role I'rab Sign Mahallu al-I'rab مَرَرْتُ Fil Madi / Aamil Mabni — — بِ Harf Jarr / Aamil Mabni — — زَيْدٍ Majrur (Ism Mu'rab) Jarr Kasrah (كَسْرَة) الدَّال

docs.title: Example 4: جَاءَ هَؤُلَاءِ (Mabni Example — Condition 3 fails)
docs.text: Word Is Ism? Is Murakab? Not Mushabih? Result هَؤُلَاءِ ✓ Yes ✓ Yes ✗ Fails (resembles Mabniyya al-Asl) Mabni — not Mu'rab

docs.title: Example 5: زَيْد (Isolated — Condition 2 fails)
docs.text: Word Is Ism? Is Murakab? Result زَيْد ✓ Yes ✗ No (alone, not in a sentence) Mabni — not Mu'rab

docs.title: Example 6: قَامَ زَيْدٌ (Teacher's analytical breakdown)
docs.text:
• Aamil: قَامَ
  • Mu'rab word: زَيْدٌ
  • I'rab: الرَّفْع (Rafa')
  • Mahallu al-I'rab: الدَّال

docs.title: Practice Examples
docs.text:
Apply the three conditions to determine if each word is Mu'rab or Mabni:

  1. تَعَلَّمَ زَيْدٌ — Is زَيْدٌ Mu'rab?

  2. Ism? ✓ | Murakab? ✓ | Not Mushabih to Mabniyya Asal? ✓ → Mu'rab, Marfu'

  3. عَلَّمْتُ زَيْدًا — Is زَيْدًا Mu'rab?

  4. Ism? ✓ | Murakab? ✓ | Not Mushabih? ✓ → Mu'rab, Mansub

  5. جَاءَ هَذَا — Is هَذَا Mu'rab?

  6. Ism? ✓ | Murakab? ✓ | Not Mushabih? ✗ (Ism Ishara resembles Mabniyya Asal) → Mabni

  7. أَسْلَمَ أُولَئِكَ — Is أُولَئِكَ Mu'rab?

  8. Ism? ✓ | Murakab? ✓ | Not Mushabih? ✗ → Mabni

  9. Identify Aamil and Mahallu al-I'rab in: مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ

  10. Aamil: الْبَاء | Mahallu al-I'rab: الدَّال (last letter of زَيْد)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Ism is either Mu'rab or Mabni. Mu'rab changes its ending; Mabni does not.

  2. Three conditions must all be met for an Ism to be Mu'rab: (1) it must be an Ism, (2) it must be Murakab, and (3) it must not resemble Mabniyya al-Asl (Huruf).

  3. Asma' al-Ishara are Mabni because they depend on a Mushaar ilayhi (context/gesture) to convey meaning — just as Huruf depend on a following word — making them Mushabih to Mabniyya al-Asl.

  4. Only two categories receive I'rab: Ism al-Mu'rab and Fil al-Mudhari'. All Huruf, Fil Madi, and Fil Amr are permanently Mabni.

  5. I'rab always resides on the last letter (Mahallu al-I'rab = Harf al-Akhir).

  6. I'rab is either Lafzi (visible) or Taqdiri (hidden). Lafzi is the default; Taqdiri cases will be studied in coming sessions.

  7. Primary I'rab signs are Dammah/Fathah/Kasrah. Secondary signs (Waw/Alif/Ya) substitute for them in certain noun types — forming the basis of the nine categories of I'rab to be covered next session.

  8. Second year is a turning point — the teacher emphasized that the material requires more focus and dedication, but mastery of this level gives a firm foundation for Years 3 and beyond.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered a review of Kalam (complete vs. incomplete speech) and the alāmāt (distinguishing signs) of fi'l, then launched into a new chapter: Faslun fī Asnāfi I'rābi l-Ism — the nine categories of i'rāb for nouns. Four of the nine categories were covered in detail, with extensive discussion of the conditions governing each type.

docs.title: Review: Kalam Tām vs. Kalam Nāqis
docs.text:
• Kalam Nāqis: Incomplete speech — e.g., Zaydun al-bā'idu (two words, no complete meaning conveyed).
  • Kalam Tām: Complete speech — e.g., Zaydun fil-bayti. Its alāma: yasiḥḥu l-sukūtu 'alayhā — it is permissible to stop/pause on it (the listener has no remaining questions).

docs.title: Review: Alāmāt of Fi'l
docs.text:
• Sawfa: Strongest alāma exclusive to fi'l — only fi'l accepts sawfa, making it the most definitive distinguishing sign.
  • Yā': Shared with other categories, so weaker as an alāma.

docs.title: New Chapter: Faslun fī Asnāfi I'rābi l-Ism (The Nine Categories of Noun I'rāb)
docs.text: The three primary i'rāb states are Raf', Naṣb, and Jarr. However, because secondary i'rāb (ḥurūf: wāw, alif, yā) can substitute for primary i'rāb (ḥarakāt: ḍamma, fatḥa, kasra), and because some nouns deviate from the default pattern (e.g., ghayr munsarif uses fatḥa in place of kasra), there are nine distinct categories of i'rāb for nouns.

docs.title: Category 1 — Raf' with Ḍamma, Naṣb with Fatḥa, Jarr with Kasra (Primary I'rāb)
docs.text:
This is the default/standard i'rāb.

Conditions — the noun must be: 1. Mufrad (singular) 2. Munsarif (not ghayr munsarif — i.e., it accepts tanwīn and kasra) 3. Saḥīḥ — defined in naḥw as: mā lā yakūnu fī ākhirihi ḥarfu 'illah — a noun whose final letter is not a ḥarf 'illah (ا، و، ي)

Note: The definition of ṣaḥīḥ differs between naḥw and ṣarf. In ṣarf, a noun is ma'tall if it has a ḥarf 'illah anywhere (beginning, middle, or end). In naḥw, only the final letter matters — if it is free of ḥarf 'illah, the noun is ṣaḥīḥ.

Also included in Category 1 (same i'rāb pattern):

  • Jārī majrā l-ṣaḥīḥ: A noun ending in wāw or yā' with a sākin (sukūn) on the letter before it.
  • Examples: Dalwun (دَلْوٌ — wāw at end, mā qabl sākin), Ẓabyun (ظَبْيٌ — yā' at end, mā qabl sākin)
  • Jam' mukassar munsarif (broken plural that is munsarif): e.g., Rijālun (رِجَالٌ)
  • Note: Madāris is also a broken plural but is ghayr munsarif, so it does not fall here.

Examples: | Case | Example | |---|---| | Raf' | جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وَدَلْوٌ وَظَبْيٌ وَرِجَالٌ | | Naṣb | رَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا وَدَلْوًا وَظَبْيًا وَرِجَالًا | | Jarr | مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ وَدَلْوٍ وَظَبْيٍ وَرِجَالٍ |

(Zayd = mufrad ṣaḥīḥ; Dalw and Ẓaby = jārī majrā l-ṣaḥīḥ; Rijāl = jam' mukassar munsarif)

docs.title: Category 2 — Raf' with Ḍamma, Naṣb with Kasra, Jarr with Kasra
docs.text:
Deviation: Naṣb does not take fatḥa; instead kasra substitutes for fatḥa in both Naṣb and Jarr.

This i'rāb is specific to: Jam' Mu'annas Sālim (sound feminine plural — every mu'annas ending in alif + tā' marbūṭa in plural form, e.g., Muslimāt).

Qur'ānic Example:

إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَالْمُسْلِمَاتِ

Inna normally causes fatḥa (naṣb). However, since Muslimāt is jam' mu'annas sālim, it does not accept fatḥa — kasra substitutes for fatḥa. So the kasra on Muslimāti is not a kasra of jarr but a kasra representing fatḥa of naṣb.

docs.title: Category 3 — Raf' with Ḍamma, Naṣb with Fatḥa, Jarr with Fatḥa
docs.text:
Deviation: Jarr does not take kasra; instead fatḥa substitutes for kasra.

This i'rāb is specific to: Ghayr Munsarif — nouns that do not accept tanwīn or kasra.

Ghayr munsarif has nine asbāb (causes); if any two of them are present in a noun, it becomes ghayr munsarif. (To be studied in detail in upcoming sessions.)

Example — 'Umar (عُمَرُ): | Case | Form | Note | |---|---|---| | Raf' | جَاءَنِي عُمَرُ | Ḍamma (no tanwīn) | | Naṣb | رَأَيْتُ عُمَرَ | Fatḥa | | Jarr | مَرَرْتُ بِعُمَرَ | Fatḥa (not kasra — ghayr munsarif rejects kasra) |

docs.title: Category 4 — Raf' with Wāw, Naṣb with Alif, Jarr with Yā' (Secondary I'rāb with Ḥurūf)
docs.text:
Here ḥurūf (letters) replace ḥarakāt entirely: - Wāw → in place of Ḍamma (Raf') - Alif → in place of Fatḥa (Naṣb) - Yā' → in place of Kasra (Jarr)

This i'rāb is specific to: Asmā' al-Sitta (The Six Nouns), with four conditions:

docs.title: The Six Nouns (Asmā' al-Sitta):
docs.text: أَبٌ، أَخٌ، حَمٌ، فَمٌ، هَنٌ، ذُو

docs.title: Four Conditions:
docs.text:
1. Must be one of the six nouns (asmā' al-sitta)
  2. Mukabbara — in their base/regular form (not muṣagghar/taṣghīr form)
  3. e.g., Akhun is mukabbara; its muṣagghar is Ukhayyun — if muṣagghar, different i'rāb applies
  4. Muwāḥada — singular (not muṯhannā or jam')
  5. If dual or plural, different i'rāb applies
  6. Muḍāf to other than Yā' al-Mutakallim
  7. If muḍāf to Yā' al-Mutakallim (e.g., Akhī — my brother), all three cases look identical → no i'rāb distinction → different rule applies

Example — Akhun (أَخٌ) muḍāf to Ḥāmid: | Case | Form | |---|---| | Raf' | جَاءَ أَخُو حَامِدٍ | | Naṣb | رَأَيْتُ أَخَا حَامِدٍ | | Jarr | مَرَرْتُ بِأَخِي حَامِدٍ |

Contrast — when muḍāf to Yā' al-Mutakallim (no i'rāb change): | Case | Form | |---|---| | Raf' | جَاءَ أَخِي | | Naṣb | رَأَيْتُ أَخِي | | Jarr | مَرَرْتُ بِأَخِي |

(All three identical — therefore a separate rule governs this situation.)

Remaining five categories will be covered in the next session (inshā'Allāh).

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning / Definition كَلَامٌ تَامٌّ Complete speech — listener has no remaining questions; pausing on it is valid كَلَامٌ نَاقِصٌ Incomplete speech — does not convey a full meaning on its own يَصِحُّ السُّكُوتُ عَلَيْهَا "It is permissible to stop/pause on it" — alāma of kalam tām سَوْفَ Particle exclusive to fi'l; strongest alāma of fi'l أَصْنَافُ الْإِعْرَابِ The categories/types of i'rāb مُفْرَدٌ Singular noun مُنْصَرِفٌ A noun that accepts tanwīn and kasra (not ghayr munsarif) غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِفٌ A noun that does not accept tanwīn or kasra; fatḥa substitutes for kasra in jarr صَحِيحٌ (in naḥw) A noun whose final letter is not a ḥarf 'illah حَرْفُ عِلَّةٍ The weak letters: ا، و، ي مَعْتَلٌّ A noun containing a ḥarf 'illah (definition differs: naḥw = at end; ṣarf = anywhere) جَارٍ مَجْرَى الصَّحِيحِ "Acting like ṣaḥīḥ" — noun ending in wāw or yā' with sukūn on the preceding letter مَا قَبْلَهُ سَاكِنٌ The letter before it carries sukūn جَمْعُ مُكَسَّرٌ Broken plural — singular form is structurally broken in the plural جَمْعُ مُؤَنَّثٍ سَالِمٌ Sound feminine plural — ends in ـَاتٌ; does not accept fatḥa in naṣb أَسْبَابُ مَنْعِ الصَّرْفِ The nine causes that make a noun ghayr munsarif (two must be present) أَسْمَاءُ السِّتَّةِ The six special nouns: أَبٌ، أَخٌ، حَمٌ، فَمٌ، هَنٌ، ذُو مُكَبَّرٌ Base/regular form of a noun (not diminutive) مُصَغَّرٌ / تَصْغِيرٌ Diminutive form of a noun (e.g., وُلَيْدٌ from وَلَدٌ; رُجَيْلٌ from رَجُلٌ) مُوَحَّدٌ Singular (as a condition for asmā' al-sitta i'rāb) مُضَافٌ A noun in an iḍāfa (possessive/genitive) construction يَاءُ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ The first-person possessive yā' (ـِي — "my") مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ The second noun in an iḍāfa; the one being possessed/specified إِعْرَابٌ أَصْلِيٌّ Primary i'rāb — by ḥarakāt (ḍamma, fatḥa, kasra) إِعْرَابٌ فَرْعِيٌّ Secondary i'rāb — by ḥurūf (wāw, alif, yā') or substitution of ḥarakāt

docs.title: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ
docs.text: • زَيْدٌ — Fā'il, marfū', alāmatu raf'ihi l-ḍamma l-ẓāhira. Mufrad, munsarif, ṣaḥīḥ → Category 1.

docs.title: رَأَيْتُ عُمَرَ
docs.text: • عُمَرَ — Maf'ūl bihi, manṣūb, alāmatu naṣbihi l-fatḥa l-ẓāhira. Category 3 (ghayr munsarif).

docs.title: مَرَرْتُ بِعُمَرَ
docs.text:
• بِ — Ḥarf jarr.
  • عُمَرَ — Majrūr, alāmatu jarrihi l-fatḥa niyābatan 'an il-kasra li-annahu ghayr munsarif. (Fatḥa stands in for kasra because ghayr munsarif rejects kasra.) Category 3.

docs.title: إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمَاتِ
docs.text: • الْمُسْلِمَاتِ — Ism Inna, manṣūb, alāmatu naṣbihi l-kasra niyābatan 'an il-fatḥa li-annahu jam' mu'annas sālim. Category 2.

docs.title: جَاءَ أَخُو حَامِدٍ
docs.text:
• أَخُو — Fā'il, marfū', alāmatu raf'ihi l-wāw niyābatan 'an il-ḍamma li-annahu min al-asmā' al-sitta. Category 4.
  • حَامِدٍ — Muḍāf ilayhi, majrūr, alāmatu jarrihi l-kasra l-ẓāhira.

docs.title: مَرَرْتُ بِأَخِي حَامِدٍ
docs.text: • أَخِي — Majrūr bi-l-bā', alāmatu jarrihi l-yā' niyābatan 'an il-kasra li-annahu min al-asmā' al-sitta. Category 4.

docs.title: Practice Examples
docs.text:
Decline the following nouns through all three cases (Raf', Naṣb, Jarr):

  1. كِتَابٌ (kitāb — mufrad, munsarif, ṣaḥīḥ → Category 1)
  2. Raf': جَاءَ كِتَابٌ
  3. Naṣb: رَأَيْتُ كِتَابًا

  4. Jarr: مَرَرْتُ بِكِتَابٍ

  5. مُسْلِمَاتٌ (jam' mu'annas sālim → Category 2)

  6. Raf': جَاءَتِ الْمُسْلِمَاتُ
  7. Naṣb: رَأَيْتُ الْمُسْلِمَاتِ (kasra, not fatḥa)

  8. Jarr: مَرَرْتُ بِالْمُسْلِمَاتِ

  9. عُمَرُ (ghayr munsarif → Category 3)

  10. Raf': جَاءَنِي عُمَرُ
  11. Naṣb: رَأَيْتُ عُمَرَ

  12. Jarr: مَرَرْتُ بِعُمَرَ (fatḥa, not kasra)

  13. أَبٌ muḍāf to زَيْدٍ (asmā' al-sitta → Category 4)

  14. Raf': جَاءَ أَبُو زَيْدٍ
  15. Naṣb: رَأَيْتُ أَبَا زَيْدٍ
  16. Jarr: مَرَرْتُ بِأَبِي زَيْدٍ

Identification drill — identify the category of i'rāb:

Noun Category Reason دَلْوٌ 1 (jārī majrā l-ṣaḥīḥ) Wāw at end, mā qabl sākin ظَبْيٌ 1 (jārī majrā l-ṣaḥīḥ) Yā' at end, mā qabl sākin رِجَالٌ 1 (jam' mukassar munsarif) Broken plural, accepts tanwīn مَدَارِسُ 3 (ghayr munsarif) Broken plural, ghayr munsarif ذُو مَالٍ 4 (asmā' al-sitta) One of the six nouns, muḍāf to non-yā'

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. There are nine categories of i'rāb for nouns, arising from the three base states (Raf', Naṣb, Jarr) combined with variations in how those states are marked (primary ḥarakāt, substitute ḥarakāt, or ḥurūf).

  2. ṣaḥīḥ in naḥw ≠ ṣaḥīḥ in ṣarf. In naḥw, only the final letter matters; in ṣarf, a ḥarf 'illah anywhere in the word makes it ma'tall. Do not conflate the two definitions.

  3. Ghayr munsarif rejects both tanwīn and kasra. When a ghayr munsarif noun is majrūr, the fatḥa you see is not naṣb — it is fatḥa standing in for kasra. Answer accordingly in i'rāb: alāmatu jarrihi l-fatḥa niyābatan 'an il-kasra.

  4. Jam' mu'annas sālim rejects fatḥa in naṣb. When you see Inna + muslimāt, the kasra is not jarr — it is kasra standing in for the expected fatḥa of naṣb.

  5. Asmā' al-sitta have four strict conditions for their wāw/alif/yā' i'rāb to apply: must be one of the six nouns, mukabbara, muwāḥada (singular), and muḍāf to other than Yā' al-Mutakallim. If muḍāf to Yā' al-Mutakallim, all cases are identical (ـِي) and a different rule governs.

  6. Reading i'rāb correctly matters more than memorizing definitions. The teacher's analogy: a skilled driver no longer thinks consciously about gears — but the student must be deliberate in the learning phase. Apply each condition consciously when parsing a text until the correct i'rāb becomes instinctive.

  7. Jārī majrā l-ṣaḥīḥ has nothing to do with Jār-Majrūr. The term means "functioning like a ṣaḥīḥ noun" — a purely morphological classification based on the final letters wāw/yā' with sukūn before them.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session continued coverage of the nine categories of I'rab (grammatical inflection) in Arabic. The teacher reviewed the remaining categories — focusing on the I'rab of Tasniyah and Kila/Kilta, Jam' Muzakkar Salim, Ism Maqsur, Ism Manqus, and Muzaf ilaa Ya' al-Mutakallim — with detailed morphological explanations of how Jam' Muzakkar Salim changes when made Mudaf toward Ya' al-Mutakallim. The session closed with study advice: reading Arabic texts daily and actively analyzing every Harakah encountered.

docs.title: Category 5 — I'rab of Tasniyah, Kila/Kilta, Isnan/Isnatan
docs.text:
Rule: This I'rab (Alif in Rafa', Ya maqabl al-Fathah in Nasb/Jarr) is exclusive (khas) to three things: 1. Tasniyah (dual) — e.g., Muslimani / Muslimayn 2. Kila and Kilta — when Mudaf to a Damir (pronoun): Kilahuma / Kilayhima, Kiltahuma / Kiltayhima 3. Isnan and Isnatan — the words for "two" themselves

Haala Muzakkar Mu'annath Rafa' جاء رجلانِ (Jaa rajulani) جاءت امرأتانِ (Jaat imra'atani) Nasb رأيت رجلينِ (Ra'aytu rajulayni) رأيت امرأتينِ (Ra'aytu imra'atayni) Jarr مررت برجلينِ (Marartu birajulayni) مررت بامرأتينِ (Marartu biimra'atayni)

Caution: Tasniyah and Jam' Muzakkar Salim share the same Ya in Nasb/Jarr, differing only in Harakah before it: - رأيت مسلمَيْن (Ra'aytu Muslimayni) — I saw two Muslims - رأيت مسلمِيْن (Ra'aytu Muslimina) — I saw many Muslims

Confusing the Fathah and Kasrah before the Ya changes the meaning entirely.

docs.title: Category 6 — I'rab of Jam' Muzakkar Salim, Ulu, and 'Ishrun wa Akhawatiha
docs.text:
Rule: Rafa' with Waw; Nasb and Jarr with Ya. This I'rab is given to:

  1. Jam' Muzakkar Salim — e.g., Muslimun / Muslimin, Mu'minun / Mu'minin, Salihun / Salihin
  2. Ulu — meaning "possessors of / those with" (equivalent to Dhu/Dhawi); used for plural persons only
  3. Rafa': اولو (Ulu) — e.g., اولو الألباب (Ulu al-albab), اولو بأس شديد (Ulu ba'sin shadid)
  4. Nasb/Jarr: اولي (Uli)
  5. Note: Ulu is inherently plural; it has no singular form in this pattern
  6. 'Ishrun wa Akhawatiha — the tens (20, 30, 40...90); these are Alfaz al-'Uqud
  7. Rafa': عشرون ('ishrun) — e.g., جاء عشرون رجلاً
  8. Nasb/Jarr: عشرين ('ishrina)

Key distinction — Noon in Tasniyah vs. Jam' Muzakkar Salim:

Form Noon type Harakah on Noon Tasniyah (e.g., Muslimani) Noon al-Tasniyah Always Maksur (كسرة) Jam' Muzakkar Salim (e.g., Muslimuna) Noon al-Jam' Always Maftuh (فتحة)

Rule of Noon dropping with Idafah: When Tasniyah or Jam' Muzakkar Salim is made Mudaf, the Noon drops: - غلاما زيدٍ (Ghulama Zaydin) — the two boys of Zayd - مسلمو مصرَ (Muslimuu Misra) — the Muslims of Egypt

docs.title: Category 7 — I'rab of Ism Maqsur and Muzaf ilaa Ya' al-Mutakallim
docs.text:
Definition of Ism Maqsur: A noun ending in Alif Maqsura (short Alif written as ى without dots), e.g., عصى ('Asa), موسى (Musa), عيسى ('Isa).

Rule: All three I'rabs (Rafa', Nasb, Jarr) are hidden (Taqdiree/Muqaddarah) — the word's form does not visibly change.

Haala Example Rafa' جاء عيسى (Jaa 'Isa) Nasb رأيت عيسى (Ra'aytu 'Isa) Jarr مررت بعيسى (Marartu bi-'Isa)

Muzaf ilaa Ya' al-Mutakallim (except Jam' Muzakkar Salim): Any noun made Mudaf toward Ya' al-Mutakallim (possessive "my") also has all I'rabs hidden in all three cases.

Example Meaning جاء ولدي (Jaa waladee) My son came رأيت ولدي (Ra'aytu waladee) I saw my son مررت بولدي (Marartu biwaladee) I passed by my son جاء أبي (Jaa abee) My father came جاء صديقي (Jaa sadeeqee) My friend came

docs.title: Category 8 — I'rab of Ism Manqus
docs.text:
Definition of Ism Manqus: A noun ending in Ya (ي) that has a Kasrah before it, where the Ya is original (part of the root), not added. e.g., القاضي (Al-Qadi — judge).

Rule: - Rafa': Hidden (Taqdiree Dhammah) — the Dhammah is not visibly shown - Nasb: Visible Fathah — this is the only case where I'rab appears - Jarr: Hidden (Taqdiree Kasrah)

Haala Example Note Rafa' جاء القاضي (Jaa al-Qadi) Dhammah hidden Nasb رأيت القاضيَ (Ra'aytu al-Qadiya) Fathah visible Jarr مررت بالقاضي (Marartu bil-Qadi) Kasrah hidden

docs.title: Category 9 — I'rab of Jam' Muzakkar Salim Muzaf ilaa Ya' al-Mutakallim
docs.text:
Rule: When Jam' Muzakkar Salim is made Mudaf to Ya' al-Mutakallim, its I'rab is: - Rafa': Hidden (Taqdiree) - Nasb and Jarr: Ya (Lafzi — visible)

Morphological derivation of مسلميَّ (Muslimiyya):

This is a detailed process the teacher explained step by step:

  1. Start: مسلمون (Muslimuna)
  2. Make Mudaf → Noon drops: مسلموي (Muslimu + Ya)
  3. Waw and Ya come together, Waw has Sukun → Waw converts to Ya (rule of Taalil): مسلميي (Muslimiyyi)
  4. Two identical letters (Ya + Ya) merge into one with Shaddah: مسلميَّ (Muslimiyya)
  5. Ya requires Kasrah before it → Dhammah on Meem changes to Kasrah: مُسْلِمِيَّ (Muslimiyya)
Haala Form Rafa' جاء مسلميَّ (Jaa Muslimiyya) — Dhammah hidden Nasb رأيت مسلميَّ (Ra'aytu Muslimiyya) Jarr مررت بمسلميَّ (Marartu bi-Muslimiyya)

Similarly for Nasb/Jarr when made Mudaf: - Base: مسلمين (Muslimina) — Noon drops → مسلمي + Ya → two Ya merge → مسلميَّ

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning التثنية (Al-Tasniyah) Dual form كلا / كلتا (Kila / Kilta) Both (Muzakkar / Mu'annath) جمع مذكر سالم (Jam' Muzakkar Salim) Sound masculine plural أولو / أولي (Ulu / Uli) Possessors of, those with (plural) العقود (Al-'Uqud) The tens (20, 30...90) اسم مقصور (Ism Maqsur) Noun ending in Alif Maqsura اسم منقوص (Ism Manqus) Noun ending in original Ya with Kasra before it الإضافة (Al-Idafah) Noun-noun genitive construction ياء المتكلم (Ya' al-Mutakallim) First-person possessive Ya ("my") تقديري (Taqdiree) Hidden/estimated (I'rab not visibly shown) لفظي (Lafzi) Visible/pronounced (I'rab shown explicitly) التعليل (Al-Ta'lil) Morphological weakening/change rule (Sarf) حروف العلة (Huruf al-'Illah) Weak letters: Waw, Ya, Alif الخامس (Al-Khamis) The fifth (category) السادس (Al-Sadis) The sixth (category) ذو / ذوو (Dhu / Dhawu) Possessor of (singular / plural) — synonym of Ulu صاحب (Sahib) Possessor, companion غير منصرف (Ghayr Munsarif) Diptote (next chapter topic)

docs.title: I'rab (Sentence Analysis) Examples
docs.text:
Jam' Muzakkar Salim — basic: - جاء المسلمون — Jaa al-Muslimuna — Rafa' with Waw; فاعل مرفوع - رأيت المسلمين — Ra'aytu al-Muslimina — Nasb with Ya; مفعول به منصوب - مررت بالمسلمين — Marartu bil-Muslimina — Jarr with Ya; مجرور بالباء

Ism Maqsur: - جاء موسى — Jaa Musa — فاعل مرفوع بضمة مقدرة على الألف (hidden Dhammah on Alif) - رأيت موسى — Ra'aytu Musa — مفعول به منصوب بفتحة مقدرة (hidden Fathah) - مررت بموسى — Marartu bi-Musa — مجرور بكسرة مقدرة (hidden Kasrah)

Ism Manqus: - جاء القاضي — Jaa al-Qadi — فاعل مرفوع بضمة مقدرة (hidden Dhammah) - رأيت القاضيَ — Ra'aytu al-Qadiya — مفعول به منصوب بالفتحة الظاهرة (visible Fathah) - مررت بالقاضي — Marartu bil-Qadi — مجرور بكسرة مقدرة (hidden Kasrah)

Jam' Muzakkar Salim + Idafah: - جاء مسلمو مصرَ — Jaa Muslimuu Misra — Noon dropped for Idafah; مرفوع بالواو - رأيت مسلمي مصرَ — Ra'aytu Muslimii Misra — Noon dropped; منصوب بالياء

Jam' Muzakkar Salim + Ya' al-Mutakallim: - جاء مسلميَّ — Jaa Muslimiyya — Rafa'; Dhammah hidden due to Taalil process - رأيت مسلميَّ — Ra'aytu Muslimiyya — Nasb with Ya (Lafzi) - مررت بمسلميَّ — Marartu bi-Muslimiyya — Jarr with Ya (Lafzi)

docs.title: Practice Examples
docs.text:
Tasniyah drill:

Meaning Rafa' Nasb Jarr Two men جاء رجلانِ رأيت رجلينِ مررت برجلينِ Two women جاءت امرأتانِ رأيت امرأتينِ مررت بامرأتينِ Two (masc.) جاء اثنانِ رأيت اثنينِ مررت باثنينِ

Kila / Kilta drill (Mudaf to Damir): - كلاهما — Kilahuma (Rafa') / كليهما — Kilayhima (Nasb/Jarr) — Both of them (m.) - كلتاهما — Kiltahuma (Rafa') / كلتيهما — Kiltayhima (Nasb/Jarr) — Both of them (f.)

Ulu drill: - جاء أولو المال — Jaa Ulu al-Mal — The wealthy came (Rafa') - رأيت أولي العلم — Ra'aytu Uli al-'Ilm — I saw the people of knowledge (Nasb) - مررت بأولي الألباب — Marartu bi-Uli al-Albab — I passed by those of understanding (Jarr)

'Ishrun drill: - جاء عشرون رجلاً — Jaa 'ishrun rajulan — Twenty men came - رأيت عشرين رجلاً — Ra'aytu 'ishrina rajulan — I saw twenty men - مررت بستين رجلاً — Marartu bisitteena rajulan — I passed by sixty men

Distinguishing Tasniyah from Jam' Muzakkar Salim (Nasb/Jarr): - رأيت مسلمَيْن (Fathah before Ya) — I saw two Muslims - رأيت مسلمِيْن (Kasrah before Ya) — I saw many Muslims

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Nine categories, not nine types of I'rab. I'rab itself remains four (Rafa', Nasb, Jarr, Jazm). The nine categories describe how and where those I'rabs are expressed — with primary markers (Harakah), secondary markers (letters like Waw/Ya/Alif), or are hidden (Taqdiree).

  2. Two categories have fully hidden I'rab: Ism Maqsur (all three cases hidden) and Muzaf ilaa Ya' al-Mutakallim (all three cases hidden). Ism Manqus has two hidden (Rafa' and Jarr) and one visible (Nasb with Fathah).

  3. Noon of Tasniyah is always Maksur (Kasrah); Noon of Jam' Muzakkar Salim is always Maftuh (Fathah). This distinction is critical and must be memorized to avoid changing meaning.

  4. Noon drops in Idafah — both Tasniyah and Jam' Muzakkar Salim lose their Noon when made Mudaf to anything.

  5. The morphological process of Jam' Muzakkar Salim + Ya' al-Mutakallim involves four steps: Noon drops → Waw+Ya come together → Waw converts to Ya (Taalil) → Two Ya merge with Shaddah → Dhammah before Ya changes to Kasrah (since Ya demands Kasrah before it). Result: مسلميَّ.

  6. Ulu and Dhu are synonymous (both mean "possessor of"); Ulu behaves like Jam' Muzakkar Salim grammatically and is inherently plural — it has no Mufrad form in this pattern.

  7. Practical study advice from the teacher: When reading any Arabic text (e.g., Al-Qira'ah al-Rashidah, Qasas al-Nabiyyin), do not just read for meaning. Stop at every word and ask: why is this Marfu'? Why Mansub? How is this I'rab being expressed — Waw, Alif, Ya, or hidden? Active analysis of Harakah is what differentiates someone who knows Arabic from someone who merely reads the script.

  8. Next session (Monday): Quick revision of all nine I'rab categories with practice, then begin the chapter on Ghayr Munsarif (Diptotes).

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session was largely Q&A-driven, covering key rules around Fi'il-Fa'il agreement (gender and number matching), the declension of Jama' Mu'annath Salim, Ism al-Manqus, and the distinction between Sahih in Nahw vs. Sarf. The teacher encouraged questions throughout and used live sentence correction as the primary teaching method.

docs.title: 1. Jama' Mu'annath Salim — Unusual I'rab
docs.text:
• Marfu': Gets Dammah (natural) → e.g. الطالباتُ
  • Majrur: Gets Kasrah (natural) → e.g. بالطالباتِ
  • Mansub: Does NOT get Fathah; instead gets Kasrah in the place of Fathah
  • This Kasrah represents/substitutes for Fathah
  • e.g. رَأَيْتُ طَالِبَاتٍ → Kasrah, not Fathah

docs.title: 2. Tasniyah vs. Jama' — Distinguishing by Ya
docs.text: Ending Indicates Example ـَيْن (Ya, ma qabl Fathah) Tasniyah (dual) الْفَائِزَيْن ـِيْن (Ya, ma qabl Kasrah) Jama' (plural) الْمُسْلِمِين

docs.title: 3. Fi'il–Fa'il Agreement: Gender and Number Rules
docs.text: This is the central rule covered in this session, applicable to Jumlah Fi'liyyah.

docs.title: Gender Agreement
docs.text:
• Always required — regardless of whether Fa'il comes before or after the Fi'il.
  • If Fa'il is Muzakkar → Fi'il must be Muzakkar.
  • If Fa'il is Mu'annath → Fi'il must be Mu'annath.

docs.title: Number Agreement
docs.text:
Case A — Fa'il is Mu'akhkhar (comes after the Fi'il): (the default/standard order) - Fi'il must match Fa'il in both gender AND number. - Wahid → Wahid, Tathniyah → Tathniyah, Jama' → Jama'

Example:

سَأَلَ الطُّلَّابُ أُسْتَاذَهُمُ    (Wahid Muzakkar — Jama' Muzakkar Fa'il)
سَأَلَتِ الطَّالِبَاتُ أُسْتَاذَهُنَّ   (Wahid Mu'annath — Jama' Mu'annath Fa'il)

Case B — Fa'il is Muqaddam (comes before the Fi'il): (inverted order) - Fi'il remains Wahid (singular) regardless of the number of the Fa'il. - Gender still must match. - The actual agreement is technically through a Dhamir referring back to the Fa'il.

Example:

الطُّلَّابُ سَأَلُوا    ✓ (Fa'il muqaddam, Fi'il matches in number)
الطَّالِبَاتُ سَأَلْنَ   ✓

Reversed back:

سَأَلَ الطُّلَّابُ      ✓ (Wahid Muzakkar)
سَأَلَتِ الطَّالِبَاتُ   ✓ (Wahid Mu'annath)
سَأَلُوا الطُّلَّابُ    ✗ — WRONG (Jama' fi'il not permitted when Fa'il is mu'akhkhar)
سَأَلْنَ الطَّالِبَاتُ   ✗ — WRONG

Summary table:

Fa'il Position Gender must match? Number must match? Mu'akhkhar (after Fi'il) Yes Yes Muqaddam (before Fi'il) Yes No — Fi'il stays Wahid

docs.title: 4. Ism al-Manqus
docs.text:
• Definition: Any Ism ending in Ya Ma Qabl Kasrah (ي preceded by Kasrah).
  • Examples: قَاضٍ (Qadi), الجَانِي (Al-Jani), المُحَامِي (Al-Muhami)
  • I'rab behavior:
  • Marfu' and Majrur: Harakah is Taqdiri (implied/estimated) — the word appears unchanged visually.
  • Mansub: Fathah appears explicitly on the Ya → رَأَيْتُ القَاضِيَ

docs.title: 5. Sahih: Nahw vs. Sarf Definitions
docs.text:
Discipline Definition of Sahih Nahw Last letter (Lam al-Kalimah) is not a Harf 'Illah (ا، و، ي) Sarf None of the letters of the word is a Harf 'Illah anywhere in the word
  • Zayd (زَيْد): Sahih in Nahw (last letter Dal, not 'Illah) — but could be Mu'tall in Sarf if examined internally.
  • 'Ali (عَلِي): Mu'tall according to both (ends in Ya, a Harf 'Illah).
  • 'Umar (عُمَر): Sahih according to both.
  • A word that is Mu'tall may carry additional ahkam (rules); otherwise the distinction is theoretical.

docs.title: 6. Ism al-Manqus in Jumlah: Inna + Jama' Muzakkar Salim
docs.text:
Sentence: إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمُونَ نَشَرُوا الْعِلْمَ فِي الْعَالَمِ

  • Error: الْمُسْلِمُونَ is Marfu' form; after إِنَّ the Ism must be Mansub.
  • Correction: إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ نَشَرُوا الْعِلْمَ فِي الْعَالَمِ ✓
  • الْعِلْمَ is Maf'ul bih → Mansub → Fathah ✓ (no change needed)
  • نَشَرُوا is Fi'il Jama'; since الْمُسْلِمِينَ is Jama', and it is the Fa'il (coming after the Fi'il implicitly through the Dhamir), this holds.

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning فَاعِل (Fa'il) Subject / doer of the verb فِعْل (Fi'il) Verb مَفْعُول بِه (Maf'ul bih) Direct object مَرْفُوع (Marfu') Nominative case (Dammah) مَنْصُوب (Mansub) Accusative case (Fathah / substitute) مَجْرُور (Majrur) Genitive case (Kasrah) جَمْع مُؤَنَّث سَالِم Sound Feminine Plural جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم Sound Masculine Plural تَثْنِيَة (Tasniyah) Dual form مُقَدَّم (Muqaddam) Fronted / placed before مُؤَخَّر (Mu'akhkhar) Placed after / deferred اِسْم مَنْقُوص (Ism Manqus) Noun ending in Ya ma qabl Kasrah تَقْدِيرِي (Taqdiri) Implied/estimated (Harakah not visibly shown) حَرْف عِلَّة (Harf 'Illah) Weak letter (ا، و، ي) مُعْتَل (Mu'tall) A word containing a Harf 'Illah صَحِيح (Sahih) Sound/correct (free of Harf 'Illah per definition) تَرْكِيب (Tarkib) Grammatical parsing / sentence structure analysis إِعْرَاب (I'rab) Grammatical case analysis جُمْلَة فِعْلِيَّة (Jumlah Fi'liyyah) Verbal sentence (begins with a verb) فَائِز (Fa'iz) The one who succeeded / passed قَاضٍ (Qadi) Judge طَالِبَة / طَالِبَات (Talibah/Talibat) Female student / female students طُلَّاب (Tullab) Students (Jama' Muzakkar Ghayr Salim)

docs.title: Example 1
docs.text:
طَبَخَتِ الطَّالِبَاتُ اللَّحْمَ (The female students cooked the meat)

Word I'rab Role Case Marker طَبَخَتْ Fi'il Madi; Ta = Ta' Ta'nith Sakinah — — الطَّالِبَاتُ Fa'il Marfu' Dammah اللَّحْمَ Maf'ul bih Mansub Fathah
  • Ta' al-Ta'nith on the fi'il is required because Fa'il (الطالبات) is Mu'annath.

docs.title: Example 2
docs.text:
رَأَيْتُ طَالِبَاتٍ فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ (I saw female students in the school)

Word I'rab Role Case Marker طَالِبَاتٍ Maf'ul bih Mansub Kasrah (in place of Fathah)

docs.title: Example 3
docs.text:
إِنَّ الْفَائِزَيْنِ جَاؤُوا — Error analysis

  • الْفَائِزَيْنِ = Tasniyah (dual), Ya ma qabl Fathah
  • جَاؤُوا = Jama' fi'il — mismatch in number when Fa'il is mu'akhkhar
  • Correction Option A: إِنَّ الْفَائِزَيْنِ جَاءَا (Tasniyah fi'il)
  • Correction Option B: إِنَّ الْفَائِزِينَ جَاؤُوا (change to Jama')

docs.title: Example 4
docs.text:
الطُّلَّابُ سَأَلُوا أُسْتَاذَهُمُ الْأَسْئِلَةَ الْكَثِيرَةَ (The students asked their teacher many questions — Fa'il Muqaddam)

vs.

سَأَلَ الطُّلَّابُ أُسْتَاذَهُمُ الْأَسْئِلَةَ الْكَثِيرَةَ (Standard order — Fi'il Wahid, Fa'il mu'akhkhar)

docs.title: Example 5 — Ism Manqus
docs.text: جَاءَ الْقَاضِي — Marfu', Harakah Taqdiri (Ya unchanged) مَرَرْتُ بِالْقَاضِي — Majrur, Harakah Taqdiri (Ya unchanged) رَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِيَ — Mansub, Fathah appears explicitly on Ya

docs.title: Practice Examples
docs.text:
1. Identify the error and correct it:
  2. إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمُونَ نَشَرُوا الْعِلْمَ
  3. Error: المسلمون is Marfu'; after إِنَّ it must be Mansub

  4. Correction: إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ نَشَرُوا الْعِلْمَ ✓

  5. Choose the correct verb form:

  6. الطَّالِبَاتُ _____ أُسْتَاذَهُنَّ: سَأَلْنَ (Fa'il muqaddam, both gender + number match)

  7. _____ الطَّالِبَاتُ أُسْتَاذَهُنَّ: سَأَلَتْ (Fa'il mu'akhkhar, Wahid Mu'annath only)

  8. Determine: Is الطُّلَّابُ Sahih or Mu'tall according to Nahw?

  9. Last letter = Ba' → not a Harf 'Illah → Sahih in Nahw

  10. Decline قَاضٍ in all three cases:

  11. Marfu': الْقَاضِي (Taqdiri Dammah)
  12. Mansub: الْقَاضِيَ (Fathah on Ya)
  13. Majrur: الْقَاضِي (Taqdiri Kasrah)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Jama' Mu'annath Salim never takes Fathah in the Mansub state — Kasrah substitutes for it. Only Dammah (Rafa') and Kasrah (Jarr and Nasb) are possible.

  2. Gender agreement in Jumlah Fi'liyyah is absolute — Fi'il must always reflect the gender of its Fa'il, whether the Fa'il comes before or after.

  3. Number agreement depends on word order: when Fa'il is after the Fi'il (standard), both gender and number match; when Fa'il is before the Fi'il (inverted), only gender matches — the Fi'il stays singular (Wahid).

  4. Tasniyah vs. Jama' Muzakkar Salim are distinguished by the vowel before the Ya: Fathah = dual, Kasrah = plural. Confusing them causes agreement errors.

  5. Ism Manqus shows its full Harakah only in Nasb (Fathah on Ya); in Rafa' and Jarr the Harakah is Taqdiri (implied, not visible).

  6. Sahih differs between Nahw and Sarf: Nahw only checks the last letter; Sarf checks all letters.

  7. Tarkib (parsing) aids I'rab but knowing meaning is often equally or more useful. Many fluent readers apply correct I'rab without formal Tarkib analysis.

  8. Recommended reading: مَاذَا خَسِرَ الْعَالَمُ بِانْحِطَاطِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ by Sayyid Abul Hasan Ali Nadwi (English: Islam and the World) — originally in Arabic; translations exist but the original carries the author's spirit most fully.

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session was a review and error-correction class focused on the nine categories of I'rab (إعراب). Students were given sentences with grammatical errors to identify and correct, covering concepts such as Taqdeeri I'rab, Mudaaf-Mudaaf Ilayh structures, Mabni vs. Ma'rab distinctions, and special cases like Ism Manqoos and Ghayr Munsarif. The sheikh also clarified the conceptual difference between Mabni and Taqdeeri I'rab, which generated significant discussion.

docs.title: 1. Taqdeeri I'rab — Hidden Vowel Signs
docs.text: When an ism is Mudaaf toward Yaa Mutakallim (the first-person possessive ي), I'rab is Taqdeeri (hidden) in all three cases (Rafa', Nasab, Jarr). - The word does not visibly change its ending. - Example: كِتَابِي — it remains كِتَابِي regardless of its grammatical position.

docs.title: 2. Noon Drop in Tasniya and Jama' Mudhakkar Salim When Mudaaf
docs.text: When a Tasniya (dual) or Jama' Mudhakkar Salim (sound masculine plural) is Mudaaf, the Noon is dropped (Noon Mahjoof/Noon Biqaya drops). - Incorrect: وَلَدَانِ حَامِدٍ (noon retained) - Correct: وَلَدَا حَامِدٍ (noon dropped) - Incorrect: مُسْلِمُونَ بَاكِسْتَانَ - Correct: مُسْلِمُو بَاكِسْتَانَ (noon drops because it is Mudaaf)

docs.title: 3. Ism Manqoos — Deficient Noun I'rab
docs.text: An Ism Manqoos is a noun ending in ي preceded by Kasra (e.g., قَاضِي). Its I'rab rules: - In Rafa' and Jarr: I'rab is Taqdeeri (hidden) — the ending appears unchanged. - In Nasab: I'rab is Zaahir (visible) — the Fatha appears: قَاضِيَ. - Therefore: رَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِيَ (not القاضي) because رَأَيْتُ requires Nasab (Maf'ool Bih).

docs.title: 4. Khabar of Inna is Marfoo'
docs.text: After إِنَّ and its sisters, the Ism takes Nasab and the Khabar takes Rafa'. - إِنَّ هُنَّ مُسْلِمَاتٌ — مُسْلِمَاتٌ is Khabar, therefore Marfoo' (with Dhamma, written with Tanween Damm). - It is NOT Maf'ool, so it does NOT take Kasra/Fatha. - Special note: when Jama' Mu'annath Salim is Mansub, it takes Kasra instead of Fatha (e.g., إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمَاتِ صَالِحَاتٌ).

docs.title: 5. Mabni vs. Ma'rab — Key Distinction
docs.text:
Category Definition I'rab Mabni Word that does NOT accept I'rab; its last haraka never changes No I'rab applied; Amil is irrelevant Ma'rab Word that accepts I'rab; haraka changes according to Amil I'rab applied (either Zaahir or Taqdeeri) Taqdeeri Sub-type of Ma'rab: I'rab comes but is hidden/unable to appear Word appears unchanged but is still Ma'rab

Categories classified as Mabni: - Zamaa'ir (pronouns) - Asmaa' ul-Ishaara (demonstrative nouns) — e.g., هَذَا، هَؤُلَاءِ - Asmaa' ul-Mawsoola (relative nouns) — e.g., الَّذِي - Asmaa' ul-Istifhaam (interrogative nouns) - Asmaa' ul-Sharat (conditional nouns) - Ba'dhul Dhuroof (some adverbs)

Examples of Mabni: - هَؤُلَاءِ: جَاءَ هَؤُلَاءِ / رَأَيْتُ هَؤُلَاءِ / مَرَرْتُ بِهَؤُلَاءِ — ending never changes (always Kasra by birth) - الَّذِي: جَاءَ الَّذِي / رَأَيْتُ الَّذِي / مَرَرْتُ بِالَّذِي — Sukoon never changes

Taqdeeri example (Ma'rab, not Mabni): - مُوسَى: جَاءَ مُوسَى / رَأَيْتُ مُوسَى — ending appears unchanged but I'rab is Taqdeeri, NOT Mabni

docs.title: 6. Ghayr Munsarif — Non-Diptote (Briefly Mentioned)
docs.text: One of the nine categories of I'rab. Full treatment deferred to the next chapter — the class has not yet covered what Ghayr Munsarif is, so its I'rab rules were not discussed in this session.

docs.title: Important Vocabulary
docs.text: Arabic Term Meaning إِعْرَاب (I'rab) Grammatical inflection / case-ending system تَقْدِيرِي (Taqdeeri) Hidden; I'rab that exists but cannot appear on the word ظَاهِر (Zaahir) Visible; I'rab that appears on the word مَبْنِي (Mabni) Indeclinable; word that receives no I'rab at all مُعْرَب (Ma'rab) Declinable; word that receives I'rab مُضَاف (Mudaaf) The first word in a possessive/genitive construction مُضَاف إِلَيْه (Mudaaf Ilayh) The second word in a possessive construction (always Majroor) يَاء الْمُتَكَلِّم (Yaa Mutakallim) First-person possessive ي (my) نُون التَّثْنِيَة (Noon Tasniya) The noon in the dual ending ـَانِ / ـَيْنِ نُون الْجَمْع (Noon al-Jam') The noon in Jama' Mudhakkar Salim ending ـُونَ / ـِينَ اسم مَنْقُوص (Ism Manqoos) A noun ending in ي preceded by Kasra; undergoes Taqdeeri I'rab in Rafa' and Jarr اسم مَقْصُور (Ism Maqsoor) A noun ending in Alif Maqsoora; undergoes Taqdeeri I'rab in all three cases غَيْر مُنْصَرِف (Ghayr Munsarif) Non-diptote; a noun that does not accept Tanween and takes Fatha instead of Kasra in Jarr خَبَر (Khabar) Predicate of a nominal sentence or of إِنَّ and sisters مَفْعُول بِه (Maf'ool Bih) Direct object; takes Nasab رَفْع (Rafa') Nominative case نَصْب (Nasab) Accusative case جَرّ (Jarr) Genitive case عَامِل (Amil) The grammatical operator that governs and determines the case of a word تَثْنِيَة (Tasniya) Dual form جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم (Jama' Mudhakkar Salim) Sound masculine plural جَمْع مُؤَنَّث سَالِم (Jama' Mu'annath Salim) Sound feminine plural

docs.title: Example 1 — Yaa Mutakallim (Taqdeeri I'rab)
docs.text: Sentence: رَأَيْتُ كِتَابِيَّ فِي بَيْتِكَ - Error: كِتَابِيَّ → Correct: كِتَابِي - Rule: When Ism is Mudaaf toward Yaa Mutakallim, I'rab is Taqdeeri in all three cases. - كِتَابِي appears the same in Rafa', Nasab, and Jarr — the haraka is hidden.

docs.title: Example 2 — Noun Drop in Tasniya Mudaaf
docs.text: Sentence: قَرَأَ وَلَدَانِ حَامِدٍ سُورَةَ يَاسِين سَبْعِينَ مَرَّةً - Errors: 1. وَلَدَانِ حَامِدٍ — Noon must drop because وَلَدَا is Mudaaf toward حَامِدٍ 2. حَامِدٍ remains Majroor (Mudaaf Ilayh) — correct as-is; it is neither حَامِدًا nor حَامِدٌ - Correct: قَرَأَ وَلَدَا حَامِدٍ سُورَةَ يَاسِين سَبْعِينَ مَرَّةً - I'rab breakdown: - قَرَأَ — Fi'l Madi - وَلَدَا — Faa'il, Marfoo', Tasniya (Mudaaf, noon dropped) - حَامِدٍ — Mudaaf Ilayh, Majroor - سُورَةَ — Maf'ool Bih, Mansub - يَاسِين — Mudaaf Ilayh (or Badal), Majroor (Ghayr Munsarif — no Tanween) - سَبْعِينَ مَرَّةً — Maf'ool Mutlaq or Zarf, Mansub

docs.title: Example 3 — Ism Manqoos in Nasab
docs.text: Sentence: رَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِي - Error: القاضي → Correct: الْقَاضِيَ - Rule: Ism Manqoos shows visible Fatha (Nasab) — unlike Rafa' and Jarr where I'rab is Taqdeeri. - رَأَيْتُ requires Nasab for its Maf'ool Bih → الْقَاضِيَ

docs.title: Example 4 — Jama' Mudhakkar Salim Mudaaf
docs.text: Sentence: بَنَى مُسْلِمُونَ بَاكِسْتَانَ هَذَا الْمَسْجِدَ - Error: مُسْلِمُونَ → Correct: مُسْلِمُو (Noon drops; Mudaaf toward بَاكِسْتَان) - Correct: بَنَى مُسْلِمُو بَاكِسْتَانَ هَذَا الْمَسْجِدَ - Note: بَاكِسْتَان is a proper name (Mabni/Alam), already Ma'rifah — no need to add ال or ي. - Note: بَاكِسْتَان is Ghayr Munsarif (no Tanween), so it cannot become بَاكِسْتَانِيّ in this context.

docs.title: Example 5 — Khabar of Inna
docs.text: Sentence: إِنَّ هُنَّ مُسْلِمَاتٌ - This sentence is correct as written. - هُنَّ — Ism of Inna, Mansub (but Mabni — pronoun) - مُسْلِمَاتٌ — Khabar of Inna, Marfoo' (Tanween Damm) - Common mistake: thinking مُسْلِمَات is Maf'ool Bih and should take Kasra → incorrect; it is Khabar, which is Marfoo'. - Contrast: إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمَاتِ صَالِحَاتٌ — here الْمُسْلِمَاتِ is Ism of Inna, Mansub → Jama' Mu'annath Salim takes Kasra (not Fatha) in Nasab.

docs.title: Practice Examples
docs.text:
Sentence Status Correction / Note رَأَيْتُ كِتَابِيَّ فِي بَيْتِكَ Incorrect → رَأَيْتُ كِتَابِي (Taqdeeri I'rab with Yaa Mutakallim) قَرَأَ وَلَدَانِ حَامِدٍ سُورَةَ يَاسِين سَبْعِينَ مَرَّةً Incorrect → قَرَأَ وَلَدَا حَامِدٍ (Noon of Tasniya drops when Mudaaf) رَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِي Incorrect → رَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِيَ (Ism Manqoos shows Fatha in Nasab) بَنَى مُسْلِمُونَ بَاكِسْتَانَ هَذَا الْمَسْجِدَ Incorrect → بَنَى مُسْلِمُو بَاكِسْتَانَ (Noon of JMS drops when Mudaaf) إِنَّ هُنَّ مُسْلِمَاتٌ Correct مُسْلِمَاتٌ is Khabar (Marfoo'), not Maf'ool

Additional practice sentences (from teacher's examples on Mabni): - جَاءَ هَؤُلَاءِ / رَأَيْتُ هَؤُلَاءِ / مَرَرْتُ بِهَؤُلَاءِ — هَؤُلَاءِ is Mabni; ending never changes - جَاءَ الَّذِي قَرَأَ الْقُرْآنَ / رَأَيْتُ الَّذِي قَرَأَ الْقُرْآنَ / مَرَرْتُ بِالَّذِي قَرَأَ الْقُرْآنَ — الَّذِي is Mabni; Sukoon never changes - جَاءَ مُوسَى / رَأَيْتُ مُوسَى — مُوسَى is Ma'rab with Taqdeeri I'rab (NOT Mabni)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Taqdeeri ≠ Mabni — Though the outcome (word appearing unchanged) looks the same, they are fundamentally different: Taqdeeri is a sub-type of Ma'rab (I'rab exists but is hidden); Mabni means no I'rab at all. Mabni words are classified as such by grammarians into fixed categories (pronouns, demonstratives, relative nouns, etc.).

  2. Noon always drops in Mudaaf — Whether it is the Noon of Tasniya or the Noon of Jama' Mudhakkar Salim, once the word is Mudaaf, the Noon is dropped. Never retain the Noon in a Mudaaf.

  3. Ism Manqoos shows I'rab only in Nasab — In Rafa' and Jarr, the Fatha/Kasra on the ي cannot appear (Taqdeeri). In Nasab, the Fatha appears: قَاضِيَ. Students must remember to write the Fatha in Nasab.

  4. Khabar of Inna is always Marfoo' — Do not confuse it with Maf'ool Bih. إِنَّ makes its own Ism Mansub; the Khabar that follows remains in Rafa'.

  5. Jama' Mu'annath Salim takes Kasra in Nasab — Unlike most nouns that take Fatha in Nasab, JMS (e.g., مُسْلِمَات) takes Kasra when Mansub (as Ism of Inna, or Maf'ool Bih, etc.).

  6. Nine categories of I'rab are now complete (except Ghayr Munsarif, to be covered in the next chapter). A summary may be shared in the class group.

  7. Next session (Monday): New chapter — beginning study of Ghayr Munsarif.
