(yataraddadoon) To hesitate / waver / be bewildered اسْتَبْدَلَ يَسْتَبْدِلُ اسْتِبْدَالًا (istabdala) To exchange / to substitute رَبِحَ يَرْبَحُ رِبْحًا (rabiha yarbaĥu ribĥan) To gain profit (in a transaction) فَمَا رَبِحَتْ تِجَارَتُهُمْ (fama rabiĥat tijaratuhum) Their trade did not profit اسْتَوْقَدَ يَسْتَوْقِدُ اسْتِيقَادًا (istawqada) To kindle a fire ظُلُمَات كَثِيفَة (thulumat kathifa) Dense / thick darkness صُمٌّ (summun) Deaf (plural); singular: أَصَم (asam) — على وزن أفعل بُكْمٌ (bukmun) Dumb / mute (plural); singular: أَبْكَم (abkam) — على وزن أفعل عُمْيٌ (umyun) Blind (plural); singular: أَعْمَى (a'ma) طَبَعَ عَلَى قُلُوبِهِمْ (taba'a ala quloobihim) Allah has sealed their hearts إِنَّ كَيْدِي مَكِين (inna kaydi makeen) "My plan is very strong" — Quranic phrase on divine strategy

docs.title: 1. The Grammatical Emphasis in "Inna Humul Mufsidoon" (Ayah 12)
docs.text:
The construction uses multiple layers of emphasis: - إِنَّ — particle of affirmation (for confirmation) - هُمْ — a separating pronoun (dameer fasl) creating a Mubtada-Khabar structure - الْمُفْسِدُونَ — the predicate with the definite article (for restriction/hasr)

All three elements together serve to restrict and emphasize: it is they — and none other — who are the corruptors. Yet they do not perceive this because the light of Iman has been extinguished in their hearts (intimas noor al-iman).

docs.title: 2. "Wa Lakin La Yash'uroon" — They Do Not Perceive (Ayah 12)
docs.text: The reason for their blindness: they have no light of Iman. A person with Iman can feel when they are doing wrong — the light of faith illuminates the conscience. Without it, there is no internal check. This is spiritual blindness at its core.

docs.title: 3. The Munafiqeen's Response to Being Called to Sincere Iman (Ayah 13)
docs.text: When told: "Aminu kama amana al-naas" (Believe as the people — i.e., the Sahabah — believed): - They responded with أَنُؤْمِنُ كَمَا آمَنَ السُّفَهَاءُ — "Should we believe as the fools believed?" - The hamza (أ) here is not a genuine question but an interrogative of mockery (hamzat al-inkaar / al-istihza') - They called the Sahabah — Bilal, Suhaib, Ammar (رضي الله عنهم) — sufaha' (fools), juhal (ignorant), and ahl al-faqr (poor/slaves) - Their motive: تحقير شأنهم — to belittle, disgrace, and degrade the status of Muslims publicly - Most early believers were poor or slaves, giving the munafiqeen social cover to demean them

docs.title: 4. Allah's Response: Restricting Foolishness to the Munafiqeen (Ayah 13)
docs.text:
أَلَا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ السُّفَهَاءُ — "Indeed, they are the fools." - أَلَا — particle for alerting attention: "Beware!" / "Listen!" - هُمُ — again a dameer fasl for restriction (hasr) - Allah uses حَصْر (restriction) to limit foolishness exclusively to the munafiqeen

Justification cited: "Whoever rides upon falsehood (batil) is undoubtedly a fool — without any doubt."

وَلَكِنْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ — They do not know (about their own condition), due to their misguidance and spiritual ignorance.

docs.title: 5. Their Double-Faced Behavior — Nifaq and Musana'ah (Ayah 14)
docs.text:
وَإِذَا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قَالُوا آمَنَّا - In front of believers: "We have believed (amanna)" - They showed Iman and muwalah (alliance) to the Muslims — out of nifaq and musana'ah (flattering/duplicity), not conviction

وَإِذَا خَلَوْا إِلَى شَيَاطِينِهِمْ - خَلَا إِلَى (khala ila) = to be alone in a place with someone - When alone with their leaders (described as shayateen — devils) — the elders of misguidance and nifaq - They said: "We are with you. We are only mocking the Muslims (innama nahnu mustahzi'un)." - They clarified: they follow the same belief as their leaders; the display of Iman is pure mockery and imitation

docs.title: 6. "Allahu Yastahzi'u Bihim" — Divine Retribution in Kind (Ayah 15)
docs.text:
This is a profound stylistic feature: - They said: نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِئُونَ (we are mockers) - Allah responds: اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ (Allah mocks them)

The same root word is used, but: - Their istihza' = mere words/actions of mockery - Allah's istihza' = actual punishment — specifically through imla' (giving respite, delaying punishment) followed by a final severe punishment

Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه): Allah's yaskhar (mocking) of them = taking revenge (linikma minhum), by giving them respite (wayumli lahum).

Ibn Katheer (رحمه الله): This is Allah informing us He will retribute the munafiqeen for their mockery — punishing them with the punishment of deception (uqubat al-khida'), because they deceived the believers.

Quranic parallel: وَأُمْلِي لَهُمْ إِنَّ كَيْدِي مَكِين — "I give them respite, for My plan is very strong."

docs.title: 7. Quranic Style: Same Word, Two Different Meanings
docs.text:
The instructor highlighted this as a recurring Quranic device: - جَزَاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُهَا — "The recompense of an evil is an evil like it" - First sayyi'ah = an evil act (Zulm / injustice) - Second sayyi'ah = the punishment for it (Adl / justice) - فَمَنِ اعْتَدَى عَلَيْكُمْ فَاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ - First i'tada = aggression/injustice - Second i'tada = justified retaliation (not injustice)

Conclusion: The word is the same; the meaning and moral status differ entirely.

docs.title: 8. "Wa Yamudduhum fi Tughyanihim Ya'mahoon" (Ayah 15)
docs.text:
• يَمُدُّ (yamuddu) — to extend, to stretch out
  • طُغْيَان (tughyan) — transgression
  • يَعْمَهُونَ — wandering blindly, floundering in confusion

Allah extends them in their transgression by way of giving them respite (imhal). Their hearts are sealed, their eyes blinded — they cannot find the right path. They wander like a blind person in a street, unable to determine direction.

Reason stated: لِأَنَّ اللَّهَ طَبَعَ عَلَى قُلُوبِهِمْ وَأَعْمَى أَبْصَارَهُمْ — Allah has sealed their hearts and blinded their sight.

docs.title: 9. The Profitless Trade (Ayah 16)
docs.text: اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلَالَةَ بِالْهُدَى - They exchanged (istabdalu) kufr for Iman — disbelief in place of belief - They took misguidance (dalalah) and paid for it with guidance (huda) - فَمَا رَبِحَتْ تِجَارَتُهُمْ — their trade earned no profit - Result: they lost the happiness of both worlds — dunya and akhirah

docs.title: 10. The Parable of the Fire (Ayah 17) — First of Two Parables
docs.text:
مَثَلُهُمْ كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ نَارًا

The example: - A person kindles a fire to get warmth and light - The fire illuminates everything around him — he feels secure and comfortable - Suddenly ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ — Allah takes away their light, extinguishes the fire entirely - The person is left in ظُلُمَات كَثِيفَة (dense darkness) and خَوْف شَدِيد (extreme fear) - He flounders (yatakhabbatoon), unable to find any way out

Application to the munafiqeen (Ibn Katheer رحمه الله): - The fire = their Iman when they first entered Islam - The light they enjoyed = the benefit and security of living among Muslims - The extinguishing = Allah taking away their light of Iman after they returned to kufr - The darkness they are left in = the darkness of doubt, kufr, and hypocrisy - Indication in this parable: annahum amanu thumma kafaru — they believed, then disbelieved

The parable illustrates: misguidance chosen after insight becomes absolute blindness.

docs.title: 11. "Summun Bukmun Umyun Fahum La Yarji'oon" (Ayah 18)
docs.text:
Three conditions of the munafiqeen: - صُمٌّ — Deaf: they do not hear / heed guidance - بُكْمٌ — Dumb/Mute: they cannot speak anything beneficial to themselves - عُمْيٌ — Blind: they cannot see the right way

فَهُمْ لَا يَرْجِعُونَ — They will not return from their state of disobedience and misguidance.

docs.title: Singular and Plural Forms (Isma Tafdil Pattern — أَفْعَل)
docs.text:
The three descriptors at the end of the passage follow the pattern of اسم التفضيل / صفة مشبهة on the وزن أَفْعَل, with broken plurals:

Singular Plural (used in ayah) Form أَصَمّ (asam) — deaf صُمٌّ (summun) فُعْل أَبْكَم (abkam) — dumb بُكْمٌ (bukmun) فُعْل أَعْمَى (a'ma) — blind عُمْيٌ (umyun) فُعْل

The plural form confirms these are referring to a group — the munafiqeen collectively.

docs.title: Key Verb Patterns Introduced
docs.text: Root / Pattern Verb Masdar Meaning فَطِنَ يَفْطَنُ يَفْطَنُ فِطْنَة To be alert/perceptive أَحَسَّ يُحِسُّ يُحِسُّ إِحْسَاس To feel/sense اسْتَوْقَدَ يَسْتَوْقِدُ اسْتَوْقَدَ اسْتِيقَاد To kindle a fire اسْتَبْدَلَ يَسْتَبْدِلُ اسْتَبْدَلَ اسْتِبْدَال To exchange/substitute رَبِحَ يَرْبَحُ رَبِحَ رِبْح To profit أَمْلَى يُمْلِي يُمْلِي إِمْلَاء To give respite/delay مَدَّ يَمُدُّ يَمُدُّ مَدّ To extend/stretch عَمِهَ يَعْمَهُ يَعْمَهُ عَمَه To wander blindly أَعْمَى يُعْمِي يُعْمِي إِعْمَاء To blind someone

docs.title: Rhetorical Device: Hamzat al-Istifham lil-Inkaar
docs.text: أَنُؤْمِنُ كَمَا آمَنَ السُّفَهَاءُ — The hamza is not a genuine question but carries the meaning of mockery and contempt (istihza' and inkaar). This is a well-known Quranic rhetorical device.

docs.title: Hasr (Restriction) Technique
docs.text: أَلَا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ السُّفَهَاءُ: - أَلَا (alerting particle) + إِنَّ (emphasis) + هُمْ (dameer fasl for hasr) + السُّفَهَاءُ (definite noun) = Complete restriction of foolishness to the munafiqeen alone

docs.title: خَلَا إِلَى vs. خَلَا بِـ
docs.text: خَلَا إِلَى — to be alone with someone in a place (implying going/returning to them); different from merely being secluded with someone.

docs.title: Lessons and Practical Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Iman is a light that enables self-awareness. Without it, a person cannot recognize their own corruption. The first casualty of spiritual blindness is insight into one's own state.

  2. The munafiqeen's defining trait is inconsistency. They perform Iman publicly and abandon it privately. Consistency between public and private is a mark of true faith.

  3. Calling believers foolish is itself a sign of foolishness. The munafiqeen mocked the poor Sahabah; Allah turned the description back on them. Social status, wealth, and lineage do not determine wisdom — Iman does.

  4. Allah's punishment can take the form of apparent ease. Respite (imla') — being left to continue in sin without immediate punishment — is itself a form of divine retribution. Not being corrected is not the same as being approved.

  5. A profitless trade: choosing dunya over deen. The munafiqeen lost both worlds by trading guidance for misguidance. The metaphor of business is deliberate — they made a calculated choice, and that calculation was catastrophically wrong.

  6. Insight given and then abandoned becomes a greater darkness. The parable of the fire is not about someone who never had light — it is about someone who had it and lost it. Apostasy and nifaq after knowledge is worse than never having known.

  7. The Quran uses the same vocabulary to distinguish an act from its just consequence. Justice is not vengeance — when Allah uses the same word for an evil act and its punishment, the first is wrong and the second is right.

docs.title: Historical Context and Stories Mentioned
docs.text:
• Bilal ibn Rabah, Suhaib al-Roomi, Ammar ibn Yasir (رضي الله عنهم): Named explicitly as examples of early Muslims the munafiqeen mocked. Bilal and Suhaib were former slaves; Ammar was among the poor early converts. The munafiqeen used their social and economic status to belittle their faith.

  • Most early believers were among the poor (fuqara'). This social reality is why the munafiqeen's taunt of "sufaha'" carried social weight — they were leveraging class prejudice to discredit Islam.

  • Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه): Cited in explaining Allahu yastahzi'u bihim — he interpreted it as Allah taking revenge (nikma) and giving them respite before punishment.

  • Ibn Katheer (رحمه الله): Cited twice: (1) on Allah's retribution mirroring their mockery in wording but constituting real punishment; (2) on the parable of the fire as illustrating the munafiqeen's trajectory of believing then disbelieving.

docs.title: Q&A Highlights
docs.text:
• Q: Does "fi" in "fi dalalihim wa jahilihim" indicate causality (because of their misguidance) or state (being in a state of misguidance)? A: The instructor clarified it refers to their state — that they are in misguidance and ignorance, and because of that state they do not know about themselves that they are doing wrong. He noted this is in fact the more severe description: they are so deep in blindness they cannot perceive their own condition. This makes the blindness more profound — not just lacking guidance, but unaware that guidance is absent.

  • Q (implicit — on the plural forms صُمٌّ، بُكْمٌ، عُمْيٌ): A student asked about the grammatical category (sighah) of these words. A: The instructor confirmed they are all plurals on the وزن فُعْل. Singulars are أَصَمّ (asam), أَبْكَم (abkam), أَعْمَى (a'ma) — all on the pattern of اسم تفضيل / صفة مشبهة (أَفْعَل). The plural context is confirmed by فَهُمْ لَا يَرْجِعُونَ which uses a plural pronoun.

docs.title: Tafseer 201 - Study Notes
docs.text: Date: 2026-08-27 Surah Covered: Surah Al-Baqarah — Ayaat covering the Munafiqeen parable (rain/storm example) and transition to Ayah 21–25 (Ya Ayyuhan-Nas)

docs.title: Session Overview
docs.text: This session covered two major sections of Surah Al-Baqarah. The first part completed the extended parable (second example) of the munafiqeen — the storm/rain parable — explaining its imagery in detail, its application to the state of the hypocrites, and Allah's declaration of power over them. The second part introduced the next set of ayaat (21–25), examining their rhetorical connection to the preceding section and beginning the tafseer of the address "Ya Ayyuhan-Nas," which calls all of humanity to worship Allah and enumerates His blessings (earth as a resting place, sky as a roof, rain and provision).

docs.title: Key Themes and Topics
docs.text:
1. The second parable of the munafiqeen — the storm/heavy rain scenario as a metaphor for their confusion and hesitation between iman and kufr.
  2. Imagery of the storm — darkness, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, and the reaction of putting fingers in ears.
  3. Parenthetical statement (jumlah mu'taridah) — "Wallahu muhitun bil-kafirin" inserted mid-parable as a warning of Allah's encompassing power.
  4. Allah's omnipotence — He could take away their hearing and sight if He willed; no one can escape Him.
  5. The munafiqeen's wavering nature — oscillating between Muslims and disbelievers based on perceived power, paralleled with the traveler walking only when lightning flashes.
  6. Rhetorical transition (munasabah) — how the shift from describing the three groups (mu'mineen, kafireen, munafiqeen) to presenting proofs of tawheed is logically connected.
  7. Iltifat (direct address) — the rhetorical shift from third-person description to direct second-person address ("Ya Ayyuhan-Nas") and its purpose.
  8. Proofs of Allah's oneness — creation of humanity from nothing, the earth as a resting place, the sky as a canopy, rain, and provision from fruits.

docs.title: The Second Parable of the Munafiqeen (The Storm)
docs.text:
• Allah gives a second example of the munafiqeen's state — intended as an increase in clarification (زيادة في الكشف والإيضاح) of their nifaq.
  • The example: their condition in their confusion and hesitation about accepting Islam is like the condition of people struck by a torrential rain (مَطَر شَدِيد), in which:
  • The earth is plunged into darkness (أَظْلَمَتْ الأَرْض)
  • The sky thunders (أَرْعَدَتْ السَّمَاء)
  • Thunderbolts (صَوَاعِق) fall

  • Lightning (بَرْق) flashes dangerously

  • In this state, the people put their fingers in their ears out of extreme fear (فَرْط الدَّهْشَة والفَزَع) to ward off (لِدَفْعِ) the danger of the thunderbolts — as if they believe this will save them from death.

  • Wallahu Muhitun bil-Kafirin — inserted as a parenthetical sentence (جُمْلَة مُعْتَرِضَة) mid-narrative. This is a Qur'anic rhetorical device: in the middle of describing a scene, Allah inserts a warning or reminder. Here it means: Allah surrounds and encircles the disbelievers from all sides with His power; they cannot escape Him, just as one cannot escape when surrounded by an enemy from all directions.

  • The lightning (بَرْق) is described as so intense it is about to take away their eyesight (يَكَادُ الْبَرْقُ يَخْطَفُ أَبْصَارَهُمْ) due to its intensity and strength.

  • Walking in the flash, stopping in the dark: Whenever the lightning illuminates the path, they walk. When it disappears and darkness returns, they stop and stand still — out of fear of falling into a hole (خَشْيَة التَّرَدِّي فِي الحُفَر).

docs.title: Application to the Munafiqeen
docs.text:
• This precisely describes the munafiqeen's spiritual condition: whenever they saw Islam and the Muslims in a position of strength, they walked with them. Whenever they saw the kuffar in a stronger position, they inclined toward them.
  • As Allah says elsewhere: مُذَبْذَبِينَ بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ لَا إِلَىٰ هَٰؤُلَاءِ وَلَا إِلَىٰ هَٰؤُلَاءِ — "Wavering between this and that, belonging neither to these nor to those."
  • They would say to the believers: أَلَمْ نَكُنْ مَعَكُمْ ("Were we not with you?") — and to the disbelievers similarly.
  • There is a full Surah dedicated to them: Surah Al-Munafiqun.

docs.title: Allah's Power Over Them
docs.text:
• وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَذَهَبَ بِسَمْعِهِمْ وَأَبْصَارِهِمْ — "Had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight."
  • Allah could intensify the thunder and deafen them; He could intensify the lightning and blind them. He has full power (قُدْرَة) over all things.
  • Ibn Jarir al-Tabari's explanation: Allah described His own power here specifically to warn the munafiqeen that they are under His total control. He surrounds them (مُحِيط بِهِمْ) and is fully capable of taking their senses — no one in the heavens or earth can make Allah incapable (لَا يُعْجِزُهُ أَحَدٌ).
  • Ends with: إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ — Allah has power over all things.

docs.title: Transition to Ayaat 21–25: Proofs of Tawheed
docs.text: Munasabah (rhetorical connection): - Having described the three groups (mu'mineen, kafireen, munafiqeen) and their characteristics, and having given parables, Allah now moves to presenting evidences and proofs (دَلَائِل وَبَرَاهِين) for His oneness (وَحْدَانِيَّة). - Purpose: to introduce His great blessings so people may be thankful (لِيَشْكُرُوا عَلَيْهَا), and to highlight the miracle of the Qur'an (بِأَنْصَعِ بَيَانٍ — with the clearest exposition), to uproot the roots of shirk and doubt from hearts (لِيَقْتَلِعَ جُذُورَ الشِّرْكِ مِنَ الْقُلُوبِ).

docs.title: Tafseer of "Ya Ayyuhan-Nas Ubudu Rabbakum"
docs.text:
• يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ addresses ALL people of the world — believers, disbelievers, munafiqeen, mushrikeen alike. Not restricted to any one group.
  • Command: اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ — Worship your Lord. This means: tawheed (making Allah one), thanking Him, and obeying Him.
  • الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ — Who created you (brought you from non-existence/عَدَم into existence by His power).
  • وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ — And who created those before you (all prior generations and nations).
  • Purpose: لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ — So that you may be among the righteous (زُمْرَة الْمُتَّقِين) — the winners of guidance and success.

docs.title: Imam Baydawi's Explanation of Iltifat
docs.text:
• In the preceding ayaat, the three groups were described in third person ("there are those who believe," "among the people are those who say…").
  • Here Allah shifts to direct second-person address (Ya Ayyuhan-Nas). This rhetorical technique is called iltifat — literally "turning toward," i.e., drawing the listener's full attention.
  • Benefit: it activates the listener, stimulates them, and signals that what follows is of the utmost importance. It is used whenever Allah wishes to address people about something critical, since most people are heedless (غَافِلُون) of that matter. The address commands their complete hearts and attention.
  • Allah uses this throughout the Qur'an: "يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ", "يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا" — each time signaling a weighty command or reminder.

docs.title: Allah's Blessings Enumerated
docs.text:
1. Earth as a Firash (bed/resting place):
  2. Allah made the earth like a فِرَاش — a furnished bed, like a cradle (مِهَاد) or stable resting place (قَرَار).
  3. Notably, the earth is spherical (كَرَوِيَّة) — it would normally be impossible to settle on a moving, spherical body. Yet Allah made it possible for humanity to live, sit, sleep, and settle upon it.

  4. Imam Baghdadi's point: this does not require the earth to be literally flat (مُسَطَّح). Because the earth's size (حَجْم) is so immense, despite its spherical shape, its curvature is imperceptible to us and does not prevent settlement on it.

  5. Sky as a Canopy (Bina'):

  6. Allah raised the sky above as a roof/dome (كَهَيْئَةِ الْقُبَّة) — a built structure over the earth.

  7. Rain from the sky:

  8. وَأَنزَلَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مَاءً — Allah sent down water from the sky, extracted as fresh and sweet water (عَذْب) from the clouds by His power.

  9. Fruits and provision:

  10. فَأَخْرَجَ بِهِ مِنَ الثَّمَرَاتِ رِزْقًا لَكُمْ — With this water, Allah brought forth various fruits, vegetables, and food as sustenance for humanity.

(Session ended here — continuation in next class.)

docs.title: Grammar and Language Notes
docs.text:
• صَيِّب — noun meaning a heavy rain shower; used as a simile marker here.
  • أَظْلَمَ يُظْلِمُ (bab إِفْعَال) — to become dark/to darken. أَرْعَدَ يُرْعِدُ إِرْعَادًا (same bab) — to thunder.
  • مُحِيط — ism al-fa'il from أَحَاطَ يُحِيطُ إِحَاطَةً (bab إِفْعَال).
  • كَادَ يَكَادُ — a "verb of approximation" (فِعْل مُقَارَبَة); means "to be about to" do something.
  • جُمْلَة مُعْتَرِضَة — a parenthetical sentence: inserted between two parts of a continuous statement to add a warning, lesson, or emphasis, without breaking the grammatical structure of the surrounding speech. This is a well-recognized device in Arabic rhetoric (بَلَاغَة) and is frequently employed in the Qur'an.
  • جَعَلَ — discussed as having multiple meanings; among them is the meaning of وَضَعَ (to place/put). Student asked whether يَجْعَلُونَ in the context of placing fingers could mean "to put" — confirmed yes, جَعَلَ carries this meaning as one of its uses.
  • إِبَاد (abad) vs. عِبَاد (ibad) — corrected in class: the plural of عَبْد (servant/worshipper) is عِبَاد (ibad), not أَبَاد (abad). Teacher corrected the student's reading.
  • نَجَّى يُنَجِّي تَنْجِيَةً and أَنْجَى يُنْجِي إِنْجَاءً — both valid verb forms meaning "to save/rescue."
  • مُنَبِّه (munabbih) — ism al-fa'il from نَبَّهَ يُنَبِّهُ تَنْبِيهًا — one who warns or draws attention.

docs.title: Lessons and Practical Takeaways
docs.text:
1. The danger of nifaq (hypocrisy): The munafiqeen are in a state of perpetual confusion — they lack the clarity, courage, and conviction of true faith. Their condition is like a person stranded in a violent storm with no fixed direction.

  2. No one escapes Allah: The parenthetical warning — Wallahu muhitun bil-kafirin — reminds us that despite apparent freedom, the disbelievers and hypocrites are entirely within Allah's grasp. True safety lies only with Allah, not in worldly calculations.

  3. Gratitude as a foundation of worship: The transition to "Ya Ayyuhan-Nas" teaches that recognizing Allah's blessings (earth, sky, rain, food) is the rational and spiritual foundation for worshipping Him alone.

  4. Heedlessness requires direct address: The reason Allah uses "Ya Ayyuhan-Nas" is precisely because people tend to be heedless of the most important things. The louder and more direct the call, the more heedless the audience being addressed.

  5. Taqwa is the goal of worship: The command to worship is connected to لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ — the ultimate aim of all ibadah is becoming among the muttaqeen (people of God-consciousness and righteousness).

  6. Preparation matters: The teacher reminded students to always prepare their reading beforehand — coming unprepared leads to mistakes and a weaker learning experience.

docs.title: Historical Context and Stories Mentioned
docs.text:
• The context of Madinah and the munafiqeen: The parable was revealed in the context of the early Madinan period when Islam was gaining strength. A group of people — the munafiqeen — were neither committed Muslims nor open disbelievers. They calculated their allegiances based on which side appeared stronger at any given time.

  • Surah Al-Munafiqun: Referenced as the dedicated Qur'anic surah exposing the characteristics of the hypocrites in detail.

  • Ayah from Surah Al-Nisa (or Al-Ma'idah — referenced as such in class): مُذَبْذَبِينَ بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ لَا إِلَىٰ هَٰؤُلَاءِ وَلَا إِلَىٰ هَٰؤُلَاءِ — describing the wavering character of the munafiqeen, oscillating between the believers and the disbelievers.

docs.title: Q&A Highlights
docs.text:
Q: Can جَعَلَ mean "to put/place" (like وَضَعَ)? A: Yes. جَعَلَ has many meanings. One of them is synonymous with وَضَعَ (to place). So يَجْعَلُونَ أَصَابِعَهُمْ فِي آذَانِهِمْ is correctly understood as "they place their fingers in their ears."

Q: What does يُنْجِيهِمْ refer to — is it that the putting of fingers will save them? A: Yes. The idea is that the people in the storm think that plugging their ears will save them from dying due to the deafening sound of the thunderbolt. In reality it cannot truly save them from death, but extreme noise can physically damage the ear system and in some cases even cause death — so the impulse to block one's ears is understandable in that state of terror.

Q: What are the two verb forms for "to save"? A: Both نَجَّى يُنَجِّي تَنْجِيَةً and أَنْجَى يُنْجِي إِنْجَاءً are valid. Both carry the meaning of saving or rescuing.

Q: Does the earth have to be flat (مُسَطَّح) for the ayah's description of it as a "bed" to be valid? A: No. Imam Baghdadi explains that because the earth's size is so immense, its spherical curvature does not prevent humans from settling and resting on it. The description of the earth as a فِرَاش (bed) refers to its function — it serves as a resting place for humanity — not its literal geometric shape.

docs.title: Concept Questions
docs.text:
1. What three conditions must a singular noun meet to take Category 1 i'rāb (ḍamma in raf', fatḥa in naṣb, kasra in jarr)?

  2. In naḥw, how is a noun classified as ṣaḥīḥ — and how does this definition differ from ṣaḥīḥ in ṣarf? What is a noun called when it ends in wāw or yā' but has sukūn on the preceding letter, and which i'rāb category does it follow?

  3. مَرَرْتُ بِعُمَرَ — عُمَرَ is majrūr here, yet it carries a fatḥa. Explain why. What is this fatḥa technically standing in for, and how would you state this in a full i'rāb sentence?

  4. State the four conditions required for asmā' al-sitta to be declined with wāw (raf'), alif (naṣb), and yā' (jarr). What happens if أَخٌ is made muḍāf to yā' al-mutakallim — i.e., أَخِي — and why does the special i'rāb not apply?

  5. Both رَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمَيْن and رَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمِين end in yā' + noon, yet they mean different things. What single feature distinguishes them, and what does each sentence mean?

  6. Describe the four morphological steps that transform مُسْلِمُون into مُسْلِمِيَّ when it is made muḍāf to yā' al-mutakallim.

In which of its three i'rāb states does a visible marker appear, and what is that marker? نُونُ التَّثْنِيَةِ What harakah does this noon always carry, and how does it differ from noon al-jam'? أُولُو / أُولِي These are the raf' and naṣb/jarr forms of a word meaning "possessors of" — which i'rāb category does it follow, and why can it never be used in the singular? تَقْدِيرِيٌّ vs. لَفْظِيٌّ Explain the difference between these two terms as applied to i'rāb.

docs.title: Concept Questions
docs.text:
1. What does خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَى قُلُوبِهِمْ (Al-Baqarah 2:7) mean according to the mufassirūn, what is the root cause that brings it about, and is it a physical or spiritual condition? What are the three faculties mentioned as sealed?

  2. Why did Allah devote 13 full verses to the Munafiqeen in Surah Al-Baqarah — more than to either the Mu'minoon or the Kafireen in the surah's opening section? What follows those 13 verses, and for what purpose?

  3. Ibn Kathir defines Nifaq with a concise Arabic phrase — what is it? Then distinguish Nifaq I'tiqadi from Nifaq 'Amali in terms of both their definitions and their consequences.

  4. Ayah 9 says the Munafiqeen attempt to deceive Allah and the believers, but then states وَمَا يَخْدَعُونَ إِلَّا أَنفُسَهُمْ وَمَا يَشْعُرُونَ. In what sense do they deceive only themselves, and why are they unable to perceive this?

  5. In Ayah 12, Allah refutes the Munafiqeen's claim of being "reformers" with maximum rhetorical force. List and explain the four Arabic rhetorical or grammatical devices used in أَلَا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ الْمُفْسِدُونَ وَلَكِن لَّا يَشْعُرُونَ.

  6. Why do detailed descriptions of the Munafiqeen appear exclusively in Madani surahs and not in Makki surahs?

docs.title: Concept Questions
docs.text:
1. Water has three qualities. What are they, and how many need to be altered by a foreign substance before the water becomes impermissible for ṭahāra? What is the ruling if only one quality is changed by a permissible additive such as soap or saffron?

  2. Distinguish between manī, madhī, and wādī. Which necessitates ghusl, and which only require wuḍū?

  3. Explain the Ḥanafī distinction between ma-e-kalīl (small stagnant body) and ma-e-kathīr (large stagnant body). What size threshold does the madhhab use, what is the "ripple test," and how does the ruling on najāsa differ between the two?

  4. What is mā' musta'mal, and at what exact moment does water acquire this status? What is the operative Ḥanafī fatwa on its purity status, and for which uses is it permitted or forbidden?

  5. Imam Malik holds that najāsa falling into a small stagnant body does not render it impure as long as the three qualities are unchanged. What hadith is his dalīl, and how do the Ḥanafīs respond to it?

  6. A mosquito dies in a jug of water. According to the Ḥanafī position, does this render the water impure? What is the Quranic dalīl for this ruling?

Give three examples. طَاهِر (not muṭahhar) Water in this category is pure in itself but cannot purify others — which type of used water receives this classification under the operative Ḥanafī fatwa? مَاءٌ مُسْتَعْمَل At what exact moment does water become this — while still on the body or after it drips off? نَجَاسَةٌ خَفِيفَة Imam Abu Yusuf classifies mā' musta'mal as this — what does the term mean and how does it differ from najasat-e-ghalizah? الشَّيْخَانِ Which two Ḥanafī scholars does this term refer to? الصَّاحِبَانِ Which two scholars does this term refer to — and which name overlaps with "the Shaykhain"? مَاءٌ جَار Najāsa entering this type of water does not render it impure — what condition must be met for the water to remain pure? إِسْرَاف Using excessive water in wuḍū is described by this term — what does it mean and what is its ruling?

docs.title: Nahw 201
docs.text:
1. The noun must be: (1) mufrad (singular); (2) munsarif (accepts tanwīn and kasra); (3) ṣaḥīḥ in the naḥw sense — its final letter is not a ḥarf 'illah (ا، و، ي).

  2. In naḥw, ṣaḥīḥ means only the final letter is free of ḥarf 'illah. In ṣarf, a noun is ma'tall if a ḥarf 'illah appears anywhere — beginning, middle, or end. A noun ending in wāw or yā' with sukūn on the preceding letter is called jārī majrā l-ṣaḥīḥ ("acting like a ṣaḥīḥ noun") — e.g., دَلْوٌ, ظَبْيٌ. It follows Category 1 i'rāb.

  3. عُمَرَ is ghayr munsarif — it rejects both tanwīn and kasra. When majrūr, it cannot take kasra, so fatḥa substitutes for kasra. Full i'rāb statement: عُمَرَ: مَجْرُورٌ، وَعَلَامَةُ جَرِّهِ الْفَتْحَةُ نِيَابَةً عَنِ الْكَسْرَةِ لِأَنَّهُ غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِفٍ — this is i'rāb far'ī (secondary i'rāb by substitution of ḥarakāt).

  4. The four conditions: (1) the noun must be one of the six nouns (أَبٌ، أَخٌ، حَمٌ، فَمٌ، هَنٌ، ذُو); (2) mukabbara — in its base form, not the diminutive (muṣagghar); (3) muwāḥada — singular, not dual or plural; (4) muḍāf to other than yā' al-mutakallim. If muḍāf to yā' al-mutakallim (أَخِي), all three cases become identical — wāw/alif/yā' cannot be distinguished — so the special i'rāb does not apply and a separate rule governs.

  5. The difference is the harakah before the yā': رَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمَـيْن has fatḥa before yā' → tasniyah (dual) → "I saw two Muslims." رَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمِـيْن has kasra before yā' → jam' muzakkar sālim → "I saw [many] Muslims." Confusing these two entirely changes the meaning.

  6. Four steps: (1) Noon drops when made muḍāf → مُسْلِمُو + يَ = مُسْلِمُوي; (2) Wāw converts to yā' (rule of ta'līl — wāw before yā' with sukūn weakens to yā') → مُسْلِمُيي; (3) Two yā's merge into one with shaddah → مُسْلِمُيَّ; (4) Ḍamma changes to kasra — since yā' demands kasra on the letter before it → مُسْلِمِيَّ.

Vocabulary:

  • غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِفٌ — Fatḥa substitutes for kasra in the majrūr state (since this noun rejects kasra entirely).
  • جَارٍ مَجْرَى الصَّحِيحِ — "Acting like a ṣaḥīḥ noun." A noun ending in wāw or yā' with sukūn on the preceding letter qualifies. It follows Category 1 i'rāb.
  • أَسْمَاءُ السِّتَّةِ — أَبٌ (father), أَخٌ (brother), حَمٌ (father-in-law), فَمٌ (mouth), هَنٌ (a vague/private noun), ذُو (possessor of).
  • يَاءُ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ — The word's form does not change across raf', naṣb, and jarr — all three cases look identical (e.g., جَاءَ أَخِي / رَأَيْتُ أَخِي / مَرَرْتُ بِأَخِي). The i'rāb is understood from context, not visible on the word.
  • اسْمٌ مَنْقُوصٌ — A noun ending in original yā' (ي) with kasra before it (e.g., الْقَاضِي). Its i'rāb is visible only in naṣb, which takes a visible fatḥa (رَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِيَ); raf' and jarr are hidden (taqdiree).
  • نُونُ التَّثْنِيَةِ — Always carries kasra (maksūr). The noon of jam' muzakkar sālim always carries fatḥa (maftūḥ). This is how you distinguish the two in naṣb/jarr.
  • أُولُو / أُولِي — Follows Category 6 i'rāb — same as jam' muzakkar sālim (wāw in raf', yā' in naṣb/jarr). It is inherently plural and has no singular form in this pattern.
  • تَقْدِيرِيٌّ vs. لَفْظِيٌّ — Taqdiree: the i'rāb is hidden/estimated — the word's written and spoken form does not change regardless of case (e.g., ism maqsur in all three cases). Lafẓī: the i'rāb is visible and explicitly pronounced (e.g., the ḍamma on a regular noun in raf').

docs.title: Tafseer 201
docs.text:
1. خَتَمَ means to seal — described by the mufassirūn as التَّغْطِيَة (covering) and الطَّبْع (imprinting/stamping). The root cause is kufr — persistent, willful rejection of the truth; accumulated sins obscure the نُور الْبَصِيرَة (light of inner insight) until no pathway (مَسْلَك) remains for imān to enter. The sealing is not physical — these people are fully healthy and functional. It is a Quranic metaphor (majāz) describing their spiritual and moral condition. The three sealed faculties are: (1) the hearts (القُلُوب), (2) the hearing (السَّمْع), and (3) the eyesight (الأَبْصَار).

  2. Allah devoted 13 verses to the Munafiqeen because of the great danger (خَطَر عَظِيم) they pose to the Muslim community from within and the great harm (ضَرَر كَبِير) they can inflict. After the 13 verses, Allah gives two parables (مَثَلَان) to further expose the inner darkness of their souls and the ultimate destination (مَآل) of their hypocrisy — destruction and ruin (هَلَاك وَدَمَار).

  3. Ibn Kathir's definition: النِّفَاقُ هُوَ إِظْهَارُ الْخَيْرِ وَإِسْرَارُ الشَّرِّ — "Nifaq is displaying goodness outwardly and concealing evil inwardly." Nifaq I'tiqadi (creedal): the person inwardly disbelieves while outwardly claiming Islam — consequence: eternal Hellfire (يُخَلِّدُ صَاحِبَهُ فِي النَّار); this is the most severe form. Nifaq 'Amali (practical): the person's aqeedah is sound but their actions resemble those of hypocrites (e.g., lying, breaking promises, betraying trust) — consequence: a major sin requiring repentance, but not eternal damnation.

  4. In reality the Munafiqeen cannot deceive Allah, since nothing is hidden from Him. The evil consequence (وَبَال) of their deception returns to them alone — they are the ones harmed most by their own nifaq. They cannot perceive this because of excessive heedlessness (تَمَادِي غَفْلَتِهِمْ) and the completeness of their foolishness (تَكَامُل حَمَاقَتِهِمْ).

  5. Four devices in أَلَا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ الْمُفْسِدُونَ: (1) أَلَا — particle of alerting (المُنَبِّه), draws the listener's full attention; (2) إِنَّ — particle of emphasis (حَرْف مُقَرِّرَة), confirms and strengthens the meaning; (3) هُمْ as ḍamīr al-faṣl (separating pronoun) between mubtadaʾ and khabar — restricts the predicate exclusively to this subject ("it is they and none other"); (4) الْمُفْسِدُونَ with the definite article — making the predicate definite intensifies the emphasis further. Together these constitute the most emphatic possible refutation in Arabic rhetoric.

  6. In Makkah, opposition to Islam was open — the Kuffar and Mushrikeen made no pretense of being Muslim. Nifaq as a social phenomenon arose only in Madinah after the Hijrah, when Islam became the dominant political and social force. Some individuals joined the Muslim community outwardly for worldly or political benefit while internally retaining kufr. Therefore all major Quranic descriptions of the Munafiqeen are found in Madani surahs (e.g., Al-Baqarah, Al-Munafiqun).

Vocabulary:

  • نُورُ الْبَصِيرَة — The light of inner insight and imān. Sins gradually obscure it; once lost, there is no pathway for imān to enter or for kufr to exit the heart.
  • النِّفَاقُ الِاعْتِقَادِيُّ — Eternal Hellfire (يُخَلِّدُ صَاحِبَهُ فِي النَّار) — the most severe consequence of all forms of nifaq.
  • الْمُزَبْزَبُ — "Confused/wavering" — the Munafiqeen waver between the Mu'mineen and the Kafireen, fully belonging to neither group.
  • وَبَال — Evil/bad consequence or result; the harmful outcome of one's own action returning upon oneself.
  • أَخْبَثُ — Superlative of خَبِيث (vile/wicked): "the most vile." The Munafiqeen are described as أَخْبَثُ الْكَفَرَة — the most vile of all disbelievers.
  • رِجْس — Moral/spiritual filth or abomination (used for Nifaq, Kufr, and idols — فَاجْتَنِبُوا الرِّجْسَ مِنَ الْأَوْثَان). نَجَاسَة is physical ritual impurity (substances affecting wuḍū/ṣalāh). Rijs is moral; najāsa is physical.
  • أَلَا — Called المُنَبِّه — the alerting/warning particle that draws the listener's attention before an emphatic statement.
  • ضَمِيرُ الْفَصْل — Placed between the mubtadaʾ and khabar; its grammatical effect is restriction — confirming that the predicate belongs exclusively to that subject and to no one else.
  • سَبَبُ النُّزُول — Reported by Ibn Abbas (رضي الله عنه). The named leaders are Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (the foremost leader of the Munafiqeen in Madinah) and Mu'tab ibn Qushayr — hypocrites from Ahl al-Kitab who outwardly professed Islam while concealing kufr.

docs.title: Fiqh 201
docs.text:
1. The three qualities are color, taste, and smell. If two or more are altered by a foreign substance, the water is no longer permissible for ṭahāra. If only one quality is changed by a permissible additive (soap, ishnan, saffron), ṭahāra remains valid — the Ḥanafī position is that altering one quality does not strip the water of its essential nature as mā'.

  2. Manī (seminal fluid discharged with desire/shahwa) — requires ghusl. Madhī (pre-seminal fluid released during foreplay) — breaks wuḍū only; wash the area and make wuḍū, no ghusl required. Wādī (slightly thick fluid sometimes seen after urination) — breaks wuḍū only, no ghusl required.

  3. Ma-e-kalīl (small): less than 10 hand-spans × 10 hand-spans in area with shallow depth — if any amount of najāsa enters, the entire body of water becomes impure regardless of whether the three qualities change (strict ruling). Ma-e-kathīr (large): 10 × 10 hand-spans or more with sufficient depth that the bottom is not exposed when scooping — najāsa does not render it impure unless one of the three qualities is visibly altered. The ripple test: if movement on one side does not cause perceptible movement on the other, it qualifies as a large body; the madhhab adopted Imam Muhammad's version (benchmarked by scooping water with the hand on one side).

  4. Mā' musta'mal is water used to remove a ḥadath — whether for a new wuḍū after ḥadath or for renewing an existing wuḍū. Water acquires this status the moment it drips off/leaves the body — while still on the skin it remains ṭahūr. The operative Ḥanafī fatwa (in line with Imam Muhammad): it is ṭāhir but not muṭahhar — pure in itself but cannot purify others. It may not be used for wuḍū or ghusl. It may be used for istiñjā', irrigation, cooking, and general purposes.

  5. Imam Malik's dalīl: the hadith of Bi'r Budha'a — a well in Madinah into which menstrual rags, dog carcasses, and refuse were thrown; the Prophet ﷺ stated: "Indeed, water is pure — nothing makes it impure." The Ḥanafī response: Bi'r Budha'a had an underground stream continuously replenishing it — it was effectively flowing water, not truly stagnant. The hadith therefore cannot override the rule for genuinely still, stagnant small bodies.

  6. According to the Ḥanafī position (and one opinion of Imam Shafi'i), an animal with no flowing blood (fly, mosquito, frog, crab, fish) dying in water does not render it impure. The Quranic dalīl is Surah Al-An'am: flowing blood (الدَّمَ مَسْفُوحًا) is declared najis — if an animal has no flowing blood to begin with, its death introduces no najāsa into the water.

Vocabulary:

  • طَهُور — (1) Pure in itself AND (2) capable of purifying others. Examples: rainwater, river/valley water, well water, seawater, spring water.
  • طَاهِر (not muṭahhar) — Mā' musta'mal — the operative Ḥanafī fatwa classifies used wuḍū water as ṭāhir (pure) but incapable of being used for ṭahāra itself.
  • مَاءٌ مُسْتَعْمَل — Water becomes musta'mal the moment it drips off the body after being used for wuḍū or ghusl — not while it is still in contact with the skin.
  • نَجَاسَةٌ خَفِيفَة — Minor/light impurity, less severe than najasat-e-ghalizah (major impurity). Imam Abu Yusuf's opinion classifies mā' musta'mal as this lighter form, whereas one opinion of Imam Abu Hanifa placed it in the heavier category.
  • الشَّيْخَانِ — Imam Abu Hanifa + Imam Abu Yusuf.
  • الصَّاحِبَانِ — Imam Abu Yusuf + Imam Muhammad (Imam Abu Yusuf is the shared scholar between both terms).
  • مَاءٌ جَار — Najāsa entering flowing water does not make it impure as long as no trace (athar) of the najāsa — no change in color, taste, or smell — remains visible in the water.
  • إِسْرَاف — Extravagance/wastefulness. Using excessive water even in wuḍū is isrāf and is impermissible (ḥarām); the Prophet ﷺ was described as making wuḍū conservatively even when standing beside a river.
